#6560. Examining the Cat's Head Nebula with the Hubble and JWST

The Cat's Head nebula gets its name from its appearance: it looks like a cat sitting so that it's facing away from the viewer, with its head turned around on the top of its neck, highlighted by a star that looks like a glowing eye. The unusual shape is made of gas and dust carved and formed by the radiation of young stars.

It's a small part of the larger Carina Nebula, a complex star-forming region about 7,500 light years away. Recently, both the Hubble and the JWST cast their gaze on the Cat's Head in an effort to learn more about star formation, a constant research subject in astronomy.

The Carina Nebula hosts some of the most massive stars in the entire Milky Way in its Carina OB1 assocation. Of particular interest is Eta Carinae, a stellar system that hosts many stars, two of which have a combined luminosity more than 5 million times greater than the Sun. Eta Carinae is also known for being at the heart of the eerily creepy Homunculous Nebula, not visible in these images. Massive stars like the ones in Eta Carinae and their powerful radiation have a pronounced effect on the region, and on star formation itself.

Hubble's image of the Cat's Head is in visible light, while the JWST imaged it in both near and mid-infrared. Each of the images shows a different aspect of the Cat's Head.

The pillar that makes the Cat's Head is composed of thick, dark dust, so far resisting the onslaught of stellar wind and radiation from massive stars. The yellow outline on its right side is likely where photoevaporation is taking place, driven by the same powerful stars. The UV radiation is ionizing the gas on the rim, and will eventually evaporate it completely.

In astronomy images like these, different filters isolate different chemicals like sulphur, oxygen, and hydrogen. The ionization level of the chemicals, along with how highly they're energized and how much dust is present, all affect the colours. Whether we know which colours represent which chemicals or not, these images are awe-inspiring.

The massive stars in the region are also responsible for the arcs and shoals in the images, again caused by their powerful radiation and stellar winds.

This zoomed-in portion of the Hubble's image highlights the "eyeball", likely a star in just the right position. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI).

The JWST, as an infrared telescope, presents different, yet no less gorgeous, images of the Cat's Head. It's infrared instruments see things differently than the Hubble does. This gives the Cat's Headâalready ethereal in the Hubble imageâan even more ghostly, almost unreal appearance. Some parts of the Cat's Head in the JWST images appear to be only half-there, with background stars shining brightly through them.

The JWST's near-infrared image doesn't show different chemical elements the same way the Hubble image does. Instead, it shows more of the stars themselves. Even background galaxies are visible beyond the Cat's Head, along with the black background of space. The JWST also shows how massive stars are shaping the region, with the wispy filaments on the images left side. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI)

Some of the turbulence in the gas, driven by the massive stars, appears more substantial in the JWST image. The star that makes the Cat's Eye is also brighter, with less of its light blocked by dust in infrared.

A zoomed-in JWST NIR image of the head in the Cat's Head Nebula. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI)

In the JWST's mid-infrared image, the Cat's Head Nebula is transformed yet again. It's muted and ghost-sheet white, surrounded by pastel gas clouds punctuated with stars. The clouds look almost Earth-like in their white colour. This time, it's carbon molecules and warm dust emissions that take the stage. What is most likely an infant star pops into view in this image, embedded in thick dust that it's yet to dissipate, to the right of the head itself.

The white colour of the gas in this mid-infrared JWST image makes it look like Earthly clouds. Fewer stars are visible in the background, their light blocked out by the gas, which appears thicker. In the gas to the left, finer detail is visible in the gas clouds. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI).

The head itself is muted in the MIR image, along with the rest of the nebula. It's eye, almost malevolent in the other images, blends in with the gas and is less striking.

In this zoom-in of the MIR image, the edges are softened, and so are the colours. The star that makes they eye blends in with the gas in gradients of white. Globules below the head look like they're reaching for the head, rather than being blown back by stellar wind and radiation. The blackness of space is visible in the upper right, and a little in the upper left. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI. Image Processing: J. Depasquale (STScI).

Though these images are easy to appreciate by almost anyone, their primary purpose is scientific. By emphasizing and de-emphasizing different aspects of the Cat's Head nebula, astronomers can see stars more clearly, along with the dust, the gas, and the chemistry. Together, they help researchers see the effects of stellar radiation and wind, called stellar feedback, on the ongoing process of star formation.

Stellar feedback can both encourage and stifle star formation, depending on circumstances. It's complicated, and it's an ongoing topic of astronomical study. One of the JWST's main, defining science themes is star formation, and images like these are one of the reasons it was built. The Hubble helps too, and illustrates how the gas, the dust, the metallicity, and the stars of different sizes and ages, all play a role. Those factors all interact in different ways, making it difficult to come up with concrete theories of how it all works.

These gorgeous images are more than eye candy to astronomers. They're working hard on understanding a process fundamental to the cosmos. Wrapped up in all this visual chaos and beauty, Nature's laws are defining how stars form. Astronomers' mission is to decipher it all.

Enjoying these images on their visual merit alone is our mission, if we accept it.

#6559. Mamdani and Hochul Visit Queens Night Market to Get Out the Vote

Zohran Mamdani wanted to share with the governor, but the vendor at the Taiwanese Yummy tent wasn’t having it. Cheng Liu insisted the New York mayor try his own bowl of beef noodle soup—the chef’s way.

Instead of trying a bite from Governor Kathy Hochul, Mamdani watched and waited as Liu arranged slippery, wide noodles underneath pickled mustard greens, herbs, and slices of succulent brisket that had been cooked for eight hours, all ladled with a delicate broth. Mamdami started to dig in with his chopsticks when Liu rushed over to spoon in a generous amount of homemade chili oil.

“The mayor is not scared of spicy food,” Liu said via his son’s translation. “We wanted to give him Taiwanese cuisine.”

At the Queens Night Market, Mamdani and Hochul struck an unusual pair: a New York mayor and governor who get along.

Three days before Election Day, the political allies arrived at Flushing Meadows Corona Park in a motorcade of black SUVs to pose for photos and get out the vote for the Democratic party. Hochul has made the city part of her final push in a reelection campaign against Republican Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive endorsed by President Donald Trump.

In a joint interview with Hochul, Mamdani told Bon Appétit that he was showing up for the governor because she was showing up for immigrant New Yorkers. Earlier this year, Hochul signed legislation to ban local and state law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration operations, and to stop police at all levels from covering their face when interacting with the public.

“The governor has stood up and called for public safety to actually be public safety and not just be an assistance and an accompaniment of ICE,” Mamdani said. “That has been part of what makes people feel like they can be part of this city.”

The mayor also mentioned that the Queens Night Market was a favorite with constituents because of the price. Every dish is capped at $6. Hochul, running on affordability, points to her expansion of free school lunch statewide. “As a mom, this is personal,” she said. “I made a lot of peanut butter and jelly sandwiches over the years for kids.”

Representing different generations and factions of their party, Mamdani and Hochul recognize what they stand to gain together. Mamdani needed Hochul to expand free childcare and greenlight plans for a second-home tax. Hochul needs the enthusiasm of the Democratic Socialist mayor’s voting bloc.

Hochul said she and Mamdani are aligned on lowering the cost of living and supporting the small business owners that make the food and nightlife scene so special.

“It’s a rare day in New York for this kind of relationship,” Hochul said, “but when we talk to each other, we don’t disagree on these issues.”

The pair of politicians approached the night market in a coordinated operation that included advance teams, extra security, and business casual ’fits: Hochul in jeans, Mamdani tie-less in a quarter-zip. The mayor—who has made his appetite a key part of his public identity—appeared less stiff in his interactions with food vendors, but Hochul gamely grabbed chopsticks and posed for selfies.

John Wang, who launched the Queens Night Market in 2015, said politicians are a regular presence here. “Every election season, they come out,” Wang said. “Even if they’ve never been here before, they’re like, ‘Yeahhh! I love the Queens Night Market.’” He said some (2020 presidential candidate Andrew Yang, for instance) get feted like Mamdani, and others (N.Y. Sen. Chuck Schumer) draw a tamer response. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez used to come a lot, Wang said, and would always get swarmed by supporters.

For the last market of the season, which fell on Halloween, Mamdani might as well have been a member of BTS. Vendors and visitors alike stared slackjawed, squealed, and uttered “oh my God!”

A young man named Asad showed up in a Mamdani costume with no idea he would meet the mayor, let alone pose for photos that brought him to tears.“This is Bruce Blakeman’s nightmare!” the mayor said of his Mamdani double.

“It was surreal, emotional a little bit,” said Asad, who declined to share his last name. Asad said he was born in Karachi, Pakistan, became a U.S. citizen in 2022, and voted for Mamdani after moving to New York from Florida.

At the Ella Spice stand, Akera Phillip represents Grenada with breadfruit croquettes, fried cou-cou, and to-go pouches of sorrel. Phillip, who named her business after her grandmother, felt “elated” and “blessed” to serve her food to the leaders of the state and the city.

“As a small island girl, it just made me feel big,” she said.

Akera Phillip holds breadfruit croquettes.

At the Epis by Steve tent, Hochul told Steve Lahens she could handle “Buffalo spicy,” a nod to her hometown, rather than admit to any trouble with his Haitian pikliz. Lahens and his wife fixed up plates of griot (fried pork) with diri djondjon (black rice) and makawoni au graten, a Caribbean mac and cheese he makes with bell peppers, “evaporated milk and a few little things I can’t talk about.”

Lahens said he was born in Haiti but came to the U.S. in 1988. A workplace injury pushed him toward cooking, “and it changed my life, for the better.” He began cooking out of his house but now works out of the Mangrove shared kitchen at the Flatbush Central Caribbean Marketplace. He was excited to hobnob with the governor and the mayor, but Lahens also said New York small businesses need more help.

“The rent could be lower so people like me could get a spot,” Lahens said. “Right now I’m stuck in catering. I love it, too, but my whole plan and goal is to get a storefront.”

#6558. Inside the New D.C. Restaurant That Only Sells Five Curry Steak Frites Every Night

In a Georgetown alleyway, Alfie’s serves northern Thai dishes that are built around local ingredients

The hottest new spot in Washington, D.C. focuses on the traditional heat-packed cooking methods of northern Thailand, while still using local ingredients from around the DMV. Alfie’s, from chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy, started as a pop-up in Petworth in 2017 before traveling around the world, serving diners in New York and London. This year, the restaurant put down permanent roots in a Georgetown alleyway. The co-owners led us through a day in the new kitchen, preparing everything from hand-cut green papaya in som tam salad to the limited-quantity Thai steak frites with a massaman curry peppercorn sauce.In the video, the kitchen team breaks down rib-eye steaks for their take on a steak au poivre, which they only make five of each night. The steaks are carefully seared for each order, with the au poivre massaman curry sauce is finished in the pan with the leftover beef fat. Classic “bar fries” are served up with the massive 26-ounce rib-eye.

Elsewhere in the kitchen, another chef carves green papayas. The irregular slices of papaya get tossed in a funky, spicy dressing for each order. Ko calls it the “most labor intensive dish on the line;” each order is carefully mixed with fresh tomatoes, peanuts, and a palm syrup and tamarind-heavy dressing. A rich pork belly curry is simmering in the background. Gaeng hung lay (a traditional northern Thai curry) cooks down large pieces of pork belly to get that fatty layer, with pickled garlic and pineapple balancing out the rich flavors of curry paste, tamarind, and fish sauce.

Right before service, the chefs begin prepping herbs and sticky rice that has been soaking overnight and is quickly steamed for that malleable, glutinous texture. McCoy talks about how being a chef is more of a lifestyle than a job, but there’s immense payoff when you get to see diners enjoy your hard work every night. He hopes that Alfie’s will become a place where “you can just forget where you are, have a good time, and just lose yourself in the experience and the food.”

Watch the kitchen team at Aflie’s cook classic Thai dishes and fusion plates like curry steak frites in this episode of Now Open.

#6557. It's a Ghost! No, It's a Stellar Crèche!

Astronomers using the Chandra X-ray Observatory (CXO) and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) zeroed in on a wispy-looking region of the Carina Nebula and found a ghostly looking cloud seemingly floating in isolation among the other clouds of gas and dust. Just in time for Halloween, although, it turns out that little cloud isn't the soul of a departed star. Instead, it's a region of the nebula that has been actively engaged in creating batches of hot, young new stars.

By studying this region in X-rays and infrared light, astronomers are getting a good look at the structure of the cloud as well as the stars it has formed. Not only that, but it helps them piece together more information about the larger Carina Nebula, which lies more than 7,500 light-years away from us.

Most of us are familiar with one of the brilliant and weird objects that lights up the nebula: Eta Carinae. It looks like one star, but is actually a binary that has a combined brightness of around 5 million times that of our Sun. Periodically, this object brightens and dims, probably due to clouds of condensed dust that coalesced around the binary stars. It experienced a huge outburst in the 1840s called the "Great Eruption", which boosted tremendous amounts of gas and dust into space. It has since experienced other, smaller outbursts.

An ultraviolet image of the Homunculus Nebula (Eta Carinae) taken by the Hubble Telescope. Credit: NASA/ESA/StSci

The Carina complex is a huge diffuse nebula containing a collection of newborn stars nestled in a sea of starmaking gas and dust. It continues to produce new stars, many of them extremely bright and massive. Many telescopes have studied it, most notably the Hubble Space Telescope and JWST. Each view brings new insights into the makeup of the cloud as well as the objects it contains. In addition, astronomers are also keeping an eye on Eta Carinae because its primary star — a luminous blue variable star &emdash; is likely to explode as a supernova. When that happens, the shock waves will transform much of the nebula, probably spurring new rounds of star birth.

A broad panorama of the Carina Nebula, a region of massive star formation in the southern skies. This new method of determining the age of stars will help astronomers better understand the process of star formation. Credit: ESO/T. Preibisch

Obviously, the Eta Carina binary is a tantalizing subject, but there are also places such as the Keyhole Nebula. It's a dark and cold molecular cloud that covers about 7 light-years of space. Ionizing radiation from the nearby Eta Carina binary is shaping and eating away at the Keyhole.

There's also the open cluster Trumpler 14, which is a six light-year-wide grouping of more than 2,000 OB-type stars. These are massive and short-lived stars and are very bright in ultraviolet light. These are very young stars, ranging in age from about 300,000 to 500,000 years old.

The ghostly nebula that CXO and JWST imaged is still making stars at its heart. At the same time, ionizing radiation from the nearby Eta Carina binary, as well as hot young stars, is eating away the materials in the cloud. Thanks to that "cannibalizing" ultraviolet radiation from those stars, the cloud has developed several comet-like "knots". Astronomers often refer to them as cometary globules because of their familiar shapes. The Carina Nebula is not the only place where such cometary knots are seen. Astronomers have spotted them in other star-forming regions as well as in planetary nebulae, where stellar winds collide with material previously ejected from a dying star like the Sun. As those collisions happen, they shape similar types of knots in the clouds of gas and dust.

Since the stars will have much shorter lifetimes than that of the Sun, someday this region will look more like a stellar graveyard. The remains of those stars we see as newborn today will, in tens of millions of years, be ghosts of their former selves, spreading their materials to interstellar space.

A new program aims to help scientists figure out how the ingredients of the universe formed early galaxies, which lit up the cosmos after a "dark age."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists are getting a new glimpse of how the first galaxies came to be. In a stunning new simulation, researchers charted the aftermath of the universe's "dark age," including the appearance of the first galaxies that began to shine about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

Lumina, the program behind the simulation, catalogs 2 billion years of cosmic time and represents a decent chunk of the 13.8 billion-year-old history of our universe. The results were published Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

"Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation."

A video published alongside the paper shows what the scientists saw. The team zoomed in on an area roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide to learn more about how the ingredients of space create galaxies.

This section of the Lumina simulation shows the gas temperature in different parts of the early universe, with redder areas showing active galaxy clusters.

In the earliest years of our universe, a fog of neutral hydrogen atoms gradually built up, blocking out the light of the first stars. The hydrogen served as a "shroud" and didn't make light visible until galaxies began to form. This ancient, enshrouded period is known as the Cosmic Dark Age.

The video begins in the middle of this epoch, at roughly 45 million years after the Big Bang. Zooming in on one small part of the simulated universe, it slowly reveals a gassy halo giving way to young galaxies shining brightly within it. Included in the calculations are dark matter, stars, gas and radiation — all contributing to the reemergence of cosmic light.

"We see this is where the first galaxies form," first author Oliver Zier, a former postdoctoral researcher and computational astrophysicist at MIT who is now at Harvard University, said in the statement. "And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Lumina aims to show off two phenomena key to the young universe's history: hydrogen reionization and helium reionization — a first for a program of its kind. Reionization describes how the intergalactic medium, or the area between galaxies, changed from neutral hydrogen to negatively charged ions.

Hydrogen reionization took place when ultraviolet light from young stars and galaxies hit the hydrogen, removing negatively charged electrons from the hydrogen molecules — a process that also allowed light to shine through the fog. Helium reionization happened when supermassive black holes, which have a lot of energy, broke apart neutral helium molecules.

The team said the simulation could eventually be used to validate telescope observations of the early universe, especially those focused on mapping many galaxies at the same time.

Zier, O., Smith, A., Shen, X., Liu, R., Kannan, R., Koehler, S. M., Springel, V., Pakmor, R., Vogelsberger, M., Bulichi, T., & Hernquist, L. (2026). Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization. Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, 552(4). https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stag1469

#6555. The 38 Best Restaurants in Barcelona, According to a Local Food Guide

From local Catalan cuisine to a burgeoning global food scene, here are the best meals in Barcelona right now

From Barcelona’s towering churches and bustling avenues to the sun-drenched beaches and idyllic plazas, it’s obvious why this city captures visitors’ hearts. You can also eat incredibly well here, and often for not very much money — though Barcelona loves a tasting menu and the World’s 50 Best Restaurant list awarded Disfrutar the No. 1 spot last year. Despite Barcelona’s famed cuisine, it’s also easy to have a downright disappointing meal if you settle for any old paella-slinging bar along Les Rambles (known in Spanish as La Rambla) or La Barceloneta. (Tip: If a restaurant has to pay someone to stand outside and hassle pedestrians, the food isn’t worth it.)

Start with some classic tapas and paella (both great but neither entirely Catalan) and be sure to seek out local gems like bittersweet vermouth, seasonal seafood, and homestyle Catalan cuisine. But after writing and revising this list for nearly a decade, I have to insist you don’t overlook the city’s burgeoning global cuisines; save room for Calabrese paninis, Northeast Asian sharing plates with natural wines, towering fried chicken sandwiches, South Indian fish stews, and nose-to-tail yakitori.

We update this list quarterly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing Barcelona dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: Lluritu, a Mediterranean marisquería with three locations across the city; a parallel universe of Catalan culinary history in a former water bottling plant at Franca; and the trendy modern Catalan cuisine of Manda Huevos.

Sam Zucker is a freelance writer, photographer, filmmaker, travel Instagrammer, and gastronomic tour guide in Barcelona. He has contributed to Monocle, National Geographic’s “48 Hours” guides, Culture Trip, and Vice Travel, among others.

Sam Zucker is a freelance writer, photographer, filmmaker, travel Instagrammer, and gastronomic tour guide in Barcelona. He has contributed to Monocle, National Geographic’s “48 Hours” guides, Culture Trip, and Vice Travel, among others.

Simplicity in concept but perfect execution is what pushes Bemba to the top of the smash burger heap. The menu is brief, with just three burger options: regular cheese, double bacon, and the house special Bemba Burger, which comes with chimichurri and a smashed patty of chorizo criollo sausage in addition to the standard beef patty. Bemba has cultivated a flock of loyal regulars with the conscious selection of quality ingredients, fast service, and careful caramelization of each smashed patty. There’s also a beet and quinoa smash burger, great fries, cold draught beer, and homemade pickles — what more is there to ask for?

Know before you go: It’s small so get there early, or order your burgers for takeaway and eat them in the beautiful Plaça de la Virreina just a few blocks away.

Open for: Lunch and dinner; closed Monday and Tuesday

An offshoot of Mantequerías Pirenaicas, whose truita de patates (Spanish omelet) is famous throughout the city, La Fonda de Pirenaicas is founder Miguel Puchol’s homage to the slow-cooked and indulgent dishes his own grandmother used to prepare; a place to sit and enjoy the flavors of honest Catalan home cooking. With a prime location at the epicenter of the Gràcia neighborhood, “La Fonda” specializes in stews and braises, with a star dish in the macarrones de la iaia Alberta (Grandma Alberta’s macaroni): a gratin of penne pasta tossed in a rich meat ragu and topped with cheese that is melted and caramelized under the searing broiler. Trying at least one of the estofats (stews) is a must — the chickpeas with black sausage and egg, for example — but don’t miss the small plates and tapas, either Here you can find Catalan classics like grilled artichokes with cured egg yolk, bombas, esqueixada de bacalao (a refreshing salad of chilled salt cod pieces with olives, onion, and tomato), and of course, the legendary truita de Pirenaicas.

Know before you go: If you enjoy La Fonda de Pirenaicas, try the affiliated Brasa de Pirenaicas literally next door, specializing in grilled meats.

Barcelona is in the throes of a natural wine renaissance, and Masa Vins is opening some of the most interesting bottles in the city. The cuisine of co-owner chef Antonella Tignanelli is rooted in the Mediterranean but globally inspired. Delicate dishes like seabass crudo with mandarin oil and sumac share space on the menu with bar snacks like the kimchi grilled cheese “bikini.” Brimming with youthful energy, Masa Vins was created by Tignanelli and co-owner Dani Bajc to be a place to hang with friends, drink unique wines, listen to music, and eat excellent food. Of the 250 natural wines on the list, there’s an emphasis on Eastern European labels, and the food menu changes every three months with the seasons.

Know before you go: The place is nearly always busy and there aren’t many tables, so get there early or expect to wait. Groups bigger than five people can book a table between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m., exclusively through Instagram direct message.

From restaurateurs Majid and Mani Alam along with Bilal Khan, Achaar Bar is part of the growing roster of restaurants under the Alam Brothers umbrella. Their latest is an Indian canteen and natural wine bar named for the ubiquitous South Asian pickled vegetable condiment (which they make in-house). The menu spans the breadth of India, as well as adding in some Pakistani favorites like the Lahori samosa, a nod to the Alam brothers’ Punjabi roots. The 150 natural wines on offer have been curated by sommelier Irene Cavalli to pair excellently with the bold seasoning, heat, and aromas of dishes like Kima Mutter Pav (spicy ground beef with peas and brioche bread), spicy coconut prawns, Madrasi vegetables, and Goan fish curry. This kitchen has breathed new life to a space that was once a warehouse, embracing the stripped-down post-industrial aesthetic in Poblenou, a district akin to the Brooklyn of Barcelona. Order as much as you can; the menu isn’t huge, so with a handful of friends you might be able to try it all, and you’ll be happy you did.

Must-try dish: If you’re a meat eater, don’t miss the tandoor-roasted lamb chops, the unassuming star of the menu.

Shoronpo is one of the most popular ramen spots in the city, and it’s equally famous for the eponymous soup dumplings, which are the Japanese version of xiaolongbao. Fillings range from classic minced pork to foie gras, and there is even a dessert shoronpo with chocolate, olive oil, and sea salt. The ramen comes in 10 varieties including three vegetarian options, but the star is the rich and creamy tantanmen with sesame-laced chicken broth, ground pork, and springy noodles that chef Keita Tanaka may have introduced to Barcelona. Booking can be done online and is a must, and keep an eye out for a new location outside the Estació Sants train station soon.

Must-try dish: The karaage (fried chicken) and the yude ebi wantan (boiled shrimp dumplings in sichuan chili sauce) should not be missed.

The team at pizzeria Sartoria Panatieri focuses on seasonality, artisan production, and ingredient provenance, taking the pies to a whole other level and making this one of the hottest spots in the city; in fact, they were awarded the title of 2nd Best Pizza in the World in 2024 as part of the the Best Chef Awards. This self-described “farm to pizza” restaurant meticulously selects every ingredient that graces their creative pizzas. Tender crust from local, organic flour is the base for toppings like sobrasada with Mahón cheese, wild fennel, honey, and mozzarella; adobo pork jowl with celeriac puree, smoked mozzarella, and Brazil nuts; or apple compote with bleu cheese, celery, freeze-dried apple, and caramelized almonds. Make sure you try their house-made salumi as well, especially the papada and the Gascón pork tartare.

Know before you go: The location on Carrer de Provença is the flagship location with the most creative and seasonal pizzas, while the location in Gràcia on Carrer de l’Encarnació serves popular classic pies.

Don’t be misled by the old-school appearance and simple menu at Ultramarinos Marín. Seats at chef Borja García’s open kitchen are among the most sought-after in the city, and for good reason. This humble-looking asador (grill-centric restaurant), only open for breakfast and lunch, is a temple of product-driven Catalan cooking, dedicated to holding classic recipes to the highest standard. Through his training at the iconic Etxebarri and Noma, García works magic with minimal ingredients, a hot plancha, and a smoldering wood-fire oven. The myriad preparations include grilled langoustines, braised pork shanks, mackerel in escabeche, stewed snails, massive steaks, smoked beef tongue, funky garum, and briny sea urchin toast. Don’t miss the fish charcuterie or the simple yet extraordinary grilled smashed potatoes with garlic alioli.

Know before you go: In April 2025, García opened Ultrapaninos Marín next door, a casual sandwich shop and grocery selling some of the house products, from pickles and garums to T-shirts. Don’t miss out on the street-style hot dogs.

Chef Rafa Panatieri, of the Panatieri-Sastre chef duo, loves to say that of all the carefully imagined and artfully presented dishes at Brabo, everyone remembers the bread. Grilled in a pan over glowing coals and served with smoked butter, this unforgettable starter is even better when enjoyed with the salumi that Panatieri and fellow co-owner Jorge Sastre have perfected at their award-winning Sartoria Panatieri pizzería. Most dishes — grilled quail with young garlic, chuletón steak of thickly-marbled Friesian, spring peas with white sobrasada sausage, whole-roasted fish of the day — pass over the grill in Brabo’s kitchen, which is open to the intimate and dimly-lit dining room.

Must-try menu: Opt for the 90 euro tasting menu which includes snacks, appetizers, main dishes, and dessert (the quivering flan with quince caramel should not be missed).

Open for: Dinner on weekdays, with lunch on Friday; closed weekends

Berbena is a leading reference in the blossoming world of chef-driven, modern Catalan cuisine in Barcelona. Take a seat at one of the handful of tables, and begin your meal with hearty chunks of sourdough smeared with rich, smoked butter. Then dive into the assortment of seasonal small plates featuring whatever is fresh that day, from monkfish cheeks with cod tripe pil-pil and beef tongue with bustard, to guinea fowl with parsnips in a Catalan vi ranci sauce and artichokes with truffle; vibrant vegetables often play a starring role in the nightly specials. The cheese selection is impressive, as is their list of the over 600 wines, with more than 30 of them served by the glass. Linger over dessert as you enjoy excellent coffee from nearby SlowMov specialty roasters and espresso from the gleaming La Marzocco machine.

Know before you go: The restaurant has a policy of no children under 12 years old allowed so keep this in mind if traveling or dining with children

Parking Pita is a virtually unmarked restaurant in the corner of what was once a cavernous parking garage. The team uses a wood-fired oven to bake fresh pitas for their popular falafel and shawarma sandwiches. The menu is packed with Mediterranean and Levantine dishes, but also includes forays into North Africa and South Asia — sweet potato and parsnip latkes, Harissa-topped French fries with roasted garlic mayo, beet hummus dotted with pine nuts and feta, grilled leeks with hazelnut dukkah, and roasted cauliflower with curry and pistachios are all great starters. The pitas range from falafel with pickled cabbage and lamb kofta with sumac, to chicken tandoori and charcoal-roasted lamb shawarma. Diners sit at a long communal table and service is quick, making it a popular lunch spot for the neighborhood working crowd.

Know before you go: Parking Pita is just a small part of the Parking Pizza concept —- the excellent and innovative pizzeria at the back of this same, former parking garage. Try their pizzas at several locations around the city, or seek out the massive, grilled ribeye at Parking Sotano, their chic underground steakhouse in Sarrià-Sant Gervasi.

Rooq makes everything in-house, from the herb breading, tangy marinade, fermented pickles, and pillowy brioche buns for their fried chicken sandwiches, to their side dishes and brownies. The menu is minimal: chicken nuggets, salads, and sandwiches. All the chicken sandwiches (fried, spicy fried, grilled, or the new Sichuan-style hotpot flavor) are made with juicy, corn-fed Catalan chicken breasts, and . vegetarians can choose from jackfruit or tofu in either nuggets or sandwiches. Pick your main course and round out the meal with twice-cooked fries tossed in the house spice blend and a side of coleslaw (vinegar- or mayonnaise-based). There’s also a wide selection of craft beers and seven house-made dipping sauces.

Know before you go: On Monday and Tuesday nights, the restaurant has fried chicken wings with special flavors that change weekly.

Seyma Ozkaya Erpul is originally from Turkey but has called Barcelona home for over a decade. She left her previous career as an engineer and marketing professional to pursue her passion for great food and design, opening the first Funky Bakers in the heart of El Born. While that original location remains a popular takeaway coffee shop, the full Funky Bakers experience can be had at the Eatery and Deli location in Eixample. One side is a highly curated gourmet grocery, gift, and coffee shop, while the other is a bistrot serving colorful and creative dishes from around Northern Europe and the Mediterranean, all paired with natural wines.

Know before you go: If you find yourself in the neighborhood of Poble Sec, check out the new Funky location inside the chic Hotel Brumell, with a beautiful interior courtyard tucked away from the busy city center.

Founded in 1898, this family-run colmado has long been one of the most iconic gourmet shops in the city. With an impressive stock of over 200 cheeses and a huge selection of wines, conservas, and cured meats, the famed dry goods store was renovated in 2022 to accommodate an array of high bistro tables, as well as a more formal dining room tucked away behind storeroom doors. The kitchen, led by chef Jordi Vilà of Michelin-starred Alkimia, offers a take on Catalan cuisine that is both elegant and nostalgic, with dishes like wild sea bass tartare with sour cream and caviar, stewed mushrooms with poached egg and zucchini panna cotta, and lamb shoulder braised with Chartreuse.

Know before you go: There are two dining areas, each with its own booking system: the less-formal Colmado Múrria shop space with high tables, and the backroom Rerebotiga with low tables and tablecloths.

Mikan comes up again and again when locals in the know are asked about their favorite spots in the city. Serving what the team calls Northeast Asian cuisine, the project, created together with partners Woody Wang and Arthur Holland Michel, is an evolution of various businesses — private dinners, a lunchbox delivery service, homemade chili crisp — that chef Dan Jin (who goes by Tan) developed at the start of the pandemic. Chef Tan has a particular passion for the dishes of her native region of Northern China, but she also loves the flavors of Japan and Korea. Mikan is a bargain for lunch, when a fixed-price menu includes a variety of dishes, soup, and dessert (including vegan and vegetarian options). In the evenings, the exciting a la carte menu is perfect for sharing. Dishes like grilled koji-cured mackerel with green onion oil, daikon, and shiso, spicy beef salad with cilantro and chile, or Iberian pork loin katsu are paired expertly with an eclectic selection of natural wines, all from small European producers.

Know before you go: One Saturday per month, the bar features rotating local DJs starting at 11 p.m., and there are often collaboration nights with unique, thematic wine pairings by visiting sommeliers, so keep an eye on their Instagram.

The exposed stone walls and traditional Catalan vaulted ceilings of the former water bottling plant that now houses Franca set the scene for what its founders call “invented local cuisine.” The kitchen imagines a parallel universe of Catalan culinary history, delivering dishes inspired by regional classics updated with creative twists. The food is unpretentious yet elegant and modern, forgoing fine-dining clichés like spherifications, heaps of microgreens, and overwrought plating. Instead, the menu focuses on fine-tuned, deeply flavored sharing plates that look deceptively simple, from a custardy Passard egg served in its shell with concentrated garum and local ratafia liqueur, to a salad of ten heirloom Spanish bean varieties, grilled monkfish tail with roasted pepper sauce, and the cuttlefish bikini — a sandwich reminiscent of shrimp toast made with cuttlefish paste pan-fried between crisp bread and served with a smoked pork demi-glace.

Must-order dish: If visiting with a group, order La Festa — a large roasted sharing platter featuring suckling lamb shoulder or pork collar depending on the season, served with seasonal side dishes like tomato and peach salad with charred onions, pork belly skewers, grilled green beans, or roasted potato terrine.

Open for: Dinner, with lunch on Fridays and Saturdays

The Palace hotel, which first opened as the original Ritz Barcelona in 1919, still dazzles with opulent, old-world decor, making it a perfect stage for chef Rafa Zafra’s homage to classic fine dining. Zafra, former head chef at El Bulli, has come to be known for his elegant and simple approach to seafood at his lauded restaurant Estimar, but at Amar the preparations and presentations are decidedly more ornate; there is even a section of dishes inspired by the original Ritz hotel restaurant. The menu also has a section of dishes that pay homage to chef Albert Adrià, as well as top-quality seafood, seven dishes highlighting caviar, a handful of modern Catalan mains, whole grilled fish and steaks, vegetable sides, and Mediterranean tapas.

Must-try menu: There is currently a special menu celebrating the 175th birthday of César Ritz himself, in addition to the standard 12-course tasting menu.

Born in Uruguay and trained in Basque, Spain — both centers for meat in their own right — chef Joaquín Ignacio Sánchez is at the helm of Carnal, a Barcelona boho take on the traditional Spanish steakhouse. At this buzzy spot, hefty cuts of dry-aged beef are charred over oak embers, served medium-rare, and finished at the table on a searing-hot stone slab, allowing diners to dial in their preferred doneness. The steaks on offer come from around the globe and are aged in-house between 45 and 150 days, with prices that range from accessible to wildly extravagant; the menu’s most luxurious item is the 120-day-aged, 2-pound ox chuletón (bone-in rib-eye) from the legendary Bodega El Capricho near León, Spain. Before the main event, warm up with some American black angus beef cheek croquettes, flame-grilled maitake mushrooms, or A5 wagyu tartare kissed with a blowtorch and served over a caveman-esque length of roasted bone marrow. For those who don’t partake in red meat, there is a decent selection of seafood, poultry, and vegetable dishes, providing some welcome balance.

Must-try dish: Do not overlook the “Jamón de vaca Rubia Gallega,” marbled beef from Galicia cured in the style of Iberian ham, which yields intense flavor and fat that dissolves on the tongue.

Chef Rafa Peña’s passion for food is as great as his disregard for formality and fine dining accolades. A favorite among the city’s chefs, Gresca is a must-visit for lovers of nose-to-tail cooking who want to experience the best of seasonal Catalan cuisine without the stuffy service and delicate portions of some Michelin-starred restaurants. The menu can change from day to day, but there are some mainstays that every first-timer at Gresca should experience, such as the roasted chicken with fines herbes, the calf’s brain with butter and lemon, the pan-roasted sweetbreads, and the grilled quail.

Know before you go: The best seats in the house are at the open kitchen pass, where diners get a front row view of the action. It’s worth calling the restaurant to reserve your spot, since they don’t provide this option when booking online.

In an antique bar space with over 100 years of history, on a coveted corner in one of the trendiest parts of the Eixample, Soma opened in 2021 to instant accolades from the gourmands of Barcelona. Cozy decor and a Parisian-style terrace set the stage for a menu of Catalan tapas with a strong Italian character and hints of France. Look for veal liver with onion and red pepper jam, socarrat de risotto (a risotto cooked until compact and crispy like the bottom of a classic paella) with kale and honey, octopus with bacon and paprika potato purée, and ragu-stuffed rigatoni.

Best for: Soma is known as a vibey spot for lunch or dinner, but weekday breakfasts on their tiny outdoor terrace with coffee, pastries, and sandwiches make a perfect, slow morning.

Created by Priscilla Alfaro, a Mexican American woman who grew up in Los Angeles, with her partner Gaston Gabrielli and chef Nick Hosea, this is an excellent, modern American diner where the draw is simple: truly delicious food and bottomless filter coffee from specialty roaster Three Marks Coffee. The pancakes are fluffy, the bacon is crispy, the breakfast burrito is hearty, and the Nashville hot chicken sandwich is tongue-numbingly good. Too many brunch spots in Barcelona rely on Instagram-worthy visuals to compensate for mediocre flavors and cookery, but Gringa All Day is the real deal. Expect a line on the weekends, but the wait is worth it. No reservations.

Know before you go: If you’re a fan of Gringa, check out their burger and fried chicken window at the rock ‘n’ roll/biker-themed cocktail bar Motor Oil BCN.

It’s rare in Barcelona to see a classic trompo slowly, perfectly charring pork, but Xuba Tacos takes tacos al pastor very seriously. The restaurant lovingly layers spiced pork on the spit, shaves it into thin slices, and serves it on supple, handmade blue corn tortillas. Alongside classics like al pastor and carne asada, there are also modern creations, like black beer-batter sea bass tacos with crispy leeks and sauteed lobster tail tacos with cilantro emulsion. Keep an eye out for seasonal specials, like wild mushroom and roasted chestnut tacos, and don’t miss the micheladas.

Best for: For a great deal, opt for their weekday fixed-price lunch menu that includes a starter of guacamole, three tacos of your choice, and a drink (water, soda, or beer).

With no signage or any identifying information visible from the street, the small Suru Bar makes meals in its intimate space feel like serendipity. A row of counter seating gives diners a view into the open kitchen, where chefs prepare star dishes like grilled chicken skin skewers with chilled shrimp tartare, vibrant spring peas with smoked chorizo and cured egg yolks, and a brochette of crunchy pig ear with charred chicken gizzard and tender squid. The cuisine is seasonal, thanks to the prime location just across the street from the famous Ninot market, and the dishes range from yakitori on a traditional Japanese grill to explorations of all things offal, with an extensive wine list to round out the meal.

Must-try dish: Don’t miss the grilled veal sweetbreads with a silky puree of toasted cauliflower and pickles.

Crowds flock to Taktika Berri to down copious amounts of ice-cold beer and funky, sour cider while perusing the platters of pintxos that adorn the well-polished bar. Highly traditional without being kitsch, this popular Basque bar, founded in 1995, feels like it’s been transported straight from the industrial port city of Bilbao, complete with old photos and jai lai baskets. The bar area at the entrance can get packed with an after-work crowd, who graze classic pintxos like fried chistorra sausage, anchovies with piquillo peppers, and tortilla de bacalao (salt cod omelette). But don’t be deceived; the pintxos on display are just a small fraction of what the menu has to offer. Take a look at the carta and order from a selection of Basque mainstays like almejas con refrito (sauteed clams with garlic, cayenne, and cider vinegar), the two-person serving of cogote de merluza (a large center-cut piece of whole hake, roasted and served with garlic and parsley), fried monkfish loin, or a well-marbled txultetón steak.

Know before you go: In addition to the cold or room-temperature pintxos on the bar, there is also a menu of hot pintxos that can be made-to-order (try the morcilla black sausage). To drink, choose a caña (small draught beer), Basque hard cider, or Txakoli (a famous, lightly-sparkling, kind of saline, low-alcohol wine from the Basque region).

True to its name, eggs take center stage at this relaxed restaurant known for spins on the classic Spanish potato and egg omelet (truita de patates). In the quiet, upscale neighborhood of Les Corts, Manda Huevos combines the relaxed energy of a trendy vermutería with sharp, modern branding. Chef and co-founder Ot Salvans draws on his experience in some of Spain’s top fine-dining kitchens while bringing flavor influences from around the globe. Catalan mainstays like cap i pota veal stew, langoustine-stuffed roast chicken, and macarrons del nét (baked pasta with meat ragù topped with a broiled cheese gratin) share the menu with fusion creations like roasted bone marrow with scallop tartare, fermented lemon, and caviar, and the chili crab-stuffed eggs. The nine truita varieties on the menu range from guanciale carbonara and Menorcan sobrasada with Mahón cheese, to red shrimp tartar with shrimp jus and the signature “bomba” omelet filled with pork ragù, spicy brava sauce, and saffron alioli. Omelets come in three flexible sizes, with the exception of the open-faced garlic lobster omelet, which skips potatoes entirely and comes topped with sherry-confited piquillo peppers and lobster roe.

Know before you go: Wednesday through Friday at lunch, take advantage of the fixed-price four-course meal. It includes an aperitivo, first course, second course, dessert or coffee, and a drink, showcasing many of the menu’s best-sellers.

With Taberna Nardi, founder Martín Pimentel of the Grup Amicks restaurant group has traded the vibrant red color scheme and meat-heavy menu of his popular Bar Pimentel for a calming vibe of deep maritime blue just a few doors down. Nardi is a self-proclaimed “irreverent seafood tavern” with a shimmering wave-like mirrored ceiling, just a handful of tables, and an inviting bar with open kitchen where the day’s catch is displayed on ice. Try the cumin-spiked hake pincho moruno skewers off the smoky Japanese robata, the grilled zamburiña scallops with tomato confit and garlic, the delicate cured horse mackerel with ginger and jalapeño, or the surprisingly meaty braised tuna cheek with potato purée. Wash it all down with a saline-heavy white wine, a natural sparkling, or their famous oyster-infused dry martini.

Must-try dish: While it may not be the immediate choice for most diners, the rich, buttery cube of toasted brioche topped with a dollop of tangy crème fraîche and a succulent cured anchovy is a single bite that should not be missed. And don’t forget the cheesecake for dessert.

Since 1946, Gelida has been an important social hub for the neighborhood, be it old friends meeting for a weekend lunch or workers loading up on calories before sunrise. The menu is full of classic Catalan dishes, but the breakfast-forward spot is best known for esmorzars de forquilla, or “fork breakfasts.” In modern Barcelona, many people opt for a light breakfast (think croissant and coffee), but the tradition of beginning your day with a hearty plate of stewed veal, tripe, snails, pig trotter, chickpeas, or pork cheeks is still alive at institutions like Gelida. You’ll see heaps of fried potatoes topped with a runny fried egg and spicy chorizo on tables as life-long regulars drink cafe con leche and mini draught beers simultaneously.

Must-try dish: Cap i pota, a gelatin-rich stew of veal head and hoof (though Gelida uses veal necks, which are meatier). The sauce is meant to be sopped up with pieces of crusty baguette and washed down with a house Gandesa, a golden, long-macerated white wine from the region of Terra Alta.

With a wave of modern kebab shops hitting Barcelona over the last year, sometimes it feels good to go back to an all-time favorite. Carrer de Joaquin Costa is always buzzing with activity, as is its most famous kebab shop, Bismillah Kebabish, a halal mainstay in the Pakistani community of Barcelona since 2003. Crowds pack into the minimalist dining room, often sharing tables with strangers, just for a taste of the famous and affordable chicken shawarma — fresh naan that is pulled by hook from a tandoor oven and loaded with fragrant, bright-red shavings of spiced chicken thigh, carved from the spinning skewer that the team prepares daily (it’s much better than the beef version). Mixed with roasted peppers and onions and topped with your choice of fresh vegetables, chile sauce, and garlic sauce, this is the go-to meal from many regular customers. However, dishes such as the lamb curry, beef shish kebab, and the tandoori chicken skewers are also quite popular; you can even mix and match multiple dishes together on the combo plates with rice and salad.

Know before you go: This is one of the last Barcelona institutions that is still cash-only, so come prepared.

La Mudana is celebrating its 10th anniversary in 2025, and over the last decade it has become an anchor of the local culinary scene of Sants, a neighborhood known for its tight-knit community and support for local businesses. La Mudana is equally suited as a spot for friends to catch up over a few tapas and a beer as it is for a refined multicourse dinner. The food draws influence as much from Mediterranean and Catalan cuisine as it does from the flavors of France and Asia, with a little Latin American influence as well. Pick from dishes like the kimchi juice and comté cheese oyster, meaty cap i pota rice with teriyaki eel, ox tail-stuffed brioche with smoked sabayon, and the Iberian pork katsu sando with mole and ají amarillo, or opt for a fixed-price two-person tasting menu of six all-star dishes, plus dessert, that includes vermouth to start and cava to finish.

Must-try dish: No table at La Mundana is complete without the picturesque patatas bravas — two perfectly-sculpted rectangles of potato, fried crisp and topped with classic spicy brava sauce as well as the funky black garlic alioli.

This small corner bar just one block from the old port of Barcelona has been serving the same four dishes since 1945. Though the salted anchovies, fried sausage, and tomato salad are all delicious, pescaditos (fresh, floured, and fried whole anchovies) are the true star. Now run by the grandson of the original founder, Bar La Plata sells over 85 pounds of the little fishes per week.

Know before you go:The place is nearly always busy and only has a few tables, so either show up right when they open, or do as the local crowd does and eat standing up at the bar or even in the street if no seats are available. Drinking alcohol outside isn’t allowed but you can get the pescaditos to-go in a paper cone.

Plump pork meatballs braised in tomato sauce, creamy stracciatella cheese, grilled zucchini, and a dusting of grated ricotta salata come together in one of the newest sandwiches on the menu at Compà, a panini shop dedicated to the flavors of Calabria. In addition to the original location a few streets over from the Barceloneta beach, owner Vittorio Cicero has recently expanded with a new shop in the uptown neighborhood of Gràcia, with panini like mortadella with burrata and pistachio pesto or Calabrese lardo with spicy ‘nduja spread, smoked provolone, and roasted potatoes. Choose from nearly a dozen sandwiches including rotating specials, all served on 48-hour slow-fermented focaccia, pressed and piping hot.

Know before you go: There are a few tables, but the sandwiches are meant as street food, so get yours to-go and head to the beach or the nearest plaza. Just don’t forget the napkins, and a tiramisu for dessert.

One of the oldest restaurants in the beachside neighborhood of La Barceloneta, this is the birthplace of the famous “bomba de la Barceloneta,” a mouth­watering fried potato croquette stuffed with savory ground beef and topped with aioli and hot sauce, which now appears on menus all over the city. In addition to the bombas, try the calamars a la planxa (grilled squid), and in summer get the grilled sardines. If you have a taste for offal, add a plate of cap i pota, an old-­school Catalan stew of tripe, veal trotters, and veal head in tomato.

Know before you go: You’ll likely see a line of people waiting outside, but don’t get behind the last person. Go straight to the door instead of queuing up and ask to be put on the waiting list. They will call out names in order, no need to wait in an orderly line, just linger nearby.

Suculent isn’t defined by one genre of cuisine, but packs its tasting and a la carte menus with as many delicious dishes as possible. It’s a favorite among chefs for nose-to-tail cooking and fine dining makeovers of grandma’s Catalan comfort food (with influences from Asia and Latin America). Dishes change with the seasons, but don’t miss mainstays such as the beets with beurre blanc and smoked eel, the royal custard of porcini mushrooms with sea urchin, and the braised hare canelon with foie gras and Codium seaweed.

The creation of chef Victor Ródenas and brothers Ignasi and Marc García, this youthful take on a simple Catalan casa de menjars (house of food) combines the best parts of a traditional vermouth bar with the refined, seasonal Catalan cooking of a fine dining veteran. The lively yet casual atmosphere is the perfect place to enjoy the varied dishes: confit artichokes with spring peas, sunchoke puree, and romesco; escabeche oyster shooters with chicken jus; beef tendon stew with fried hake and pickled chile peppers; and mini paella with shrimp tartare and pig trotter carpaccio. This is a gathering place for neighborhood regulars first and foremost.

Must-try dishes: There are always some special off-menu treats to be discovered, just ask your server.

This beachside restaurant has had five different names since it opened in 1942, but has always stayed within the same family. In 2023, it was born once again as Casa Costa, a modern concept with playful branding, refined food, and natural wines that still gives timeless Mediterranean flavors and aesthetics — few places capture the true essence of Barcelona as well as Casa Costa. Start your meal with a spicy bomba croquette of potato and slow-cooked beef, clams in green sauce, or tomato salad with rosemary gelee, to be followed by star dishes like the whole roasted seabass for two with Mediterranean vinaigrette, and the pig trotter roulade with red prawns. There are always seasonal specials too, from tuna tartare with pickled summer cherries and confit spring artichokes with pancetta, to fire-charred calçots — the iconic Catalan winter onions.

Know before you go: The outdoor terrace is always bustling, but the best sea views are to be had from the second-floor dining room with panoramic windows and cozy banquets.

Now with three locations across the city, Lluritu’s stripped-down approach to a Mediterranean marisquería has made it a must-visit in the Barcelona food scene. Its ethos of shunning complex sauces, tablecloths, and deep fryers in favor of simple, wood-fired and planxa grilling means diners get the pure flavors of the region’s best seasonal seafood. With a fishmonger aesthetic of white tiles, marble counters, and stainless-steel serving trays paired with the energetic service of a festive neighborhood bar, Lluritu is one of the best spots in the city for grilled razor clams, zamburiñas, giant prawns, and whole roasted fish — all washed down with a cold beer or house vermouth. Don’t miss the famous polp sec (dried, flash-grilled octopus), the smoked eel and tomato salad, the crispy lluritu (a small, hyper-seasonal fish and the restaurant’s namesake), or any of the daily blackboard specials.

Know before you go: While all three locations share core menu highlights, each has unique offerings, most notably the rice dishes like the squid ink-infused arròs negre and traditional suquet seafood stew, which are exclusive to Lluritu 3 on Passeig de Sant Joan.

Some high-end seafood spots in the city are places to see and be seen; this intimate, traditional marisqueria is a place to eat. For nearly 30 years, the supreme quality and freshness of the fish has kept any desire to modernize or adulterate classic Catalan cuisine at bay. Just a block from Plaça d’Espanya, El Camarote d’en Tomàs displays the day’s catch on heaps of ice at the bar, an impressive sight that immediately greets visitors. Expect wild-caught fish roasted whole, grilled giant prawns, impossibly tender sauteed baby squid, clams, scallops, and plump sea urchin roe scooped from the shell and laid across a butter-smeared cracker with a dash of lemon on top. Whatever you pick, be sure to start with the superb and refreshing esqueixada de bacallà, a popular cold preparation of salt cod bathed in olive oil, tomato, and olives that is near and dear to the hearts of many Catalan people.

Must-try dish: If you want to experience the legendary Spanish delicacy that is percebes (gooseneck barnacle), this is a perfect place to try them — just brace yourself for the lavish cost per kilo.

Open for: Dinner, with lunch on the weekends

Tiberi Bar was born from the Tiberi Club, a popular organizer for creative events and pop-ups that fuse eating and art. Tucked away on a quiet street in Poble Sec, the minimalist, airy interior, with high ceilings and plenty of windows, is the perfect scene for a rotating roster of colorful sharing plates inspired by Catalan traditions and the flavors of the Mediterranean, paired with natural wines from small local producers. Duck terrine with pistachios, crunchy polenta with sage, smoked sardine with sour cream and whole grain mustard, and a pork confit sandwich with red cabbage play upon well-worn local staples with surprising flavors.

Know before you go: Tiberi Bar organizes a periodic Sunday morning special menu, dubbed Granja Tiberi, with novel takes on brunch such as croissant with ricotta, sobrassada, and honey, and fried eggs with peas, artichokes, mint, and ham. Check the Tiberi Bar Instagram for scheduling and booking info.

Open for: Dinner, with lunch and brunch over the weekend

At Margarit, on a narrow tree-lined street on the slope of Montjüic, Greek chef Stefanos Balis paints with broad Mediterranean brushstrokes while paying homage to his Hellenic homeland. There’s a standout list of both traditional and natural wines, with some especially interesting and potent Greek reds, which pair nicely with refined dishes dispatched from a sleek open kitchen. Favorites include the salty taramas fish roe spread with cured bonito tuna, the grilled eggplant with pistachios and honey harissa, the mini chicken souvlaki on fresh sourdough pita, and the braised lamb neck with yogurt sauce and tender root vegetables — dishes built on tradition and memory.

Know before you go: Weekends are a bit different at Margarit, with a rotating daytime menu that captures the flavor and energy of a slow Sunday meal around the Mediterranean.

Today guests expect more than a Michelin-starred restaurant. They want to get into the kitchen and out in the field.

No more generic resort food. These culinary-savvy properties bring a distinct sense of place to the all-inclusive experience.

#6554. How You Squeeze Planetary Minerals Changes Everything

Studying the interiors of planets is essential for understanding planetary formation, evolution, and their ability to potentially host life as we know it. To accomplish this, researchers use a combination of Earth as an analog, computer models, meteorites, and data collected from other planetary bodies for studying their interior compositions. As a result, scientists have determined that the elements of magnesium and silicon are the most abundant planetary building blocks. And, under extreme pressures like the interior mantle of our planet, it forms magnesium oxide (MgO) crystals. But how does this same process occur under different pressures and temperatures on other planets like gas giants and larger rocky exoplanets called super-Earths?

Now, a collaborative team of researchers from the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) and Johns Hopkins University might be one step closer to solving this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in Physical Review X, the researchers unveiled intriguing findings that could solve a 12-year investigation regarding the geochemical processes that occur deep inside planets, specifically related to the formation of magnesium oxide. This study is a third study in a series that builds off two previous studies, a 2015 study published in Physical Review Letters and a 2024 study published in Science Advances.

Artist's impression of the interior layers of Earth, Mars and the Moon. (Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

For the study, the researchers conducted a series of laboratory experiments using lasers on a cubic crystal structure of magnesium oxide to compress and simulate the extreme temperatures and pressures it experiences in planetary interiors. For example, the researchers tested as high as 572 Gigapascals (GPa) and 13,000 Kelvin (K) (12,927 degrees Celsius/23,300 degrees Fahrenheit), which are much higher than the pressures and temperatures near the center of the Earth at about 360 GPa and 6,000 K (5,727 degrees Celsius/10,340 degrees Fahrenheit), respectively.

The laser compressed the MgO cube from various directions, which challenged longstanding scientific theories that the extreme temperatures and pressures made the direction of compression irrelevant. The three directions included diagonally along the face, perpendicular to a cube face, and along the diagonal through the face.

Credit: NASA/Lunar and Planetary Institute

In the end, the researchers found that the direction of the incoming laser onto the MgO cube resulted in different responses regarding its compression. For example, while the cubeâs transformation along the diagonal through the cube, whereas the other two directions resulted in different responses, specifically disordered and irregular crystal growth behind a shock wave from the compression. While this finding refuted longstanding theories regarding the behavior of crystals based on direction, the researchers also found that the MgO cube melted at 572 GPa and 13,000 K, which set a new experimental known material record for pressure and temperature.

âMagnesium oxide is an important ingredient in our understanding of planetary interiors,â said Dr. June Wicks, who is a professor in Johns Hopkinsâ Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences and a co-author on the study. âThese experiments help us determine where it can remain solid and where it becomes liquid, which matters for how planets transport heat and evolve.â

As noted, magnesium and silicon comprise the most abundant elements in planetary interiors, with its combined form of MgO revealing the temperatures and pressures of those same planetary interiors. The three main geologic layers of a rock planetary object are the crust, mantle, and core, with the Earth having a liquid outer core and a rocky inner core, with MgO forming near the bottom of the mantle near the core-mantle boundary. However, this process is different depending on the type of planet.

For example, on super-Earth exoplanets, MgO can transform into a conductive liquid within the mantle (whereas this conductivity exists within the Earthâs outer core), resulting in magnetic fields much stronger than Earthâs. Additionally, MgO on gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn can exist either as a solid or liquid deep within their cores and depending on the temperatures.

What new insights into planetary interior processes will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

As always, keep doing science & keep looking up!

#6553. Even for Desperate Restaurants, Fake Reviews Just Aren’t Worth It

A new report proves that planting fake Yelp reviews has dire long-term impacts on restaurants

When Yelp was first launched in 2004, it flopped. The company’s initial model of an email-based referral service failed to take off until its creators realized users were taking the platform into their own hands; in lieu of sending one another recommendations via email chain, they began using a “hidden” link at the bottom of the startup’s website to write unsolicited reviews of everything from doctors to restaurants. Yelp 2.0 launched in 2005, and gave those reviews a more visible place to live online — one that emboldened users to feel more authentic stewardship, by way of direct authorship, over hyping up the businesses they enjoyed (or didn’t). The startup bought a whopping 20-million-business database, and amplified a world of reviews outside of the restaurant- critic echo chamber. It was a fresh democratization of information, which was itself one of the more optimistic legacies of the Y2K internet.

It’s been over 20 years since Yelp was founded. At its best, the platform still feels like a place where the voices of hungry, curious diners can share their personal experiences and offer recommendations and tips; at its worst, it feels like a bloated repository for reviews filled with misdirected anger, unreasonable expectations, or else completely fake customer reviews. Initially, unsubstantiated and unreliable reviews were more often written by a person — either someone from the business itself, or paid by the business; now, a fake review can be penned by a paid influencer, a detailed generative AI prompt, or purchased from third-party agencies that will produce fake bot reviews in bulk.

Fake reviews were perhaps inevitable. Bot-driven comments became ubiquitous during an overripe moment in the untamed internet’s lifespan. But how does a restaurant shamed for gamifying its reviews — even if it was, presumably, out of desperation in a tough economic landscape — regain customers’ broken trust?

… The offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp.

In 2026’s AI-addled digital ecosystem, researchers are starting to understand even more about how paid-for, planted reviews impact the restaurants behind them, and whether trying to gamify platforms to achieve high ratings is worth it at all for businesses. A recently published working paper on the consequences of restaurants flagged by Yelp for fake (planted, incentivized) reviews found that since 2023, more than 4,900 businesses have been flagged with Yelp’s “Consumer Alert” banner, which exists on the penalized business’ page for a 90-day period and lets Yelp users know that the business has been caught peddling fake reviews. In 2020, the fast-casual chain Burgerim was found guilty of planting fake reviews, and received over 200 digital warning banners across its various locations’ Yelp pages.

The impacts of that digital pillory extend far beyond its 90-day duration. Yi Cao is an assistant professor of accounting at George Mason University, and the co-author of the paper; almost immediately, Cao noticed the offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp. Cao’s team cross-analyzed the business’ performance on Yelp with real-life foot traffic reports (from global location data firm SafeGraph) and credit card transaction data (courtesy of Consumer Edge), and discovered that most of the penalized restaurants struggled to recover to pre-alert traffic even after a year and a half. The stink of chicanery lingered.

While Cao says his team doesn’t know every signal that Yelp uses to identify fake reviews, they do know that it relies “substantially on reports from consumers and business owners,” and that “they also have an algorithm running in the background to screen reviews for AI-generated language — which is a sign of possible review inflation.” At this point, the cost of planting a good review is only getting steeper as the technology capable of detecting it improves. “This is a classical theory of a trade-off between the benefits of manipulating reputation and the risks of getting caught,” Cao explains, “When the risk is relatively low, the business owners decide the incremental benefits are worth the risk.”

Yelp’s real restaurant reviews don’t necessarily need to be etched in stone, but as AI-penned reviews become less detectable and more sophisticated, what diners want now, more than ever, is a human touch and a sense of authenticity.

#6552. Scientists Discover a New Type of Depression That Common Antidepressants May Miss

For some people with hard-to-treat depression, the body’s internal clock may help explain why standard antidepressants fall short.

University of Sydney researchers have identified a proposed subtype called “circadian depression,” marked by disrupted sleep and daily rhythms. It accounted for nearly a quarter of participants in a study of more than 10,000 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.

The findings, published in the British Journal of Psychiatry, suggest that recognizing this pattern could help clinicians identify people who may benefit from treatments targeting the body clock earlier in their care.

“Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression,” said first author Dr. Emiliana Tonini, from the university’s Brain and Mind Centre.

Using clinical and genetic information from the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study, the researchers classified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Its features included seasonal episodes, sleeping longer when depressed, waking up exhausted, and a tendency to stay up late.

These symptoms point toward the circadian system, the body’s internal 24-hour timekeeping network that regulates sleep and wakefulness. The researchers identified genetic characteristics of the subtype that could help explain why treatments aimed at other brain pathways are less effective.

Participants with circadian depression were more likely to have developed depression earlier in life and experienced more severe symptoms (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). They also had greater genetic susceptibility to inflammatory and cardiovascular conditions and major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.

“Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them,” Tonini said.

SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are commonly offered as initial treatments for depression. People with the circadian subtype reported less benefit and more side effects from these medications.

The researchers suggest that this group may respond better to behavioral and medical therapies targeting the brain circuits involved in circadian rhythms. Options include light therapy, melatonin, and antidepressants that act on melatonin pathways.

Co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse, from the Brain and Mind Centre, said, “Because circadian depression is linked to people’s internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.

“For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances.”

For young people, identifying this pattern early could help avoid unsuccessful initial treatments and additional side effects, according to Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist.

“We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.

“Most young people will be offered SSRIs first up, but for at least a quarter there are better circadian-focused medical and behavioral options to help treat and manage their condition.”

Reference: “Clinical and genetic correlates of a circadian subtype of depression in the Australian Genetics of Depression Study” by Emiliana Tonini, Jacob J. Crouse, Mirim Shin, Joanne S. Carpenter, Brittany L. Mitchell, Enda M. Byrne, Penelope A. Lind, Scott D. Gordon, Richard Parker, Samuel J. Hockey, Timothy To, Andrew Shim, Alex Hill, Anna Treneman, Elizabeth Scott, Jan Scott, Kathleen R. Merikangas, Naomi R. Wray, Nicholas G. Martin, Sarah E. Medland and Ian B. Hickie, 20 October 2026, The British Journal of Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1192/bjp.2026.10798

This work was further supported by philanthropic donations from families who are affected by mental illness (who would like to be left anonymous) awarded to Dr. Mirim Shin.
