#6543. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee

Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings?

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee.

Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout.

Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue.

Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami.

The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?”

As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.”

“Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?

#6542. A Simple Tongue Exercise Could Hold the Key to Fighting the Devastating Effects of ALS

Researchers at the University of Missouri have uncovered a promising way to help surviving nerve cells compensate for damage caused by ALS and other motor neuron diseases.

The loss of tongue control in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) can affect far more than speech. It can make swallowing increasingly difficult and interfere with breathing during sleep. Now, researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that tongue exercise can increase the activity of surviving nerve cells in a preclinical model, potentially offering a new approach to preserving these essential functions.

ALS, also called Lou Gehrig’s disease, progressively damages the motor neurons responsible for muscle movement and currently has no cure. However, not all neurons controlling the tongue are lost, particularly during the early stages. Researchers are investigating whether these surviving cells can compensate for damaged neurons and help maintain muscle function.

The findings center on neuroplasticity, the nervous system’s ability to adapt to damage or changing conditions. In the preclinical model, tongue exercise increased the activity of surviving motor neurons, suggesting that targeted training may help the remaining cells compensate for those lost to disease. Scientists have not yet determined exactly how exercise produces this response.

“This adaptation is called neuroplasticity, meaning the nervous system changes how it operates to compensate for damage, and this finding offers hope for those with motor neuron diseases,” said Nicole Nichols, an associate professor in the College of Veterinary Medicine and coauthor of the study. “By boosting the activity of the surviving neurons, we can help preserve the quality of life for those with ALS, spinal muscular atrophy and other motor neuron diseases.”

The tongue plays a central role in speaking, moving food during swallowing, and keeping the airway open during sleep. As the muscles weaken in people with ALS, eating can become difficult enough to require a feeding tube. Reduced tongue muscle function can also contribute to sleep apnea, a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep.

“For those with ALS, preserving swallowing function not only reduces the chance of developing sleep apnea, it could also mean the difference between needing a feeding tube or continuing to eat normally,” she said. “That’s incredibly meaningful for quality of life.”

Although the results are promising, the benefits have so far been demonstrated only in a preclinical model. Researchers now want to understand the biological mechanisms that allow tongue exercise to increase neuronal activity. Identifying those mechanisms could eventually support the development of medications that reproduce the effects of exercise without requiring patients to perform physical training.

“If we can figure out exactly how and why the tongue exercise helps the remaining neurons function better, that can help the development of treatments that mimic the benefits,” Nichols said. “For example, for someone with a very poor prognosis who may not be able to do tongue exercise, is there an injectable that we can give them that would activate those surviving motor neurons to improve their function? While both tongue exercise as a therapy and an injectable would require human clinical trials in the future, this finding is a step in the right direction.”

Nichols and her colleagues hope to advance tongue exercise toward human clinical trials within the next several years through collaborations at Mizzou’s NextGen Precision Health.

Reference: “Impact of tongue exercise on hypoglossal axis survival, structure, and output in a rodent model of hypoglossal motor neuron degeneration” by Amy N. Keilholz, Stephanie Lopez, Minasadat Attari, Nguyen P. Nguyen, Jay Henry, Catherine L. Smith, Ashley Feldberg, Kate L. Osman, Mojgan Golzy, Filiz Bunyak, Teresa E. Lever and Nicole L. Nichols, 12 May 2026, Journal of Neurophysiology. DOI: 10.1152/jn.00631.2024

#6541. Queen's University Belfast Students Find Neptune's Elusive Trojan Asteroids

An international team led by researchers at Queen's University Belfast has made a discovery that has eluded astronomers for decades. Beginning in 1906, telescope observations revealed a population of asteroids leading and trailing Jupiter, which came to be known as the "Trojan" and "Greek" populations. Since then, astronomers have discovered similar "families" orbiting Saturn and Uranus, but not Neptune. Thanks to the Queen's-led team, the mystery of the missing Trojans has now been resolved!

As detailed in a paper that appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, the team found these distant icy bodies by analyzing data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the next-generation telescope perched high atop the Andes in Chile. Thanks to Rubin's sharp optics and ability to rapidly survey the night sky (the fastest of any ground-based telescope), the team identified two asteroids and a candidate as permanent members of Neptune's trailing Trojans.

The team was led by Dr. Meg Schwamb, an astronomer and lecturer at the Astrophysics Research Centre, Queen's University Belfast (QUB). She was joined by researchers from the Instituto de Astronomia, GeofÃ­sica e CiÃªncias AtmosfÃ©ricas (IAG), the Planetary Science Institute (PSI), the DiRAC Institute, the Michigan Institute for Data and AI in Society (MIDAS), JHUAPL, the NSF's NOIRLAB, and multiple universities worldwide.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's LSST survey will help scientists create a census of Solar System objects. Credit: Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA H.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory combines the resolution of its 8.4-meter Simony Survey Telescope with the LSST Camera, the largest digital camera ever built. Having commenced operations in June 2025, Rubin is currently conducting the largest survey of the southern sky - the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). At the same time, it is mapping the northern sky to create an ultra-wide, ultra-high-definition time-lapse record of the cosmos.

Through these surveys, Rubin will provide new insight into the mysteries of the cosmos, including Dark Matter and Dark Energy. It will map the Milky Way and its faint satellite galaxies, detect transient phenomena (supernovae, variable stars, rogue planets, etc.) and create an inventory of objects in the Solar System. This last objective was what drew Schwamb and her team to analyze data from Rubin's early test observations last year.

After combining this massive trove of data, the team identified the objects as primordial members of the elusive trailing Neptune Trojan population. "Early data from Rubin Observatory is already expanding our knowledge of the solar system's 'small bodies,' including asteroids, comets, and other minor planets," Schwamb explained in a QUB press release. "And these early observations have provided our clearest view yet of Neptune's trailing Trojan cloud."

A rendering of the inner Solar System showing the asteroids discovered by Rubin in light teal. Known asteroids are dark blue. Credit: NSFâDOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NSF NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R/NASA/Goddard/ESA/Gaia/DPAC

Previously, astronomers struggled to find Neptune's Trojan populations because of the difficulty of spotting such distant, faint objects as they moved across the night sky. For the past ten years, the Trojans have been crowded in a region of the sky that placed them in front of the Milky Way's center (relative to Earth-based observers), an extremely dense and bright part of the night sky that obscured any tiny light sources in the foreground. Said Schwamb:

The Trailing Cloud has now begun to move out of this region of sky and combined with the Rubin Observatory's unmatched depth and sky coverage, we've been able to double the number of known objects in this population on long-lived orbits. These discoveries offer a glimpse of just how transformative Rubin's data will be, with even more exciting findings expected in the years ahead.

The Rubin Observatory obtained images of these objects using different filters, which allowed Dr. Schwamb and her team to show that the Trojans leading and trailing Neptune have similar surfaces. As Rubin continues the LSST survey over the next nine years, it is expected to discover tens to hundreds of Neptune Trojans in both its leading and trailing population, plus tens of thousands of icy bodies in the Trans-Neptunian Region and Kuiper Belt.

Further Reading: Queen's University, The Astrophysical Journal Letters**

See the new facial reconstruction of a man from Roman-era Scotland who was decapitated after his death and buried near a Roman fort.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers have virtually reconstructed the face of a man who was decapitated after his death almost 2,000 years ago and then buried near a Roman military fort in Scotland.

While it's unclear why the man was beheaded, other burials hundreds of miles away may offer a clue. A chemical analysis of the man's remains suggests that he grew up in southern Britain. Beheading bodies may have been an obscure burial rite for some southern Britons, as other decapitated bodies from about the same time have been found in that region, John H. Reid, an archaeologist at the Trimontium Trust who was not involved in the excavations, told Live Science.

Another mystery is why a southern Briton was on the Roman frontier, but it seems that he was working for the Roman army when he died, researchers at National Museums Scotland said in a statement. However, his skeleton shows the man's right arm had such limited movement that he could not have used a sword, so he was probably not a soldier, they added.

Despite this disability, however, it's possible that the man used weapons in his other hand, or had a job in the Roman army that did not require frontline fighting, such as a clerk.

"He could have been left-handed, or he could have had a 'desk job'," said Reid, who is the author of the book "The Eagle and the Bear: A New History of Roman Scotland" (Birlinn, 2023).

The man was probably about 50 years old when he died between A.D. 142 and 165. His remains were then buried near the Roman fort at Inveresk, on Scotland's east coast just southeast of what's now Edinburgh, according to the statement.

An analysis of the man's skeleton indicated that he had lived an active life. His nose had been broken and healed, and his right elbow showed extensive bone growth, perhaps from arthritis. Reid said the bone growth may have been his body's response to a physical injury.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Researchers at National Museums Scotland and the independent U.K.-based forensic anthropologist Christopher Rynn created the facial construction based on the man's skull.

The facial reconstruction is based on the shape of the man's skull. He is shown here without a beard, which was based on what was common at this time.

The Roman fort at Inveresk was built around A.D. 140 and acted as a command-and-supply center for Roman forts along the Antonine Wall, which ran along the shortest route between Scotland's west coast and east coast — roughly the line between Glasgow and Edinburgh, although neither city existed at the time.

The Romans had hoped to secure all of Scotland under their rule after their invasion of Britain under Emperor Claudius in A.D. 43. They tried to impose control after their victory against a coalition of native Caledonian tribes at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly near the Scottish city of Perth) in about 83. But by about 120, the Romans had retreated to the heavily fortified line of Hadrian's Wall, near the modern border of England and Scotland.

The fort at Inveresk was built for a second push that aimed to secure Roman control over southern Scotland by establishing the Antonine Wall. But this failed too, and after A.D. 162, the Romans withdrew again to Hadrian's Wall, until the final collapse of Roman rule in Britain in the early fifth century.

Jess Turner, an osteoarchaeologist at National Museums Scotland, with the skull of the man buried outside the Roman fort at Inveresk.

Reid told Live Science that Scotland's soil seldom preserved human skeletons, making the discovery of a Roman-era burial an uncommon find. Although the man had been decapitated after his death, other aspects of his grave indicated he was buried with dignity. In other words, his burial was unlike those of executed criminals, who were often decapitated in Roman-era Britain, he said.

The remains from six Roman-era burials have been found at Inveresk, and four of the dead had been similarly beheaded, the statement said.

There are several ways non-Romans could have served with the Roman army, Reid told Live Science. They might have been employed as servants or artisans attached to the Roman legions, or they might have been soldiers in Roman auxiliary units or even citizen-based legions, he said. By the time of the Antonine Wall, few members of the Roman army in Scotland would have been from the Italian peninsula, he added.

The chemical analysis looked at the ratios of isotopes, or variations of chemical elements, in the man's remains. This analysis suggested that the man had grown up in southern Britain. Alternatively, he may have been recruited from a nearby region, such as the coast of what's now the Netherlands, that gave the same isotopic profile, Reid said.

Reid and his colleagues have found extensive evidence of the Roman army at the Burnswark site in southern Scotland, including the deadly whistling sling bullets they used against their "barbarian" foes. Archaeological work there is ongoing.

What do you know about the Empire's conquest of the British Isles? Find out with our Roman Britain quiz!

#6539. Scientists Discover a Powerful New Way To Destroy Toxic “Forever Chemicals”

Scientists have developed a new way to destroy toxic “forever chemicals” in water rather than simply filter them out. During a 58-day experiment, the system removed more than 90% of each of six PFAS compounds and stripped away approximately 83% of their fluorine, providing evidence that the pollutants were being chemically broken down.

PFAS are widely used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, food packaging, and firefighting foam. Their exceptional durability also allows them to persist in soil, water, wildlife, and the human body. Exposure to certain PFAS has been linked to cancer, thyroid disorders, immune system problems, and reproductive health risks.

Conventional treatments capture PFAS using filters, membranes, or other materials, leaving contaminated waste that must still be managed. Researchers at Arizona State University and their collaborators instead developed a system that attacks the chemicals’ molecular structure.

“PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” said Bruce Rittmann, director of the Biodesign Swette Center for Environmental Biotechnology.

The challenge lies in the carbon-fluorine bonds that make PFAS exceptionally stable. “It’s called the strongest bond in organic chemistry,” Rittmann said. With fluorine atoms shielding the carbon backbone, ordinary degradation processes struggle to attack the molecules. “There’s really no place to get a start to break it down,” he explained.

The researchers created tiny membrane fibers coated with palladium nanoparticles. Hydrogen gas travels through the fibers to the palladium, which activates the hydrogen and helps it break carbon-fluorine bonds in PFAS molecules approaching from the surrounding water.

“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann said.

The system builds on earlier membrane technology that supplies hydrogen to pollutant-degrading bacteria. In the new approach, palladium replaces the microbes. During continuous testing, the technology successfully treated all six PFAS compounds examined. “We showed that this mechanism worked for all six,” Rittmann said. “It’s a universal mechanism.”

The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

PFAS contamination affects groundwater, wastewater, soil, and food supplies. Particularly high concentrations occur near landfills, airports, military bases, and facilities where PFAS-containing firefighting foams have been used.

“We all have PFAS in us,” Rittmann said. “They stay in the environment. They move up the food chain, and so they’re a big legacy problem.”

Although the 58-day test demonstrated sustained treatment, scaling up the technology presents challenges, particularly the cost of palladium. “Palladium is expensive,” Rittmann said. “It’s around $50,000 a kilogram” (about $22,700 per pound).

The researchers are working to reduce palladium requirements and explore combining the technology with existing filtration systems. They are also developing hybrid membranes that pair palladium with pollutant-degrading bacteria, allowing contaminants to be attacked through different mechanisms. “We’ve shown that this works too,” Rittmann said.

Reference: “Catalytic reactive-hydrogen membranes for rapid capture and hydrodefluorination of six PFAS of regulatory concern” by Min Long, Ai-Shi Wang, Welman C. Elias, Chen Zhou, Thomas P. Senftle, Michael S. Wong, Jie Cheng and Bruce E. Rittmann, 19 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2613985123

#6538. Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days on Prince Edward Island

Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

Recently I spent a few days exploring Prince Edward Island, a place that embraces its local foodways with gusto. There’s a complex history here, with roots in Indigenous Mi’kmaq, Acadian, Irish, Scottish, and other cultures. And if one thing unites these histories, it’s the island’s abundance of seafood and produce, which have helped earn it the nickname Canada’s Food Island. How can you not want to visit Canada’s Food Island?

On a stretch of land only about 140 miles long, you can eat oysters pulled out of nearby waters, potatoes grown on local farms, dig into a juicy burger made with PEI beef, and lick ice cream made with milk from the cows you pass along those famous red-dirt roads. That’s a lot of good eating packed into a place you can drive across in an afternoon.

I had to structure my visit, therefore, around where to dine, but also include a bucket-list visit to Green Gables Heritage Place. (I am a complete freak for L.M. Montgomery’s novel Anne of Green Gables, set on PEI around the turn of the last century.) I also had to schedule time at the PEI International Shellfish Festival, which promised endless trays of freshly shucked oysters and clams, hot buttered lobster rolls, steaming bowls of mussels, and plenty of entertainment, from shucking competitions and cooking demos to live music and dancing.

My husband and I rented a car and stationed ourselves in Charlottetown, the island’s main hub. Prince Edward Island is situated in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, just a hop away from Nova Scotia. You’re never far from the ocean here, and on a sunny day, the air seems to sparkle. The island is known for its red-sand cliffs and beaches, rolling landscapes, fishing harbors, and lighthouses. If you’ve read Anne of Green Gables, you’ll know just how pretty PEI is.

We landed late Thursday afternoon, ready to hit the ground running. With just shy of three days, I had carefully mapped out the places I wanted to visit, using Charlottetown as my base.

Charlottetown isn’t big, and most things here are walkable within 20 minutes or so. First stop in PEI: Slaymaker & Nichols, a gastropub and inn with the feel of an old-fashioned supper club. It takes its name from the 19th-century circus that once performed on the site. They take cocktail making seriously here. The summery feel of the day prompted me to try the watermelon mule, with hibiscus-infused vodka and chunks of pickled watermelon. I liked it, especially alongside the creamy lobster dip with tomatoes and harissa, and the buttery shrimp pil pil, with lots of tasty little spears of asparagus.

I was saving myself for my first lobster roll, which we grabbed up the street in an unremarkable spot. It was pretty mediocre, so I won’t go on about it. But after eating, we stopped into Reddins, a speakeasy that channels PEI’s Prohibition history in a dark, intimate third-floor bar with vintage furniture, good jazz, and whimsical cocktails. Our excellent bartender, AB, told us the space had once been a pharmacy where folks came during Prohibition to get their “medicine” — drugstores could legally dispense alcohol by prescription. We tried a few of the signature cocktails, and the one that stood out was the Pink Canary, with vodka, rose, lychee, citrus, and rosé bubbles, served in a small bathtub. Yup, you heard that right. It was sweet and awfully fun to sip.

Tip: You need a secret password to get in when you buzz from downstairs. You can get it online, or just do as we did and ask the hostess next door for help.

In the pouring rain, we made our way to nearby Victoria Row for breakfast at local roaster Receiver Coffee. Fuel for the day included strong coffee, a particularly good cup of Earl Grey cream tea, and the Ham Slam, a big fluffy cheddar biscuit layered with a runny fried egg, Black Forest ham, Swiss, and Dijon mayo.

We swung by the shellfish festival (more on that later) but the rain wasn’t welcoming, so we got back in the car and drove out to tiny and charming Victoria-by-the-Sea. When I say tiny, I mean it: The town is half a square mile, with a population under 200. Despite the town’s size, Landmark Oyster House, set there in an old general store with pretty green shingles and a steep gabled roof, thrives.

Our friendly waiter (everyone is abundantly friendly on PEI) suggested Raspberry Point oysters to start. They hit the spot: medium-sized, briny, and sweet, served with lemon wedges and freshly grated horseradish, which is now how I think every oyster should be eaten. We also tried the scallop dog, with buttery sweet scallops, bacon jam, red pepper aioli, and pickled shallots nestled in a toasted bun. It came alongside a very good, eggy potato salad.

After seeing the cheery lighthouse and visiting a couple of little gift shops, we popped into Island Chocolates, a family-run shop and café where bars and truffles are hand-crafted, often using local ingredients like haskap, a berry that tastes somewhere between a blueberry and raspberry. That fruity haskap truffle had a nice thick shell of milk chocolate.

Sun out? Check. We spent the afternoon at the festival and got a substantial fix of oysters and clams. The lobster rolls here were stuffed with unadorned lobster meat, then melted butter from a gigantic vat was ladled over the top.

For dinner, both our bartender and waiter at Slaymaker recommended North Shore Canteen in French River, a local haunt for sure. (A slew of chefs from the shellfish festival were two tables down from us.) The menu, which changes with the current haul, hit on the day’s best ingredients: halibut, striped bass, the aforementioned shellfish, beef, and potatoes. We opted for a very generous portion of local beef tartare, amazingly tasty with capers, roasted garlic, and freshly grated Parmesan, served with Covered Bridge potato chips. We wanted to try more PEI beef and opted for a juicy hanger steak with chimichurri and black garlic, which showcased it well. Dessert was a must: parsnip cake drizzled with caramel sauce for the win.

It was time for me to check Green Gables off my bucket list. This is an article about where to eat, so suffice it to say that if you’re a fan, this is 100 percent worth a visit to see the house, wander the Haunted Wood and Lover’s Lane, and taste some nonalcoholic raspberry cordial (IYKYK).

All that walking made me hungry, which was good because this was a much anticipated two-lunch day.

First stop: Blue Mussel Café, a bright and very welcoming, beloved PEI restaurant set just back from the water in Rustico Harbor. I think it’s obvious what to order, and for good reason: These are excellent mussels — plump, fresh, and brought to the table piled high in a large stainless steel bowl. You can have them prepared with rosemary and lemon or beer and wine. I’d rate them equally, but I did like the hit of rosemary. Melted butter comes in a small ramekin on the side; I used it to dip each mussel, and my husband poured it all over the top. I didn’t have it, but the other signature, seafood chowder, looked popular. It’s made with haddock, salmon, scallops, mussels, and PEI potatoes, and served with a giant biscuit. Noted for my next visit.

We hightailed it to our next meal because I had yet to have the perfect lobster roll. Richard’s Fresh Seafood in Covehead Wharf delivered. This is one of the island’s longest-running fish shacks, where you can savor fish and chips and beer on the deck overlooking the fishing boats, or camp out on the nearby beach under the lighthouse with a lobster roll. no mistake: This is the quintessential lobster roll. It was an exercise in abundance, packed with sweet lobster meat that managed to be chunky and fine, bound with lemon and chive mayo and tiny bits of onion, all stuffed in a buttery toasted bun. It came with crunchy coleslaw, crispy fries, and a paper cup of ketchup. There are other menu items, but this lobster roll alone is worth the trip to PEI.

For our final dinner, we drove back toward North Rustico Harbor to Rustico Cannery, which opened this past spring. The airy, modern space has giant windows and a big deck that takes in super sunset views.

I needed greens, and Rustico delivered. We had crisp romaine hearts with a creamy, spicy charred jalapeño dressing, lardons, Parmesan, and sourdough crunchies. My husband hit the jackpot with his dinner: panko crusted, pan-fried haddock with pickled beet remoulade, jalapeño relish, confit potatoes, and coleslaw.

A final note: Many places are seasonal, so check if they’re open if you’re visiting in cooler months.

#6537. What Could Split a Black Hole in Two?

We all know that black holes can collide. It has happened since black holes began to form, early in cosmic time. The result is always a clash that gives off gravitational waves and a giant bang. Since black holes have such strong gravity, it's almost impossible to imagine a way that any force could break one apart. Yet, that's the task that a group of scientists in Europe set for themselves.

In a study of possible mechanisms for black hole fragmentation, Francesco Sannino of the University of Naples Federico II in Italy and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark, along with Giacomo Cacciapaglia (Laboratoire de Physique ThÃ©orique et Hautes Ãnergies) and Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center, conducted a series of calculations showing that under the right conditions, a black hole could split up into two black holes. It's an unusual possibility, to say the least, but the team has calculated what needs to happen if such an event were to occur.

The two pieces would have to stay apart, according to Sannino. "The two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate," he said. If such a split-up could happen, the event horizon of the black hole would form a trouser-like shape as the split-up proceeded. Essentially, it would form two legs of a pair of pants, which is why the team called it a "pair-of-pants topology."

That's one possibility for what happens if/when a black hole splits into pieces. No one has seen such an event (yet), so it's still largely theoretical. There's one major impediment, however. That's called entropy, the measure of how many different microscopic ways a physical system can be arranged while still appearing the same from the outside. For example, a rock's shape can remain solid and static until some outside force changes it, such as heating. In the case of an ordinary, non-rotating black hole, breaking it into two pieces would reduce its entropy and make the process thermodynamically unlikely.

The black hole at the centre of M87. It has a measured spin, so theoretically, if conditions were right, it could break apart, according to a new study. Credit: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration

However, let's say we have a rotating black hole, spinning very rapidly. According to the team, such a system could break up into two pieces. However, they have to separate quickly, or risk falling back together. So, it turns out it could happen if both black holes have to keep rotating as fast as they possibly can (or close to it). But what would cause the split to occur? The answer lies in the rotation. It alters the relationship between black hole mass, its angular momentum as it spins, and entropy. It's possible that change could lead to the black hole fragmenting. If so, then the next steps are for the black hole "twins" to move apart and retain the momentum and speed of the original.

Focusing just on black holes, it seems pretty unlikely that such events have happened, but they don't want to say it's never happened. According to Sannino, the possibility is there, but in specific cases. "We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einsteinâs theory, and we are working to quantify this," he explained. "We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers."

When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies

#6536. Dry-Brined Turkey With Tangy Honey Glaze

This dry-brine turkey recipe produces a Thanksgiving centerpiece that’s full of flavor and juicy as heck. The brine is just kosher salt and brown sugar, applied at least 12 hours and up to 2 days ahead. The salt helps the meat retain moisture, while an uncovered rest in the fridge dries the skin for better browning—no bucket required.

Roasting the bird on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet (instead of a high-sided roasting pan) lets hot air circulate around it, encouraging browning all over. We’ve also done away with the turkey baster in favor of a buttery honey-vinegar glaze you’ll brush over the bird while it cooks. Fragrant with rosemary, garlic, and orange zest, with Worcestershire sauce for savory depth, the repeated brushing builds an even, glossy lacquer.

Let the cooked turkey rest uncovered for 30 minutes to 1 hour before carving. Resist the urge to tent it with foil, which traps steam and softens that hard-earned crispy skin. Use the downtime to put the finishing touches on your Thanksgiving side dishes.

What kind of turkey should I buy for dry-brining?

Choose an unseasoned turkey. Kosher, self-basting, and enhanced turkeys have already been salted, so adding this dry brine can make them overly salty. Check the label for an added salt solution before buying. A frozen turkey is fine; thaw it in the refrigerator for at least 24 hours before starting the brine.

No. In this recipe, the brine stays on the bird; Step 2 calls for rinsing the baking sheet and rack to prevent the drippings from becoming too salty, not the turkey. Follow the measurement for your brand of kosher salt, and don’t feel compelled to use every last grain of the mixture—the recipe intentionally makes extra.

Yes, but taste them first: The dry brine and glaze make these drippings especially flavorful, and they may be quite salty. Skim off the excess fat to make your roux, then add the juices a little at a time, followed by low-sodium chicken broth (or homemade unseasoned turkey stock).

Our Make-Ahead Gravy doesn’t need drippings, but you can stir some in as it reheats. Taste before adding salt.

Can I use a larger or spatchcocked turkey?

Yes, but not with the same roasting schedule. This dry brine recipe is written for a whole 12–14-lb. bird; a larger turkey or one that’s been flattened will cook differently. For a spatchcocked bird, follow our Spatchcock Turkey With Anise and Orange rather than transferring this recipe’s roasting and glazing times.

See why each step works in our guide to cooking Thanksgiving turkey →

4 hours 45 minutes, plus at least 12 hours brining

Place ½ cup Diamond Crystal or ¼ cup plus 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar in a small bowl and work together with your fingers until incorporated. Place one 12–14-lb. turkey, neck reserved for gravy, giblets discarded, on a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and pat dry with paper towels. (If you don’t have this setup, place your turkey on a V-shape rack set inside a large roasting pan.) Sprinkle salt mixture all over outside of the turkey as well as inside the cavity of the turkey, patting to adhere and nudging some into every crevice. You won’t need all of the dry brine, but it’s good to have extra since some of it will end up on the baking sheet as you season the turkey. Chill bird, uncovered, at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.

Remove turkey from wire rack and rinse baking sheet and rack if needed (turkey will most likely release some liquid onto pan). Line baking sheet with 3 layers of foil and set rack back inside. Place turkey, breast side up, on rack and tuck wings underneath. Let turkey sit at room temperature 2–3 hours.

Place an oven rack in middle of oven; preheat oven to 450°. Using your fingers, loosen turkey skin on breast. Work 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, under skin, spreading evenly over both breasts. Smear outside of turkey with another 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature.

Tie legs together with kitchen twine and pour 1 cup water into baking sheet.

Roast turkey, rotating pan halfway through, until skin is mostly golden brown all over, about 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook ¼ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. honey, 4 tsp. Worcestershire sauce, 3 sprigs rosemary, 3 garlic cloves, crushed, two 2x1" strips orange zest, and remaining 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, in a small saucepan over medium heat until bubbling and slightly thickened, about 5 minutes. Reduce heat to lowest setting and keep glaze warm.

Reduce oven temperature to 300° and continue to roast turkey, brushing with glaze every 30 minutes and adding more water by ½-cupfuls as needed to maintain some liquid in baking sheet, until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of breast near the neck registers 155° (don’t worry; the temperature will continue to climb while the bird rests), 65–85 minutes longer. Skin should be deep golden brown, shiny, and crisp. Transfer turkey to a cutting board and let rest at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour before carving.

Editor’s note: The dry-brine turkey recipe was first printed in our November 2018 issue as ‘Dry-Rubbed Roast Turkey.’ Head this way for more of our best Thanksgiving recipes →

#6535. NYC’s Hottest New Wine Bar Started With a DM Slide

An interview with the team behind El Camarón Peludo.

Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants. Throughout the year, we’ll check in with teams in Chicago, New York City, and Washington, D.C., to hear what it’s really like behind the scenes of a buzzy opening. Then, we’ll host exclusive meals at these restaurants as part of Dinner Party, presented by Capital One. Read along for challenges, candid reflections, and advice from the proprietors behind some of the country’s hottest new openings.

Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar spent the last five years slinging tacos at breakneck pace to keep up with the lines at Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez and rowdy World Cup crowds at Socceria. Now the duo is slowing things down a bit for their first full-service restaurant El Camarón Peludo, a playful wine and seafood spot in the West Village where guests linger over mariscos.

At the tiny, walk-in-only restaurant, the menu fuses Mexican seafood dishes with Spanish influences and excellent wine from around the world. For the project, Cervantes and Apolinar teamed up with chef Carlos Barrera, a Mexico City-born chef who has worked in Michelin-starred restaurants in Spain and hosted dozens of popular pop-ups around NYC. When I sat down with Cervantes and Apolinar, I planned to pick their brains about how and why they manage four wildly popular (and very different) New York City restaurants. Then I learned how much El Camarón Peludo was the result of fate: If it weren’t for space constraints, a tapas-fueled trip, and a social media superfan, the duo may have had an entirely different restaurant on their hands.

Pre Shift: Where did the idea for El Camarón Peludo come from?

Tania Apolinar: When we were looking at [the space], we considered making it a taqueria, but because of the [long shape of the restaurant], it wouldn’t have worked for that concept. We knew we wanted to do something different, focused on seafood and wine.

Giovanni Cervantes: I was in conversation with Carlos about this idea to serve mariscos in New York when we saw the space. We didn’t know [at the time], but we were setting up the basis of the menu because we were talking about what we like and what we miss a lot [from Mexico]. We also talked about [our past trips] to Europe. We were really interested in how to match [the style of European tapas and wine bars] with what we do, which is the Mexican approach.

How did you connect with Barrera for the project?

Cervantes: Carlos was one of the first clients that we ever had in Taqueria Ramírez. We met basically through that and through Instagram. He was always commenting a lot...

Cervantes: Exactly. Sending the flame emoji. Then soon enough, we find out that we were neighbors because he lives in Greenpoint, so we started seeing each other more often.

Apolinar: Then we did a pop-up with him serving his famous Trompo Negro, which is like al pastor with [a smoky black spice paste that is widely used in Yucatán and surrounding regions], and that was the first time we actually connected in a working setup. We’re really aligned and happy with the partnership.

Can you tell me about how you balance Mexican and Spanish influences on the menu?

Cervantes: When we found the space, we knew it was the perfect setup to try something different. Then we made a trip to Europe and a trip to Mexico. After we came back from Europe, I think I was feeling very “Europeanized.” I remember having a conversation with Tanya and Carlos about making it even more Spanish, and both of them were like, “What?” And I’m glad they [pushed back], because we definitely found the right balance.

Apolinar: We’re talking about Mexican and Spanish, but in the end, it’s about the seafood and the freshness, the product that we really want to stand out. That’s why [we serve a] very simple gambas a la plancha, and the carpaccio has that approach as well, but then other more Mexican classics [like tostadas topped with tuna or aguachile] have more sauces and all of that.

Cervantes: And it’s not just the food. The influence that we took from different parts of Europe is the setup, the vibe, the size of the plates, the type of space. We want the space to feel cozy and friendly.

How is the service different from your other spots?

Cervantes: At Taqueria Ramírez and Carnitas Ramírez, it’s all about efficiency. Making it right, as fast as you can, and getting people in and out of the place. It’s nonstop volume. The consistency is awesome over there, and that’s [how we] measure that we’re making it right. Here it’s different. It’s more about the experience of the space and the music and the wine. [Our staff are] with these people for an hour or two, so you try to make it personal in a way. It feels different when you have that much time to see how people are enjoying the experience and transporting people to that world through what we’re doing. That’s comforting to me.

Now that you have four different restaurants around the city, how do you balance your time between them?

Cervantes: For Taqueria Ramírez, the very first one, we can sleep very well because almost everybody on the staff has been there since we opened. I’m just mentioning that because it’s all about building the right team because you can only be in one place at a time. Then at Carnitas, our partners [Yvon de Tassigny and Kari Boden] are really great and the plan was for them to be the day to day operators from the beginning. So right now we’re between El Cameron Peludo and Socceria because they’re the new babies and there’s a lot of work to do there.

Tania: It’s tiring, but at the end of the day, I’ve been enjoying it a lot. It’s nonstop but it feels rewarding to see the point of view of customers and make people feel happy and connect to them.

#6534. Earth’s Oceans Were Slowly Suffocating Millions of Years Before a Devastating Mass Extinction

As today’s oceans lose oxygen, Alaskan rocks trace a similar decline that began millions of years before the end-Triassic mass extinction.

Dinosaurs survived the end-Triassic mass extinction 201 million years ago, but roughly 60 percent of Earth’s species did not. New evidence from Virginia Tech geologists suggests that the crisis in the oceans began about 8 million years earlier, when oxygen levels in shallow waters started to decline.

Scientists have long linked the extinction to enormous volcanic eruptions that tore apart landmasses, warmed the planet, and triggered widespread environmental changes. As temperatures rise, rocks break down faster, releasing nutrients that contribute to increasing ocean acidity. Warmer seawater also holds less dissolved oxygen, creating conditions that can lead to oxygen-depleted dead zones where marine organisms struggle to survive.

The combination of rising acidity and falling oxygen is “kind of like a one-two punch,” said geochemist Ben Gill. “It wouldn’t have been a very happy place to be.”

Although scientists had previously found evidence of widespread marine oxygen loss around the end-Triassic extinction, much of it came from a limited geographic area. Researchers still lacked a clear understanding of when the decline began and how extensively it affected the oceans. Recent studies had also raised the possibility that environmental conditions started deteriorating far earlier than previously believed.

“It’s a 200-million-year-old cold case,” said Kayla McCabe, a former Virginia Tech geosciences graduate student and first author of the study, published in Communications Earth & Environment.

To investigate, McCabe and her colleagues turned to sedimentary rocks at Grotto Creek in Alaska’s Wrangell–St. Elias National Park. The remote location is accessible only by small aircraft, and the team traveled there in 2017, 2019, and 2022 to collect evidence of ancient ocean conditions.

Sedimentary rocks form as layers of material accumulate over time, preserving chemical traces of the environments in which they were deposited. By comparing layers formed before, during, and after the extinction, the researchers could reconstruct how oxygen conditions changed across millions of years.

The geochemical analyses revealed a prolonged deterioration rather than a sudden collapse. The earlier decline likely placed marine ecosystems under stress long before the main extinction event. Conditions then worsened considerably during the extinction itself, with the rock record showing a much more severe loss of oxygen. The findings indicate that oxygen starvation became a major contributor to the disappearance of marine species.

What triggered the initial decline remains uncertain. The massive volcanic eruptions associated with the end-Triassic extinction have long been considered a major cause of the environmental catastrophe, but the newly identified timeline raises questions about what was happening millions of years beforehand.

“There’s evidence of another volcanic province that roughly lines up with this time interval,” Gill said. “But we’re in the very beginning of trying to understand what happened.”

The ancient rock record also offers a way to examine the potential consequences of environmental changes unfolding today. Modern oceans are experiencing rising temperatures, acidification, and declining oxygen levels. Ocean deoxygenation is an ongoing concern, including in coastal environments such as the Chesapeake Bay.

Although the ancient and modern circumstances are different, understanding how warming and oxygen depletion affected marine life in the past could help scientists anticipate the combined pressures facing ocean ecosystems today.

“Earth has run this experiment in the past. We have evidence that the climate gets warmer, and then all these other knock-on effects come afterwards,” Gill said. “It gives us some sense of what we can expect to happen.”

Reference: “Deoxygenation in the equatorial Panthalassan Ocean predated the end-Triassic mass extinction” by Kayla E. McCabe, Selva M. Marroquín, Andrew H. Caruthers, Jeremy D. Owens, Martyn L. Golding, Rachel E. B. Reid, Theodore R. Them II, João P. Trabucho-Alexandre, Yorick P. Veenma and Benjamin C. Gill, April 01 2026, Communications Earth & Environment. DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-03362-w

This research was supported with funding from the National Science Foundation, National Geographic Society, Alaska Geological Society, Virginia Tech Department of Geosciences, and the Virginia Tech College of Science Dean’s Discovery Fund.

“As temperatures rise, rocks break down faster, releasing nutrients that contribute to increasing ocean acidity.”

The oceans are NOT acidic, probably never have been except locally such as in stagnant pools enriched in hydrogen sulfide, and probably never will be, according to Stanford Professor Konrad Krauskopf who is considered by some to be the father of geochemistry.

It isn’t just the decomposition of carbonate rocks (e.g. limestone) by carbonic acid that results in the accelerated release of carbon dioxide. All chemical reactions are accelerated by warmth, including the silicate weathering that buffers pH declines in sea water.

My main complaint about research such as this is that I can’t be certain whether it is the result of a disingenuous attempt to convince the lay public that the oceans are acidic and becoming more so because of anthropogenic emissions, or that it reflects a defective educational system.

On the last day of an ecology field trip to Virginia's Eastern Shore, a biology undergraduate student discovered more than she expected. While searching for shark teeth, Brooklyn Rolph, a student at Mary Baldwin University in Virginia, stumbled upon a stone spearpoint estimated to be around 4,500 years old.

"Wow, this is so crazy," Rolph said in a statement. Already primed to look for pointy objects underwater, Rolph found a stone spear and immediately alerted the professors running the trip. "They were ecstatic," she recalled.

The stone artifact is about 6 inches (15 centimeters) long and, according to local archaeologists, a type known as a Lehigh/Koens-Crispin point. This kind of stone tool was made by Indigenous people across the East Coast of the U.S. from around 4,500 to 3,000 years ago. Sometimes called a "broadspear," the stone point also may have been used as a knife by prehistoric hunter-gatherers in the Late Archaic period.

The stone point is likely 3,000 to 4,500 years old.

The field trip was part of an ecology course led by Mary Baldwin University faculty members who had secured a permit from the state to explore the barrier islands off the Eastern Shore, the southern part of the Delmarva Peninsula that includes most of Delaware and parts of Virginia and Maryland.

Just after a lunch break on Sept. 21, the last day of the excursion that aimed to let students study plants and animals in the coastal ecosystem, Rolph set out to quickly explore a mound of shells on the island and noticed the spearpoint at the edge of an inlet. Her professors were blown away by the lucky discovery.

"The set of circumstances that came together that made this possible is quite unbelievable," Paul Callo, a biology professor at Mary Baldwin University who was co-leading the trip, said in the statement. "The tide was coming in, so the spear point was soon to be buried."

When Rolph showed Callo the artifact, he was "truly at a loss for words," he said. "It is certainly awe-inspiring to see and touch something that was made by human hands thousands of years ago."

The barrier island where Rolph found the stone point is part of a natural area owned by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, which means the artifact is now the property of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Archaeologists collected it from the Mary Baldwin group and have taken it to the Virginia Department of Historic Resources for further study.

Rolph was fine with not keeping the spearpoint. "That's how you get cursed!" she said.

#6532. Hera Probe Sees Asteroid Pair Separately for First Time

Planetary defense is a growing concern among the scientific community, as efforts have been made to design and implement missions meant to deflect incoming threats to the Earth well in advance. In 2022, NASA intentionally collided the Double Asteroid Redirection test (DART) planetary defense spacecraft into the smaller asteroid of the binary asteroid, Didymos and Dimorphos, with the latter being the smaller one. While the goal was to ascertain if deflecting an asteroid is feasible, how did this influence the geological characteristics of Dimorphos, and what can it teach us about planetary defense missions?

This is the task of a brave robotic explorer known as Hera, which is a spacecraft mission led by the European Space Agency (ESA) in cooperation with NASA and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Hera recently sent back its first image of Didymos and Dimorphos, which orbit each other as they orbit the Sun, with the image revealing the two asteroids separated, as opposed to seeing a single dot. This comes after Hera was launched in October 2024 and is now about 1,280 kilometers (795 miles) from the well-known binary asteroid, the latter of which is about 197 million kilometers (122 million miles) from Earth. While the larger Didymos is estimated to be 780 meters (2,559 feet) in diameter, the much smaller Dimorphos is estimated to be about 151 meters (495 feet) across.

âFor the very first time we are seeing through Heraâs own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for,â said Ian Carnelli, who is the ESA Head of the Systems Department and the Hera mission manager. âOur views will much grow sharper as Hera comes closer. We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos â the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action â on 25 November [2026].â

As noted, the goal of the Hera mission will be to conduct follow-up observations and data collection for NASAâs DART planetary defense mission. For this mission, the DART spacecraft intentionally impacted Dimorphos with the goal of ascertaining whether impacting an object could deflect it away from impacting Earth. The intentional impact occurred in September 2022 at 6.1 km/s (3.8 mi/s), resulting in not only slowing Dimorphosâ orbit around Didymos by 32 to 33 minutes, with the initial goal being at least 73 seconds. Thus, the mission was deemed a resounding success, and the researchers even observed an ejecta plume from the surface of Dimorphos as far as 10,000 kilometers (6,214 miles) into space.

Aristic rendering of Hera approaching Dimorphos. (Credit: ESA-Science Office)

Along with conducting observational analyses of the post-collision Dimorphos surface, Hera will also deploy two shoebox-sixed CubeSats named Milani and Juventas since Hera canât fly that close to the surface. While Milaniâs task is to perform a close-up mineralogical analysis of the DART impact site, Juventas will be tasked with using ground-penetrating radar to peer about 100 meters (328 feet) beneath Dimorphosâ surface to ascertain whether its interior is solid rock or a loose rubble pile which has been proposed by researchers.

As noted, planetary defense is rapidly becoming a growing concern among not only the scientific community, but governments worldwide. This is primarily driven by our growing awareness of the number of asteroids in our solar system that cross Earthâs orbital path, but also the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor that blew out windows and injured more than 1,500 people, primarily from broken glass. But with this concern comes how to address, and a combination of NASAâs DART and Hera missions are providing key insights into how to deflect potential asteroid impactors that could cause widespread death and destruction if one impacts Earth.

What new insights into Didymos and Dimorphos will Hera and other space missions make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6531. Scientists Reveal How 60% of Medieval Stories May Have Disappeared Forever

The medieval world may have produced far more stories of knights, legendary heroes, and epic adventures than historians will ever recover. A new study suggests that up to 60% of medieval chivalric works and more than 95% of their handwritten copies may have disappeared over the centuries.

Jean-Baptiste Camps and colleagues reached these estimates by combining computer simulations with historical evidence from approximately 2,000 medieval manuscripts spanning four centuries. Their research examines how stories survived through repeated copying, why others vanished entirely, and how much of a surviving work’s original history may be missing.

Before the printing press, preserving a literary work depended on scribes making copies by hand. Each new manuscript could introduce accidental errors, deliberate revisions, or adaptations for different audiences. These changes accumulated across generations, producing branching family trees resembling those used to trace evolutionary relationships in biology. Scholars call these textual genealogies stemmata.

The simulations suggest that a work’s earliest years were especially critical. When only a few copies existed, the loss of those manuscripts could cause the entire text to disappear. The authors describe this vulnerable early period as a “danger zone.” Producing numerous copies soon after a work’s creation could substantially improve its chances of surviving for centuries.

The researchers tested several scenarios, including steady copying rates, declining popularity, and sudden destruction of manuscripts during a major crisis. Depending on the scenario, their models estimated that just 1.4% to 4.4% of individual manuscripts survived, illustrating how extensive the losses could have been.

The disappearance of manuscripts did more than eliminate entire works. It also erased branches of the textual family trees that connect surviving copies to their origins.

The simulations indicate that surviving manuscripts often descend from later versions rather than directly preserving an author’s original text. The Song of Roland, one of the most famous medieval epics, may be an example. Its earliest form is probably lost, leaving scholars with later versions and rewritings that cannot fully establish what the original contained.

Historical events may have further influenced which stories endured. The Black Death, the Hundred Years’ War, and changing literary tastes could have disrupted manuscript production or contributed to the destruction of existing copies. Although the simulations demonstrate the substantial role chance can play, they do not establish which individual works disappeared because of particular historical events.

“Our results expose the fragility of cultural heritage and offer new tools to understand how randomness, historical contingencies, and human choices have shaped the legacy we inherit today,” the authors write.

Reference: “On the transmission of texts: Written cultures as complex systems” by Jean-Baptiste Camps, Julien Randon-Furling and Ulysse Godreau, 7 July 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag207

#6530. $22 Fries at Marcel Are One of New York's Finest Little Luxuries

This is Highly Recommend, a column dedicated to what we’re eating, drinking, and buying.

I recently celebrated a dear friend's birthday at Marcel 945 Madison, the much-buzzed about restaurant at Sotheby's global headquarters (RIP, old Whitney) on the Upper East Side of New York. Inside the Breuer Building, named for its Brutalist architect, it is a space to behold, equal parts concrete and midcentury walnut accents. Every detail—the luscious lighting, the forged flatware, the tufted mohair banquettes—is exquisitely considered and, likely, for sale.

In this beautiful room full of beautiful people, I could not take my eyes off the frites, priced at $22 under the "Accompagnements" section of the menu in Chroma sans serif type.

Skinny but not shoestring, long, golden, and perfectly salted, they practically glowed from within a napkin-lined bread basket. Every frite was pert, not a single one enervated under a mountain of hot fries. There was no oily outline at the bottom, either.

When I first saw the large portion, I felt a brief wave of doubt: Could we even finish these? How silly of me. We made quick work of the basket, with not a single spud left behind. These fries are so good, they do not need the crutch of a condiment—though they did reach another stratosphere when dipped in plain mayonnaise.

“I like them best with the chicken jus in the roasted chicken dish, or sauce au poivre with the filet de boeuf,” recommends Marie-Aude Rose, chef-partner at Marcel.

When people talk about life's little luxuries, they're talking about these frites. If the best McDonald's fries spent a transformative semester in Paris, they would be a little closer—but still untouchable—to Marcel's frites.

Is $22 pricy? Yes. But we're not talking about a paltry handful landing in a stainless steel cup lined with parchment. These are impeccable, best-in-class wonders, elegantly and generously presented.

I was so in awe that I had to know the deliberate thinking that must be responsible for such perfection. Rose says it is a long process. The kitchen begins with Idaho Russet, chosen not just for taste, but for length and sugar and moisture content that she calls “adequate to frying.”

The potatoes are cut with a French fry cutter, soaked in water, then dried and pre-fried in peanut oil at 160C (320F). During service, they are fried again in clean peanut oil at 180C (356F) and then seasoned with La Baleine fine sea salt, Rose’s salt of choice for seasoning all food at the restaurant.

"Time is important,” Rose said. “You cannot rush cooking.”

Please, chef, take all the time you need.

#6529. Space Outposts Beyond the Moon May Rely on Planetary AI

NASA plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028 for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972. But the famed agency has no intention of stopping there, as they plan to establish a permanent human presence on the Moon through a slow and meticulous process involving power, resource extraction, and habitat technologies. However, with the soaring use of artificial intelligence (AI) in our everyday lives, how could this emerging technology be used to identify new landing sites for future outposts on the Moon and possibly Mars?

Now, a team of researchers from The Ohio State University might have contributed to how AI can be used for future space outposts. As discussed in a recent study presented at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS 58) of the American Astronomical Society, the researchers introduced how a novel AI model could be used to both identify safe landing sites and develop a human outpost strategy at those landing sites. The model is called LUMINA, which is an agentic AI framework designed to help mission planners evaluate safe landing sites on the lunar surface, specifically focusing on key resources like water ice, along with potential scientific value.

To identify prime landing sites, LUMINA doesnât just rely on orbital images. It incorporates a myriad of lunar surface data, including topography and terrain hazards, scientific value, geology, surface properties, and even comparing the candidate landing sites to each other. As a result, LUMINA demonstrates a keen ability to identify landing sites across the lunar surface that could maximize mission success and effectiveness for both human habitation and science. But the researchers donât want to limit LUMINA to the Moon, as they envision LUMINA contributing to other planetary bodies, specifically Mars.

âAI systems are going to become critical tools for space exploration that will help humans analyze the millions of images and datasets that future missions will require,â said Gokce Inal, who is a PhD candidate in Civil Environmental and Geodetic Engineering at The Ohio State University and lead author of the study. âThis work is meant to serve as a bridge between those two worlds, AI and planetary science.â

LUMINA is built upon previous research by this same group called the Large Language-and-Vision Assistant for Lunar Exploration (LLaVA-LE), which demonstrated its ability to analyze and describe orbital images of the lunar surface. The LLaVA-LE model is currently available on arXiv, was recently presented at the CVPR2026 AI4Space Workshop in June 2026 and can be found on GitHub.

As noted, NASA has ambitious plans to establish a permanent human presence on the lunar surface with the long-term goal of sending humans to Mars. Developing the necessary technologies to accomplish both goals is part of NASAâs Moon to Mars Architecture, which is a constantly evolving strategic framework designed to develop and test vital technologies that will allow humans to work and live on the Moon that can then be used for human missions to the Red Planet. These technologies include power systems, transportation, habitation & life support, robotics & construction, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), communications, and more. The question then becomes how can AI, and specifically the LUMINA model, be used to further develop these technologies?

âNASAâs Artemis program creates important opportunities for our research,â said Inal. âAs new lunar data becomes available, their results can improve systems like ours and better support future mission planning.â

Of the technologies listed above, ISRU plays a crucial role in using local and available resources for crew use and survival. This includes water ice for drinking, bathing, fuel, and even oxygen from electrolysis, and using the lunar regolith to potentially grow plants and for construction. Also known as âliving off the landâ, ISRU aims to reduce, and potentially eliminate, the need for resupplies from Earth. Essentially, it wants to create a self-sustaining system exactly like life on Earth.

How will LUMINA help plan future space outposts on the Moon and Mars in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

As always, keep doing science & keep looking up!

#6528. Beyond the Iconic Potato Dish at New NYC Restaurant Somssi

There’s plenty of creative dishes coming out of this West Village kitchen

You’ve probably heard of the Potato Potato Potato dish at Somssi, the newest restaurant from Na:eun Hospitality. The triple-layered potato dish is the most labor-intensive dish on the menu but has also become the most popular order, with the kitchen going through up to 100 pounds of potatoes each week. The whimsical, caviar-topped dish really encapsulates what the restaurant is trying to achieve: “We should have serious food, serious hospitality, but we shouldn’t take ourselves too seriously,” says managing partner Ahris Kim. Here’s how the Somssi kitchen preps to create the newly famous potato and plenty of other dishes before a night of service.

Yukon gold potatoes are put through a ricer to become a cream and butter-heavy puree that is set in molds in the freezer. After being toasted in breadcrumbs, the logs of potato are wrapped in russet potato ribbons before being fried up to order.

Next is the ox tongue, which is brined for just over 16 hours before being slow-cooked in herbs, aromatics, and beef tallow for four hours. Huge cuts of tongue are carefully scored so they will get a great sear when they hit the grill. It’s served on a romesco sauce with just a bit of wasabi on the side.

Finally, pork loin is coated in ground shrimp for a creative schnitzel that is reminiscent of shrimp toast. The schnitzel is topped with a sweet-and-sour plum sauce that balances out the thick, crispy fried exterior. Scallop crudo is made up of pressed scallops surrounded with a strawberry sauce and topped off with gooseberries and peppers.

#6527. Hubble Uncovers a Mysterious 93-Billion-Mile Structure Hiding in a Nearby Star System

Astronomers have finally detected a mysterious, enormous dust structure in visible light, uncovering new details about what may be the remains of a violent collision between planetary bodies. Known as the “Cat’s Tail,” the feature stretches across as much as 1,000 astronomical units (about 93 billion miles) in the young Beta Pictoris star system.

Located 63 light-years from Earth in the constellation Pictor (which is Latin for “painter”), Beta Pictoris is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rocky debris. The Cat’s Tail was discovered in infrared observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, but had remained hidden from telescopes observing shorter wavelengths. Now, new Hubble Space Telescope images, combined with observations spanning more than 14 years, are helping astronomers investigate its composition, geometry, and possible origins.

“Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while,” said Arin Avsar, a doctoral student at the University of Arizona who led the research.

The explanation may lie in the dust itself. “We think the Cat’s Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it’s made of,” Avsar explained. “It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they’re quite black.”

The observations also suggest that the structure contains microscopic dust grains with an exceptionally porous, fluffy composition. Although the particles are only about a micron across, their internal structure is difficult to explain through conventional models of planetary collisions. “How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that’s part of why we study this feature,” Avsar said.

Beta Pictoris is roughly 20 million years old, making it a valuable laboratory for studying the turbulent environments in which planets develop. Its debris disk contains material left behind from planet formation, including particles produced when larger objects collide.

“The Cat’s Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies – think something like Pluto,” said Avsar, who works with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona’s Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory. Such an impact could have scattered enormous quantities of dust, although the exact process that produced the observed particles remains uncertain.

One possibility is that the impact generated enough heat to transform solid carbon into vapor, which later cooled and formed new particles. “It’s possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that’s how they became so porous,” said Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at Steward Observatory.

The new observations have also changed astronomers’ understanding of the Cat’s Tail’s position in space. Earlier interpretations suggested that the feature extended far behind Beta Pictoris from Earth’s perspective, creating the appearance of a long structure stretching away from the star.

By combining Hubble’s visible-light images with Webb’s infrared observations and computer modeling, the researchers developed a revised picture of its three-dimensional geometry. “We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat’s Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it,” Avsar said. “It’s essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it.”

The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, suggest that much of the structure’s apparent length lies across our field of view rather than extending deep into space. Its precise three-dimensional arrangement remains dependent on the models used to interpret the observations.

Using Hubble in a new observing configuration, the team also identified a previously unseen warp in the dust halo surrounding Beta Pictoris. The distortion may result from the gravitational influence of Beta Pictoris b, one of three known planets in the system and a gas giant approximately 10 times Jupiter’s mass.

“This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force,” Avsar said. “It’s a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units.”

Similar gravitational interactions likely occurred during the early history of our solar system. When the Kuiper Belt was about 20 million years old, it may have contained hundreds of Pluto-sized objects packed into a much denser region than exists today. Over time, the gravitational influence of the giant planets altered the orbits of many of these bodies, scattering some into different regions or ejecting them from the solar system entirely.

The Beta Pictoris observations provide a way to investigate comparable processes in a much younger planetary system, where collisions and gravitational disturbances are still shaping the distribution of material around its star.

Reference: “Deep HST/STIS Coronagraphic Imaging of the β Pictoris Debris Disk: On the Scattered Light Component of the Cat’s Tail” by Arin M. Avsar, Kevin Wagner, Dániel Apai, Isabel Rebollido, Antranik A. Sefilian, Marshall D. Perrin, Christopher C. Stark, Gabriel Weible and András Gáspár, 7 October 2026, The Astrophysical Journal Letters. DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/aeac4a
