#6526. Ceres' Water Ice Can Mask Massive Surface Salt Deposits

The dwarf planet Ceres is arguably one of the most overlooked and underappreciated planetary objects in the entire solar system. This could be because while Ceres has the same dwarf planet designation as Pluto, Ceres is largely considered an âasteroidâ since it resides the in main asteroid belt. However, along with being the largest object in the main asteroid belt, Ceresâ mass comprises between 25 to 30 percent of all the mass of the entire main asteroid belt. Despite its lack of recognition, Ceresâ interior is layered like most rocky planets, including Pluto, and its surface displays evidence of past water ice activity (also called cryovolcanism) with several âbright spotsâ, which are highly reflective salt deposits. But what can these salt deposits teach scientists about Ceresâ formation and evolution?

Now, a pair of researchers from the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) might have inched our way to better understanding a connection between Ceresâ water ice activity and surface salt deposits. As discussed in findings published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets (JGR: Planets), the researcher presented evidence that past data might have been incorrect regarding the amount of salt deposits previously observed by NASAâs Dawn spacecraft, which explored Ceres from 2015 to 2018.

For the study, researchers used a combination of Dawn spacecraft data and a series of computer models to examine the evolution of surface water ice and salt deposits on Ceresâ surface. The primary motivation behind the study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding observational results of surface water ice and salt deposits versus whatâs actually happening. Specifically, this study focused on the transition of water ice to salt deposits through evaporation (scientifically called sublimation) and whether data collected from Dawn accurately estimated the amount of water ice and salt.

In the end, the researchers found that the salt deposits might be hidden by the water ice deposits theyâre mixed with, with the salt deposits potentially existing in larger amounts than previously hypothesized, estimated to be between 30 to 50 percent greater. Additionally, they found that landslides (scientifically called mass wasting) contribute to more surface ice being exposed, which then evaporate, leaving behind the salty bright spots observed by Dawn. They note some water ice deposits could have been observed by Dawn that could have been recently exposed from landslides.

âWe proposed a qualitative model of long-term surface evolution of Ceres' salty ices based on observations that is akin to thermal segregation [sorting] on icy satellites,â the study notes. âIce in deposits with salts sublimates more readily and may move to colder areas, resulting in a feedback that creates compositional differences between colder, icy surfaces and warmer, salt-richer regions. Ongoing replenishment of ice at the optical [visible] surface is required to reconcile multiple detections with geologically negligible lifetimes of ice. The finding resolves an existing paradox about how salt-rich deposits arise in the Ceres near-surface; they are likely not initially salt-rich but instead result from enrichment of salt at the optical surface by sublimation of salty ices.â

Essentially, the salt-water ice deposits are sorted based on heat and evaporation, the salt within water ice mixture causes the water ice to evaporate faster, leaving behind the salt deposits. This creates a feedback loop that results in different mixture amounts and types among separate water ice and salt deposits. Additionally, the surface water ice is exposed from landslides, adding to this evaporation feedback loop. Finally, the study fills a longstanding misunderstanding between how salt deposits are formed and evolve, in that they donât start out with heavy amounts of salt. Instead, they start out with low amounts of salt but have their salt contents increase from the evaporation of water ice that also contains salt.

What new insights into Ceresâ salt deposits and water ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6525. How Flavored Syrup Became a Coffee-Shop Culture War

For some coffee shop customers, premade syrups are now a major red flag. It presents a new opportunity for small business owners.

In a TikTok video with over 82,000 likes, the person behind the camera zooms into the shelves at a Pennsylvania coffee shop, three rows stacked with an array of Torani syrups in flavors like blueberry, brown-sugar cinnamon, English toffee, and salted caramel. “I just know my latte isn’t going to be good,” the caption reads. Across social media, similar sentiments appear. “If I see these at a cafe, I’m walking out immediately,” says one tweet, co-signed by many commenters. In a multipart video series, another creator documents her journey of replacing all of her Torani syrups with ones from small businesses instead. Last year, the niche food newsletter Unsnackable published what was described as a “Torani tirade.”

It’s not just a Torani problem, though the brand — by virtue of its market dominance — tends to get the most flack on social media. While some people seem to prefer competitor Monin, it, too, draws backlash over allegations of tasting “like chemicals.” The problem, for some drinkers of dessert-like specialty beverages, is premade syrups across the board.

For a certain sect of consumers, they’ve become a coffee shop red flag, a sign that a so-called “specialty” establishment asking them to fork over $8 plus tip for a latte is unfairly cutting corners when it comes to quality or craft. For these consumers, mass-market syrups now symbolize exactly that: They’re synonymous with coffee chains and corporations, the kind of impersonal institutions that many people are trying to get away from when they patronize a small business. The flip side: For independently owned coffee shops across the country, house-made syrup now represents a major opportunity.

When Carrie and Dennis Medina first envisioned their coffee shop, Room Service, in Ventura, California, they thought they would take an approach similar to the one at Sightglass Coffee, where they’d both gotten their start. “Very purist, with no syrups, no specialty drinks,” Dennis says. They imagined eight kinds of pour-over coffee and an emphasis on single-origin beans, since the couple also runs a roastery. “We said we’re never gonna do cream tops; we’re never gonna do these crazy drinks,” Carrie says. But in the first week alone, every customer was asking for them.

Now, Room Service offers 10 to 12 different syrups at any given time (and six different cream tops), all of them made in-house. It offers drinks such as a cinnamon roll latte topped with a cinnamon roll, and a honey cornbread latte with an ube cream top. “I hear that question all the time,” Dennis says. “‘Hey, do you guys make your syrups in-house?’” To him, a shop that isn’t trying to do at least the basics — like vanilla — in-house is “falling behind what the times are pushing for.”

The demand for syrups and other embellishments is so intense that the Medinas have brought on a full-time prep person who works exclusively on “all these things that we do in-house that make us special,” Carrie says. Room Service’s PSL, for example, starts with kabocha squash. It’s roasted, blended with spices such as cloves and cinnamon, and cooked into syrup, a process that takes two days. Echoing a sentiment that seems common among coffee shop owners right now, Carrie describes their current approach as “not necessarily the coffee shop we wanted, but it’s more like the coffee shop we have to be.” And if the market demands syrups and cream tops, then the Medinas wanted to ensure that the intention and emphasis on quality that they applied to their coffee beans also carried over.

In 2025, Michael Smith opened Trust Coffee Co. in Bay Village, Ohio, taking over, remodeling, and rebranding an older coffee shop. He, like the Medinas, imagined a more “pour-over, third-wave” style establishment. “But I’ve been a business owner for a long time,” says Smith, who also runs a restaurant and a catering business. “I’ve realized over the years that your customers tell you more about who you are than who you actually think you are.” His customers, it turned out, wanted seasonal syrups in niche flavors like maple rosemary, caramelized banana, and strawberry rhubarb.

The purist is no longer coffee’s north star; the maximalist is.

Syrups like Monin, which the shop’s previous iteration used, “serve a purpose in the industry,” Smith says, but he wanted more control over the menu. The two full-time pastry chefs from Smith’s other businesses oversee the shop’s syrups. “It’s become such a huge thing,” he says: Every time Trust’s social media manager posts a new syrup, the line is out the door for a week. “It sets us apart,” he explains.

When Sabrina Kaylor opened the first location of Bizarre Coffee in Canton, Georgia in 2020, the shop used bottled syrups. She hadn’t worked in coffee prior, and she said that approach felt like the norm at the time. “It allowed us to hone our craft and learn what we were doing,” she says. Over time, Kaylor — who’s quite active on the company’s official social media platforms — noticed that the tenor of the conversation was changing: In the immediate post-COVID years, people were making more things at home and there was more pride to be gained in “scratch-made.” With her business becoming known for lattes in flavors such as blueberry, banana, and guava, Kaylor decided to shift toward more house-made syrups. Previously, her customers didn’t ask about their sourcing, but now, they ask all the time.

As much as there is a sense of valor in the entirely from-scratch approach, Kaylor retains some skepticism about the current torrent of Torani and Monin backlash. Today, 90 percent of Bizarre’s drinks use house-made syrups, though one of its best-selling drinks still relies on the bottled stuff; Bizarre’s menu is extensive and making everything in-house would be a significant investment of labor. On the part of coffee shops, “I think a lot of [the house-made syrup conversation] is marketing, quite honestly,” Kaylor says. As for the bandwagoning that is all the anti-Torani memes, “I think it’s part of consumer behavior,” she says. And that, she acknowledges, can be really “discouraging” for small business owners.

In a sense, that’s what the premade-versus-house-made-syrup conversation boils down to: the stand between small businesses and big ones. For more consumers, the economic and social conditions of the current moment have inspired increased skepticism toward the influence of corporations and private equity in the food and beverage world.

The Minnesota coffee shop Little Joy has become famous across social media for posting the recipes of its signature drinks in detailed DIY videos. It has since launched a membership program through which other coffee shop owners can purchase its recipes, scaled up for commercial usage; gain access to training videos; and sell its drinks without even needing to attribute them to Little Joy, though the ones that would like to can pin their use of Little Joy’s recipes to a Drink Finder map.

Yes, these might just be recipes for syrups and foams, but in an interview with Eater’s industry newsletter Pre Shift earlier this year, Little Joy owner Cody Larson described the system as a way to build solidarity among independent businesses. “The big coffee chains, they’re never gonna do house-made syrups, so I think that’s where independent shops can get a leg up,” he said. “Ultimately, the chains are our competition... If independent shops can, in any way possible, raise the bar across the board, that’s good for all independent shops, including us.”

It’s hard to look at the drinks coming out of specialty coffee shops today — fluffy with foam, flavored to emulate nuanced desserts like princess cake and tiramisu— and not think of the Starbucks Frappuccino. The combination of app-ordering and social media “hack” culture have mainstreamed super-elaborate beverage requests, allowing Starbucks and coffee chains like it to become purveyors of highly complicated customizable beverages, mainstreaming the mindset of the aforementioned “hyperflavor.”

When it comes to why consumers have moved away from the single-origin pour-over approach at shops like his, “my guess is that these are a lot of people who used to be Starbucks loyalists and they’re looking for something that’s more local,” Smith says. “It’s a trend across everything where people want local, and we’re able to provide what Starbucks did, but in a more high-quality, more local way.”

Intentionality is what people are gravitating towards, especially as prices rise. If consumers are spending so much on a drink that’s undeniably a luxury, then they want to know that every part of that drink has been made carefully. And if they’re going to make the trip to a new, independent shop, they want to know that the offerings there aren’t the ones they can get anywhere, made with easily attainable, big-brand flavorings. For small coffee shops, the key to success could be as simple as syrup.

#6524. Researchers Discover a New Way To Control Magnetism Without Changing a Material’s Chemistry

Neutron experiments have uncovered an unexpected connection between magnetic structure and electrical behavior.

A gentle squeeze can change the magnetic structure of certain crystals and alter their electrical behavior. Scientists at the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) demonstrated this effect in altermagnets, an emerging class of magnetic materials being investigated for advanced electronics.

Using neutron beams to examine the materials at the atomic scale, the researchers found that mechanical strain could shift their magnetic organization and influence an electrical response associated with electron transport. The findings, published in back-to-back papers in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials, point to a possible method for controlling magnetic properties without altering a material’s chemical composition.

The researchers placed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between two titanium plates and applied mechanical pressure. They then used neutron diffraction at ORNL’s Spallation Neutron Source to investigate how the strain affected magnetic domains, regions within a material that have different orientations of magnetic order.

The measurements showed that squeezing the crystals changed the relative populations of these domains. The researchers also detected changes in the anomalous Hall effect, an electrical response that produces a voltage perpendicular to the direction of an applied current. Together, the results connect changes in magnetic domain organization with changes in electrical transport behavior.

“By controlling the magnetic domains, we can directly influence the transport behavior, and that opens the door to exploring these materials for spintronic technologies,” said Pengcheng Dai of Rice University, a former neutron scientist at ORNL.

Altermagnets are attracting research interest because their unusual magnetic properties could support spintronics, a technology that uses electron spin alongside electrical charge to store and process information. Conventional electronics relies on electron charge, while spintronics could provide additional ways to control information in electronic devices.

Developing practical spintronic technologies requires materials whose magnetic and electronic properties can be reliably manipulated. Altermagnets are among the candidates being explored for potential applications ranging from wireless communications to quantum computing. The ORNL experiments suggest that mechanical strain could offer another way to adjust these properties, although translating the findings into working devices will require further research.

“What’s exciting is that one creative experimental idea — a small mechanical squeeze between two plates — can reveal entirely new magnetic behavior and push the field forward, and neutron scattering plays such a critical role, revealing the underlying change in magnetism,” said Feng Ye, an ORNL neutron scientist and co-author of both studies.

“Uniaxial Strain Tuned Magnetism of the Altermagnet Candidate H-FeS” by Weiliang Yao, Feng Ye, Zachary J. Morgan, Douglas L. Abernathy, Ruixian Liu, Sijie Xu, Yuxiang Gao, Kevin Allen, Yuan Fang, Emilia Morosan, Qimiao Si and Pengcheng Dai, 6 August 2026, Advanced Materials. DOI: 10.1002/adma.74398

“Strain-Tunable Anomalous Hall Effect in Hexagonal MnTe” by Zhaoyu Liu, Sijie Xu, Jonathan M. DeStefano, Elliott Rosenberg, Tingjun Zhang, Jinyulin Li, Matthew B. Biological Pre-Ribosome Assembly & Gravitational Reconnection: Across all these examples—from cellular field locking down to 4D gravitational field sheet reconnection—mainstream models keep discovering that phase, orientation, and geometric strain control energy flow, rather than particle statistics or static chemical affinity.

#6523. Martian Polar Crater Ice Shifts with Seasonal Frost

The planet Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with the Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms and dust devils, and water ice. But one feature that Earth and Mars share among the eight planets in our solar system are polar ice caps. Both are one of each planetâs striking features, but the major difference is while Earthâs polar ice caps are both comprised of water, Marsâ north polar ice cap is only comprised of water while its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. The reasons for this are determined by altitude, but Marsâ northern polar ice cap is one of the most studied regions primarily due to its water ice composition. But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Marsâ climate history?

Now, an international team of researchers might have shed new light on this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, the researchers challenged our understanding of ice deposits in Marsâ northern polar ice cap region. The primary motivation behind this study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding the seasonal changes in Martian polar ice deposits, specifically focusing on craters. The researchers note that better understanding seasonal changes in polar ice cap deposits could help gain insights into long-term climate changes on the Red Planet.

For the study, the researchers analyzed images of 36 craters within the northern polar ice cap region of Mars. The images were obtained from NASAâs Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera between 2006 and 2025. This time period is also referred to as Mars Years (MY) 28â38 since one year on Mars is 668 Earth days. The goal of the study was to identify how polar ice deposits on crater floors changed with seasons, specifically whether the deposits increased or decreased in size based on winter or summer months, respectively.

In the end, the researchers found that 32 of the 36 craters exhibited changes in bright deposits, broadly indicating ice deposits are expanding and shrinking with the seasons. Of the remaining four craters, the researchers didnât observe changes in brightness. The researchers note that seasonal frost deposits on the outside of each crater could be responsible for the changes in brightness.

âNot all craters exhibit changes in frost coverage from one Mars year to the next,â the study notes. âFor a given Mars year, only a subset of craters show altered frost conditions relative to previous years, while others maintain similar or nearly identical frost extents. This spatial heterogeneity suggests that seasonal frost cycles and interannual mass balance are localized processes rather than cap-wide phenomena. Local topography, crater geometry, and microclimatic conditions likely modulate energy balance and vapor transport, leading to crater-specific responses to broader climatic forcing.â

Essentially, the researchers found the changes in crater ice deposits are triggered by local climate changes, as opposed to being triggered by larger climate changes. The reason why understanding Marsâ climate changes is important is to help pin down specific triggers, whether itâs seasonal or related to other factors. For example, Mars experiences much larger climate changes on grander scales compared to Earth due to the Red Planetâs planetary tilt having much larger swings than Earth. However, as this study demonstrates, local climates are still capable of delivering their own changes disconnected from the larger climate picture. This study identifies seasonal changes in polar ice deposits while providing motivation for future modeling work that could help expand our understanding of localized climates on Mars.

What new insights into Mars polar crater ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a new dwarf planet in our solar system, orbiting the sun on an inclined plane past Pluto.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what might be a tiny new world in the far reaches of our solar system, hidden beyond the orbit of Neptune — and it is among the largest and brightest objects ever discovered beyond Neptune.

If confirmed, the miniature world would increase the number of officially recognized solar system dwarf planets to six. Upper estimates of the object's size place it at more than half the diameter of Pluto, the largest known dwarf planet.

"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Matthew Holman, an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and member of the Rubin team who wrote the code that helped discover the prospective dwarf planet, said in a statement. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

The potential dwarf planet, designated 2026 ED138, orbits the sun at roughly 46 times the distance between Earth and the sun. The potential new planetoid has been hiding behind galactic camouflage; with its orbit tilted at a 25-degree angle from the solar system plane, it's at just the right angle to get lost in the light from the inner Milky Way, the researchers said.

Many telescopes struggle to see past the millions of stars making up our galaxy's bulge. The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, however, images the entire southern sky every few nights with the largest digital camera ever built, sending out millions of nightly alerts for every object that has changed brightness or position. This makes it exceptional at identifying anything that moves, from solar system objects to transient events like supernova explosions.

The observatory had only just begun its 10-year mission of scanning the sky in July, and ED138 stood out in the data.

Holman works on the software algorithms that process the extreme amounts of data the observatory collects. The code he developed with his colleague, Kevin Napier, compares billions of observations to determine which ones are detections of the same moving object. Running data from Rubin through the code revealed the unusually large object.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By looking at past data from Rubin and archival images from the Dark Energy Camera mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (both in Chile), the team was able to map out ED138's orbit over the past 10 years.

The Kuiper Belt is a region of the solar system beyond Neptune that is a wild frontier of small, mostly icy bodies made from frozen methane, ammonia, water and rock. It ranges from roughly 30 to 50 times the distance between Earth and the sun, and is home to most of the known dwarf planets, including Pluto. Thousands of Kuiper Belt objects have already been discovered. These space rocks can be frozen time capsules that hold clues about the early solar system's formation.

A model of the solar system showing the five dwarf planets officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) and the orbit of the newly discovered dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138.

Dwarf planets are the largest Kuiper Belt objects that we know of. Bigger than asteroids but not quite planets, dwarf planets are big enough to be rounded under the force of their own gravity but too small to clear their orbits like planets do. While the International Astronomical Union (IAU) has officially confirmed five dwarf planets — Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake — astronomers studying dwarf planets often recognize at least nine, with several more candidates whose properties are still unknown.

Depending on which astronomer you ask, there could be anywhere from a handful to hundreds of dwarf planets in this part of the solar system. Identifying which Kuiper Belt objects are dwarf planets is tricky because they are often very dim and move very slowly from Earth's perspective, since their orbits are so large and distant. The likeliest candidates have high albedo (surface reflectivity) and diameters greater than roughly 370 to 500 miles (600 to 800 km).

What makes ED138 special is its size, inferred from its brightness, albedo and distance from the sun. It's estimated to have a diameter between 370 to 930 miles (600 to 1,500 km). For comparison, Pluto — the largest dwarf planet recognized by the IAU — is 1,477 miles (2,377 km) in diameter. Ceres, the smallest IAU-recognized dwarf planet, is 595 miles (958 km) in diameter. Future observations of ED138 will give researchers a more accurate idea of its diameter and density to determine if it's round enough to join the dwarf planet club.

"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said in the statement. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for ten years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."

#6521. New Research Resolves the Mystery Behind Van Gogh's The Starry Night

Starry Night, the iconic painting by legendary Impressionist Vincent Van Gogh, has inspired debate among art historians and astronomers for decades. Was the painting something that Van Gogh was spontaneously inspired to create in the early morning hours in July 1889, or did it present a realistic depiction of the night sky over Saint-RÃ©my (where he painted it)? According to a recent study conducted jointly by South Korean telescope manufacturer SLLAB and the School of Space Research at Kyung Hee University, it's the latter.

For over a century and a half, scholars focused primarily on religious and symbolic interpretations of the painting. It was not until the mid-1980s that studies were presented that analyzed its astronomical aspects. These were conducted by UCLA art historian Albert Boime (1984) and Harvard astronomer Charles Whitney (1986), who examined celestial correspondences and proposed constellation identifications based on a mid-June date. However, the two reached conflicting conclusions, and no studies since have examined the painting using observational geometry.

The study, presented in Scientific Reports (a Nature journal), instead narrows the dates on which a crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades star cluster (which appear closely together in the painting) fell within Van Gogh's field of view. The study's first author, Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, has spent years building telescopes and observing the night sky and was inspired to weigh in on the debate.

(a)The stars in The Starry Night (1889) overlaid by the real stars after matching for size, orientation, and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences. (b) The stars in CafÃ© Terrace at Night (1888), left, and the stars around the Summer Triangle. Credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports

"To an observational astronomer, the cluster of stars in The Starry Night is the Hyades in Taurus," he said. "But the moment I read the earlier studies explaining it as Aries, I heard the painting calling to me." The research builds on Kim's previous book (released in 2025) and began with two field trips to France in 2019 to gather additional evidence and add quantitative data. Traditionally, the painting was dated to June 18th, 1889, based on a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother, Leo.

However, on that date, the Moon was in its waning gibbous phase, which does not match the slender crescent in the painting. On July 22nd, the Moon was a crescent, and the Hyades cluster would have been seen rising in the east alongside Venus (placing it in the Taurus constellation). In the past, that date was thought to be one when Van Gogh experienced one of his seizures, but cross-analysis of the original French and Dutch letters and the details mentioned in both suggests his seizure began in late July.

Using on-site photographs taken in Arles, the team verified Van Gogh's field of view overlooking the RhÃ´ne River. Afterward, they traveled to Saint-RÃ©my, where they located the spot where Van Gogh drew the landscape in preparation for his painting. They then conducted a statistical shape analysis to confirm that the five central stars in the painting corresponded to the Hyades cluster, which matched even more closely in the pen drawing Van Gogh made after he finished the painting.

These results suggest that the sky in the painting was based on actual observation rather than pure impressionist feeling. The methods employed could also be extended to other historical night paintings, leading to collaborative efforts between astronomers and art historians. The team has already used the same method on another of Van Gogh's famous creations that features stars in the sky - CafÃ© Terrace at Night (painted in 1888) - and found a possible match to the Summer Triangle asterism.

"I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-RÃ©my paintings, and at Van Gogh's movements that summer," Kim said. "Our conversation with Van Gogh's other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one."

#6520. A Hidden Nanoscopic Effect Is Disrupting Some of the World’s Most Sensitive Sensors

Nanomechanical resonators are vital to precision sensing and emerging quantum technologies, but their extraordinary sensitivity comes with an unexpected vulnerability.

A nanomechanical device can lose much of its ability to sustain vibrations without ever touching another object. Researchers at EPFL have discovered that placing insulating materials just a few hundred nanometers from these tiny structures can dramatically increase energy loss, reducing their mechanical quality factor by as much as tenfold.

The findings, published in Nature Physics by scientists in the group of Tobias J. Kippenberg, identify a previously underappreciated limitation for ultrahigh-precision sensors and quantum technologies. The source of the problem is an electrical interaction that allows energy to escape across an otherwise empty gap.

The mechanism begins with static electric charges trapped inside a mechanical resonator. As the structure vibrates, those charges move with it, producing a changing electric field in the surrounding space. When an insulating material such as silicon dioxide or silicon nitride is nearby, the fluctuating field interacts with the material and causes energy to dissipate through its small electrical losses.

This process is related to “noncontact friction,” a phenomenon previously observed in atomic force microscopy. Although the surfaces never touch, mechanical energy is transferred away from the vibrating structure. The resulting damping lowers its quality factor, which measures how efficiently a resonator stores vibrational energy rather than losing it.

The researchers developed a theoretical model predicting that lower-frequency vibrations would experience greater energy losses. To test this, they studied silicon nitride strings suspended approximately 500 nanometers (0.00002 inches) above a dielectric layer. By measuring how quickly different vibrational modes decayed, they confirmed that the lowest-frequency modes suffered the strongest additional damping, consistent with the model.

A second experiment examined resonators designed for exceptionally high quality factors. The team positioned vibrating strings between photonic crystal cavities, with separations of only a few hundred nanometers (roughly 0.00001 inches). As the gaps narrowed, the quality factor declined sharply, sometimes falling by a factor of ten. The researchers also demonstrated that their modeling approach could reproduce the effects of trapped charges in these more complicated device geometries.

Nanomechanical resonators are microscopic vibrating components fabricated on chips, operating at frequencies from a few kilohertz to several gigahertz. Their sensitivity makes them useful for detecting extremely small changes in mass, force, temperature, and pressure. They also serve as components in radiofrequency filters and chip-based clocks. Advanced versions can even be used to prepare quantum states of comparatively large mechanical objects and investigate fundamental physics.

Many of these applications require resonators to operate extremely close to other structures, particularly when measuring motion or coupling mechanical vibrations to light and electrical systems. The EPFL results show that trapped charges and dielectric losses must be considered when designing such closely integrated devices, even when no physical contact occurs.

The same interaction could also have practical uses. By measuring how mechanical vibrations lose energy near insulating surfaces, researchers may be able to characterize electrical losses in thin films or develop controlled interactions between mechanical resonators and other electrical systems. Understanding these effects could help engineers preserve mechanical coherence while integrating increasingly sensitive resonators into complex quantum and sensing devices.

Reference: “Non-contact friction in ultracoherent nanomechanical resonators near dielectric materials” by Amirali Arabmoheghi, Alessio Zicoschi, Guillermo Arregui, Mohammad J. Bereyhi, Yi Xia, Nils J. Engelsen and Tobias J. Kippenberg, 7 July 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03350-z

Funding: Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF)

Non-Contact Boundary Drag and Spatial Impedance Leaks

Recent research out of EPFL’s laboratories (led by Tobias J. Kippenberg’s group) has identified a hidden limitation affecting state-of-the-art nanomechanical resonators and quantum sensors. These ultra-sensitive nano-strings boast vanishingly low internal thermal noise and near-zero physical friction, yet scientists discovered that they experience unexpected energy losses. Even when surfaces never touch, the nano-strings interact with electrical and mechanical drag from nearby objects across empty microscopic gaps, causing their quality factor to plummet by up to a factor of ten.

Mainstream physics identifies this as non-contact electrical interaction and charge-trapping across empty boundaries. When evaluated through continuous field dynamics and the Torsion Hill Framework, this discovery highlights a critical baseline rule of spatial impedance:

The Illusion of Empty Space: Conventional engineering treats an empty gap as a total insulator—a void where mechanical and electrical fields terminate. Under field mechanics, space is a continuous medium. An adjacent static surface introduces an abrupt local spatial impedance profile (Z_T), meaning that a vacuum gap does not isolate a vibrating structure from surrounding boundary forces.

Non-Contact Boundary Drag as grad Z_T Interference: When a nano-string oscillates, its mechanical motion generates localized torsional and spatial pressure waves. If a nearby boundary introduces an un-optimized impedance mismatch, field energy bleeds across the gap. This leakage acts as an invisible aerodynamic brake, degrading the resonator’s coherence without physical contact.

Two-Layer Isolation (Ribbon Substrate & Surface Coating) – EPFL Laboratory Link: To protect these nanomechanical sensors, EPFL’s research parameters can be met by deploying a dual-layer boundary configuration along the surrounding chamber walls—strictly isolating the cavity walls rather than coating or covering the active vibrating sensor itself, which would add mass and destroy resonance. Remarkably, the same Kippenberg laboratory at EPFL exploring these non-contact boundary leaks is renowned for pioneering the ultra-precise dual-layer ribbon and surface-coating fabrications needed to decouple mechanical stress, smooth out local spatial impedance steps (delta Z_T), eliminate charge-trapping, and prevent field leakage across microscopic gaps.

The Limit of Precision: Whether observing macroscopic gravitational field sheets, strain-tuned altermagnets, or EPFL’s nanomechanical resonators, precision is never limited solely by internal material friction. It is governed by how effectively boundaries are managed to maintain rotational phase clearance (Omega_pi) and eliminate spatial impedance drag. #6519. Researchers May Have Solved a Puzzling Contradiction in the Ryugu Sample

The Solar System's asteroids are sometimes referred to as fossils because they preserve evidence of the conditions when the Solar System formed. Asteroids are critically different than their planetary counterparts. On the rocky planets, the rock itself has been subjected to billions of years of change. On Earth, tectonic plates have melted rocks, exposure to water has altered its mineral content, and pressure deep inside the Earth has transformed its crystalline structure. Cosmic and solar radiation has also driven fundamental changes on some worlds, and across Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, a mixture of these factors have altered the rock.

But asteroids and the parent bodies they came from haven't been subjected to all of these forces. In many ways, they remain unchanged from the early days of the Solar System, 4.5 billion years ago. They haven't remained completely unchanged; that would be next to impossible. But their ancient state and what it can teach us about the Solar System's history is why we've sent missions to collect samples and return them to Earth.

In 2020, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA)Hayabusa 2 successfully completed its sampling mission to asteroid Ryugu and returned its precious sample to Earth. Almost six years after its arrival on Earth, the Ryugu sample is still generating valuable scientific results, as researchers examine its mineralogical and chemical composition.

The newest results are in research titled "Pervasive poorly crystalline Mg-rich hydrous silicate material in C-type asteroid matrices." It's published in Nature Communications Earth and Environment, and the lead author is Reon Okumura from the Division of Geosciences and Civil Engineering at Kanazawa University, Japan.

Ryugu and other carbonaceous chondrites present an apparent contradiction. It involves aqueous alteration, where contact with water creates mineralogical and chemical changes in rocks and minerals. Aqueous alteration isn't a rare action that happens only in space environments; it's common on Earth. The best-known example is how clay forms from common silicate rocks in Earth's crust, from exposure to water. It's basically how soil is created.

A JAXA official successfully retrieving the 16 kg capsule that it contained a sample from the asteroid Ryugu. (Courtesy: JAXA)

There's obviously no soil on Ryugu, but there is aqueous alteration. "C-type asteroid-derived samples, including Ryugu and carbonaceous chondrites, consist primarily of fine-grained matrices of magnesium-rich hydrous silicates formed by aqueous alteration," the paper states.

The contradiction stems from the matrix of minerals in the asteroid. There seems to be two components, each altered under a different set of aqueous conditions. That implies that Ryugu's interior matrix is patchy, which is highly improbable. An asteroid can be clumpy on a macroscale, but how can it have two components in the same mineral matrix? That's been a nagging question in cosmochemistry: how can aqueous alteration happen to some of the matrix while leaving some of it more intact?

The authors write that Ryugu's matrix is "commonly interpreted as mixtures of serpentine- and saponite-like phyllosilicates..." Serpentine and saponite are both found on Earth, where they're created when rock is aqueously altered. But despite the fact that they're generally interpreted to be these substances, "their mineralogical characteristics do not fully correspond to these well-crystalline terrestrial layered silicates."

To dig into this apparent contradiction, the researchers used the SPring-8 synchrotron radiation facility and the Photon Factory High Energy Accelerator, both in Japan. Both of these research facilities use powerful x-rays to look deeply into the Ryugu sample.

They found the expected serpentine and saponite, but they also identified something else: poorly crystalline magnesium silicate hydrate (M-S-H).

âWhat makes M-S-H particularly interesting is that it can accommodate a wide range of magnesium-to-silicon ratios,â said study corresponding author Keisuke Fukushi of Kanazawa University. âThis flexibility may be key to understanding how water-rock interactions proceeded without erasing pre-existing chemical differences within their parent asteroids.â

The composition of most materials remains stable when subjected to the same aqueous conditions. But previous research and lab work shows that M-S-H is a bit of an oddball: it can exist in the same aqueous conditions and have different magnesium to silicon ratios. So this work suggests that M-S-H is the initial starting point, and that if it formed into serpentine and saponite phases, the presence of M-S-H can explain the two different outcomes without necessarily requiring a different aqueous alteration for each one.

This illustration helps explain the findings. The previous interpretation on the left shows tighly packed grains of serpentine and saponite, with the parallel lines representing their orderly crystal structure. The alternating blue and green lines in some grains represent interleaves of serpentine and saponite layers in the same crystal. There's almost no empty space between grains. The image on the right shows the new model, with a background of poorly crystalline M-S-H, making up the bulk of the matrix. In this model, serpentine and saponite are a minor part of the matrix, and are poorly-formed intrusions. Image Credit: Keisuke FUKUSHI, Kanazawa University (2026)

The study says something not only about Ryugu, but about carbonaceous chondrites. Much of their matrices could be poorly crystalline M-S-H. If this material precipitated first and then was transformed later, the different compositions of clay-like minerals found in the matrix could have arisen without a separate, distinct water environment for different regions of the parent asteroid.

"Assuming its initial precipitation and subsequent mineralogical transformations, a wide range of compositional variation can be produced without requiring separate aqueous conditions for each local composition," the authors write. "This framework provides a physicochemical basis for explaining the compositional variability and associated phyllosilicate diversity of C-type chondritic matrices within a parent-body alteration scenario."

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is developing a reputation for successful sampling missions, one of the most difficult type of missions to complete. The original Hayabusa mission, though plagued with difficulties, still managed to return a small sample from asteroid Itokawa in 2010. Hayabusa 2 was a complete success, as this research shows. And at this moment, JAXA's Martian Moons eXplorer mission is on its way to collect a sample from Phobos, the largest of Mars' two moons.

That sample should be on Earth five years from now. What questions will it answer?

Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors.

In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models.

RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development.

This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input.

The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest).

At the lower levels, development remains largely human-led. As AI systems move up the scale, they become increasingly capable of identifying their weaknesses and deciding how to address them, eventually gaining the ability to make their own “meta-improvements” — improving how they improve themselves.

Whether AI could ever achieve this level of sustained self-improvement remains an open question. Previous experiments have, however, demonstrated more limited forms of RSI.

In one study earlier this year, an AI system called A-Evolve-Training was tasked with improving the performance of a 30 billion-parameter large language model (LLM).

Over four rounds, A-Evolve-Training modestly improved the LLM's benchmark performance by testing different training techniques and using the results to change how it approached subsequent experiments.

Peter Bentley, a professor of digital biology at University College London, questioned whether such experiments offer a credible route to RSI.

"This idea that some AI is magically going to start generating better and better AIs by themselves [is] nonsense," Bentley told Live Science in an email.

Bentley pointed out that self-improving computer systems have been around for decades. Evolutionary computation and reinforcement learning, for instance, are both based on the principle of systems refining their performance over time in response to feedback.

Could AI really self-improve? Some experts are skeptical.

The much greater challenge, he said, is developing AI systems capable of autonomously conducting the research needed to create more powerful successors — not to mention overcoming their dependence on human expertise and physical computing infrastructure.

"You can't 'recursively self-improve' unless you can also enhance your own training, enhance your hardware, and test it exhaustively in real world settings," Bentley added.

The study's authors acknowledged some of these challenges. Developing RSI-capable systems could require enormous investments in computing power, as well as human supervision to ensure successive improvements delivered meaningful gains. All of this becomes effectively redundant if the resources needed to develop and test subsequent AI models outweigh any benefits they offer, the authors noted.

Scientists would also need a reliable way to determine whether an AI system was genuinely becoming more capable over iterations, rather than exploiting weaknesses in tests used to measure its capabilities. This is a known problem in AI development, where models can achieve higher benchmark scores by exploiting testing methods or cherry-picking results.

Kayla Blomquist, an AI researcher at the University of Oxford and co-founder of the Oxford China Policy Lab, said that, while the paper doesn't provide a practical road map to RSI, it could help developers and policymakers understand the technical challenges and safety risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.

She also questioned whether there would ever be a clear point at which AI became completely independent of human development. "The paper describes a gradual handover of responsibility rather than a single moment, so there may never be an obvious 'last' model built by humans," Blomquist added.

#6515. Something Remarkable Is Happening to Dogs Living Near Chernobyl’s Nuclear Plant

Scientists studying wild dogs near the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant have uncovered unusual genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than radiation-induced mutations.

Dogs living near the Chornobyl (previously called Chernobyl) Nuclear Power Plant carry genetic differences that may reflect natural selection rather than mutations caused by radiation exposure. A new genomic analysis identified more than 100 locations in their DNA showing signs of directional selection, including regions associated with DNA repair, cancer development, and immune function.

The findings suggest that environmental pressures may have favored certain inherited genetic variants, potentially helping some dogs survive in a contaminated environment. However, researchers have not established whether radiation or other environmental hazards directly caused these patterns.

Earlier research revealed substantial genetic differences between dogs living at the nuclear power plant and those in Chornobyl City, just 10 miles away. City dogs closely resembled populations from Russia, Poland, and surrounding regions, while dogs near the plant had distinctive genetic features, particularly in areas associated with DNA repair.

“This work ties up some of the loose ends from our previous work, where in characterizing the population’s genetic structure we found that while these two dog groups are geographically very close, they have a very high degree of genetic difference, and those differences aren’t due to mutation,” said Megan Dillon, postdoctoral research scholar at North Carolina State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine.

“With this work, we wanted to explore two additional larger-scale evolutionary drivers – are the genetic differences due to selection, or are they due to genetic drift over time in an isolated population?”

Natural selection occurs when inherited traits that improve survival or reproduction become more common across generations. Directional selection is a form of this process in which particular traits become increasingly favored, often in response to environmental conditions. Genetic drift, by contrast, involves random changes in the frequency of genetic variants. It can have especially strong effects in small, isolated populations and may reduce genetic diversity over time.

To distinguish between these processes, researchers compared the two Chornobyl dog populations with free-breeding dogs from Eastern Europe and an isolated population from the Galápagos Islands. This allowed them to examine whether geographic isolation alone could explain the unusual genetic patterns near the nuclear plant.

Although the plant dogs had a small effective population size, a measure of how many individuals contribute genetically to future generations, it was not significantly different from that of the city dogs. The plant population also lacked the reduction in genetic diversity expected from substantial genetic drift. Moreover, its genetic makeup differed markedly from other isolated populations, including the Galápagos dogs. Surprisingly, the Chornobyl City dogs were genetically more similar to the Galápagos population than to the dogs living at the nearby nuclear facility.

The researchers found evidence consistent with directional selection in genomic regions containing genes involved in DNA replication and repair, cell cycle regulation, cancer-related processes, and immune responses. These biological functions could influence how animals respond to harmful environmental exposures, although the analysis cannot determine whether particular variants actually improve survival.

“While we can’t say for certain whether what we’ve found can be directly confirmed as selection, we do find these genomic signatures suggestive of selection,” Dillon said.

“When we dig deeper into those genomic regions, we find that these genes are involved in biologically relevant pathways that could allow them to overcome the effects of being exposed to toxicants in this environment.”

The genetic differences do not necessarily mean that dogs developed new adaptations after exposure to radioactive contamination. Another possibility is that individuals carrying advantageous genetic variants were more likely to survive earlier environmental pressures, allowing those variants to become more prevalent in subsequent generations.

“When we consider the toxic environment around Chornobyl, I can see why most people would think, ‘Surely there’s got to have been some consequence of living in that environment,’” said Matthew Breen, Oscar J. Fletcher Distinguished Professor of Comparative Oncology Genetics at NC State’s College of Veterinary Medicine and corresponding author of the study.

“But what we’re saying is the consequence may not have gone as far as changing the dogs’ genome in order to adapt, it could be the ones that were able to survive the initial exposures had this level of underlying genetic diversity and variants to offer a higher degree of fitness,” Breen added. “Obviously that’s speculation, and we don’t know exactly what’s happened. But it is fair to say that we used a very robust analysis and found signatures of selection in biologically relevant regions.”

Reference: “Evidence of Selective Response in the Free-Breeding Dog Population in Chornobyl” by Megan N. Dillon, Reade B. Roberts, Jennifer A. Betz, Timothy A. Mousseau, Norman J. Kleiman and Matthew Breen, 26 September 2026, Genes. DOI: 10.3390/genes17101195

#6512. Too Much Exercise Could Change Your Brain Chemistry in Unexpected Ways

Two days after an exercise test, mice subjected to weeks of grueling training still had elevated dopamine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and emotional regulation. The findings suggest that excessive exercise without adequate recovery can produce lasting changes in brain chemistry.

The study, published in the journal Neuroscience, was conducted by researchers in Brazil. Because dopamine helps regulate motivation and alertness, the results raise questions about whether similar disruptions could contribute to sleep problems, anxiety, and persistent fatigue in overtrained athletes. However, these possible effects have not been demonstrated in humans.

To investigate how different levels of physical exertion affect the brain, the researchers compared mice subjected to two exercise protocols. One group completed a single treadmill session until exhaustion. The other underwent eight weeks of progressively more demanding training designed to simulate the physical strain associated with overtraining syndrome.

During the final week, the heavily trained mice exercised twice daily, with just four hours between sessions. Researchers then examined the animals’ hippocampi, measuring dopamine, serotonin, and proteins involved in neurotransmitter production and regulation.

The mice that completed a single exhausting run showed a rise in dopamine shortly afterward. In contrast, the chronically trained animals had elevated dopamine levels even 48 hours after their performance test, during a period intended for recovery. Levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme essential for dopamine synthesis, also remained elevated.

Dopamine is involved in several functions, including motivation, reward processing, and wakefulness. Its presence is not inherently harmful, but changes in its regulation could affect brain activity during periods when the body would normally be recovering.

Interestingly, the researchers found no significant changes in serotonin levels. Serotonin has long been investigated as a possible contributor to exercise-related fatigue, but these results suggest that the neurochemical effects of excessive training cannot be explained by serotonin alone.

“Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain,” said Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study’s first author. He conducted the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP), with support from FAPESP.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when prolonged physical demands exceed the body’s ability to recover, potentially causing declining athletic performance, chronic fatigue, muscle pain, loss of appetite, increased injuries, and changes in immune and metabolic function. Researchers suspect that changes in brain signaling may also contribute to some symptoms.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, suggested that similar dopamine disturbances in humans might help explain connections between excessive training and sleep disorders. However, the researchers did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness in the mice, so the findings cannot establish a connection between the observed chemical changes and those symptoms.

The research team is now participating in an international project to identify which biological systems first begin to show abnormal responses when excessive exercise interferes with the body’s usual adaptations to training. Such work could help clarify how beneficial physical activity progresses into a state of insufficient recovery and impaired performance.

Reference: “Excessive training alters hippocampal tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine homeostasis in mice” by Alisson Luiz da Rocha, João Pedro Floriano, Ana Paula Pinto, Dennys Esper Cintra, Eduardo Rochete Ropelle, Ellen Cristini de Freitas, José Rodrigo Pauli and Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, 4 August 2026, Neuroscience. DOI: 10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.08.006

#6511. The JWST May Have Found Where Heavy Black Hole Seeds Formed

Astrophysicists think that the supermassive black holes (SMBH) we see in the modern Universe are the result of a long drawn-out process. That process is referred to as the hierarchical black hole mergers framework. It explains how some SMBH can reach such staggering masses. Some of the most massive appear to have billions of solar masses.

The idea is that these SMBH start out as seeds, and those seeds are stellar-mass black holes. Two processes create them. One is when massive stars between about 8 and 50 solar masses reach the end of their lives of fusion. They either explode as supernovae, and their cores collapse, forming black holes, or they collapse directly into black holes. The other is when two neutron stars merge.

In between stellar mass black holes and SMBH are intermediate mass black holes (IMBH.) These black holes range in mass from about 100 solar masses to 100,000 solar masses. The observational evidence for IMBHs is still thin, but it's persistent.

A 2024 paper focused on Omega Centauri, a globular cluster on the outskirts of the Milky Way, as the site of an IMBH. A group of fast-moving stars in the center of Omega Centauri can only be explained by the presence of an IMBH with about 8,200 solar masses, according to that work.

Gravitational waves from a black hole merger are also evidence of an IMBH. A 2020 paper presented the only direct evidence of an IMBH when the waves showed that two black holes, with 85 and 66 solar masses, merged to create an IMBH with about 142 solar masses.

But what are the birthplaces of these IMBH? Some must have formed in the early Universe to act as seeds for the SMBH we see today.

Research titled "Massive star clusters detected by JWST as natural birth places to form intermediate-mass black holes" may have the answer. It's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics, and the lead author is Viola Bocchi. Bocchi is from the Sapienza University of Rome.

"The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of dense stellar systems at high redshifts, including the âCosmic Gemsâ arc (zââ¼â10.2) and the âFirefly Sparkleâ (zââ¼â8.3). With masses in the range 105 Mââ107 Mâ and half-mass radii in the range â¼0.4â15 pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models," the authors write.

The Cosmic Gems arc is a gravitationally lensed galaxy, and the JWST observed its light when the Universe was only about 460 million years old. The JWST found five dense star clusters there.

The Cosmic Gems was first discovered by the Hubble during its Reionization Lensing Cluster Survey (RELICS) and was identified as a powerful source of radiation during the Epoch of Reionization. In 2024, the JWST took another look and found the five Young Massive Clusters (YMC), the first discovery of such ancient clusters.

The Firefly Sparkle is another gravitationally lensed early galaxies, imaged only about 600 million years after the Big Bang. The JWST found 10 YMCs in the Firefly Sparkle.

This image shows the Firefly Sparkle galaxy, where the JWST found 10 YMCs. It also shows a pair of companion galaxies. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Chris Willott (National Research Council Canada), Lamiya Mowla (Wellesley College), Kartheik Iyer (Columbia University)

This research shows that not only were all these YMCs sources of ionizing radiation, they may have been the birthplaces of IMBH.

Due to the density in these YMCs, n-body simulations weren't viable. Instead, the researchers used a model based on runaway collisions and mass-loss by stellar winds to estimate the resulting IMBH masses. They then validated these results against direct N-body simulations of compact star clusters.

"With masses in the range 105 Mââ107 Mâ and half-mass radii in the range â¼0.4â15 pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models," the authors write. "Our estimates yield typical IMBH masses in the range â¼102 Mâ to â¼4âÃâ103 Mâ, implying typical formation efficiencies on the few percent level."

The clusters in the Cosmic Gems yieled the heaviest IMBH, with masses ranging from 1600â2700 Mâ. "The extreme compactness of the Cosmic Gems clusters (Rhââ¼â1 pc) facilitates the formation of black hole seeds with high masses of 1600â2700 Mâ," the authors write. Rh â¼â1 pc is the radius of the sphere that contains half of the clusterâs total mass and measures how compact a cluster is.

"The low metallicity (Zââ²â0.02âZâ) is a critical factor for retaining the seed mass despite stellar winds," the authors write.

These young clusters also have low metallicities because not enough stars have lived and died in them to generate higher metallicity. Their low metallicity played a critical role in forming IMBH. Low metallicity limits mass-loss due to stellar winds, and that let the objects keep growing.

The results from the Firefly Sparkle are different. "In contrast to the Cosmic Gems, these clusters exhibit significantly larger radii (Rhââ¼â4âââ6 pc) for typically lower total masses (105âââ106âMâ)," the authors write. That creates cores that are less massive, limiting the potential for the runaway collision process to create IMBH. The black hole masses in Firefly Sparkle range 1.8âÃâ102âââ8.1âÃâ102âMâ. That's about 180 to 810 Mâ, which represents the lower boundary for IMBH masses.

This artist's illustration shows what the Firefly Sparkle galaxy looked like about 600 million years after the big bang if it wasnât stretched and distorted by gravitational lensing. This illustration is based on images and data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Ralf Crawford (STScI). Science: Lamiya Mowla (Wellesley College), Guillaume Desprez (Saint Mary's University)

Overall, the lower range for IMBH masses in this work (~100 solar mases) is comparable to black holes formed by massive Population III stars, the Universe's hypothetical first stars, which were likely extremely massive. But, "the upper bound extends significantly higher, allowing the most massive clusters to produce objects firmly in the âheavy seedâ regime," the authors write. "Forming such heavy seeds is highly beneficial to form SMBHs at high redshift."

These results aren't observational in the sense that the JWST didn't observe any IMBH. But they do show a plausible environment where IMBH could form and potentially lead to the SMBH we see in the centers of galaxies like ours.

These results could also explain the JWST's Little Red Dots. Their spectra are often interpreted as being powered by SMBH. "Our results suggest that dense massive star clusters could provide possible massive seeds from which the SMBHs in the LRDs may have grown," the researchers write.

The researchers state some caveats, based on some acknowledged weaknesses in their work. Many properties of these clusters are unknown, including their rotation and their internal structure, which could change the outcomes and lower the IMBH masses.

The initial mass function also isn't known, but it could be top-heavy. "This possibility, along with a possible primordial mass segregation, would favor the formation of massive IMBHs, though we did not explore it here in detail," the authors explain.

Researchers will no doubt dig deeper into these young massive clusters and try to fill in some of the blanks that remain. But this research shows that they could be the source of the heavy seed IMBH that eventually form SMBH.

"Our results suggest that these dense, metal-poor clusters are viable factories for heavy seeds that are capable of growing into the supermassive black holes observed in the early Universe," the authors conlude. .

#6510. The Vera Rubin Has Found Two More of the Milky Way's Dim Satellites

Massive galaxies like the Milky Way have a retinue of smaller, dim satellites on their outskirts. They're hard to detect, and while astronomers have found about 65 of the Milky Way's dwarf satellite galaxies, and about 40 globular clusters in its halo, they suspect there are many dwarf satellites and globular clusters yet to be found. Now the Vera Rubin Observatory has found two more.

The Milky Way's satellites are either small dim galaxies or globular clusters, and both are part of the assembly history of the Milky Way through mergers. These two detections by the Rubin, found in its Early Data Preview 2 (EDP2) released in July 2026, are almost certainly the beginning of many more discoveries of Milky Way satellites by the powerful observatory. One is a most likely a dim dwarf galaxy named Aquarius IV, and one is a globular cluster named Rubin-GC1.

This figure shows the locations of both Rubin-GC1 and Aquarius IV. Rubin-GC1's detection was particularly impressive, since it's in the direction of the Milky Way's bulge, a region with a dense stellar population and thick dust. Image Credit: NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA, ESA/Gaia/DPAC, W. Cerny

The discoveries are presented in two new papers.

One is titled "Discovery of the Distant, Ultra-faint Milky Way Satellite Aquarius IV with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Early Data Preview 2." It's published in Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society, and the lead author is William Cerny, an astronomy student in Yaleâs Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.

"We present the discovery of Aquarius IV (RubinâJ2201â0234)âthe first ultra-faint Milky Way (MW) satellite to be identified using data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory," the authors write. It was confirmed in images from the Dark Energy Camera. The authors say it's a low-luminosity, compact stellar system in the outer Galactic halo.

It's stellar population is ancient and low-metallicity. "These properties closely resemble those of the smallest and faintest confirmed ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs), though a globular cluster classification is not ruled out," the researchers write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies can have as little as a few hundred stars, which makes them smaller than some globular clusters (GCs). But there's one critical difference between UFDs and GCs: UFDs have dark matter while GCs don't (except for a few possible outliers).

Only a small number of the stars in Aquarius IV have been detected so far, so whether or not it is a UFD for sure will depend on deeper imaging and spectroscopy.

âWhat I find especially exciting is that these discoveries are just the beginning for Rubin,â said first author Cerny. (He is also the second author of the Rubin-GC1 study, which has been accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters.)

âIf the observatory can find systems this faint and difficult with only its preview data, its full 10-year survey will undoubtedly provide us with many more Milky Way satellite discoveries,â Cerny said. âThese new satellites will give us new opportunities to test models of galaxy formation, trace the assembly history of the Milky Way, and investigate the nature of dark matter.â

These panels are images centered on Aquarius IV. The star in the lower panel marks a Blue Horizontal Branch star used to determine the distance to Aquarius IV. The stars in the bottom panel are also coloured according to their probability of being members of Aquarius IV. The grey stars are almost certainly not members, while colours ranging from purple through red, orange, and yellow represent increasing probability. Image Credit: William Cerny et al 2026 Res. Notes AAS 10 239

The second paper is "Rubin Observatory Reveals a Dust-Shrouded Halo Globular Cluster in Ophiuchus," and it will be published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. It's currently available at arxiv.org and the lead author is Aashay Pai. Pai is a graduate student in the Department of Physics at the University of Chicago.

"We present the discovery of the Milky Way satellite Rubin-GC1 (Rubin J1628â1735) using data from the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatoryâs Early Data Preview 2," the authors write. The stars in Rubin-GC1 have an intermediate age of about 9.2 billion years, and are moderately rich in metals, meaning it's most likely a very faint GC. "Together, these properties suggest Rubin-GC1 is most likely a star cluster in the faint tail of the luminosity function of globular clusters surrounding the Milky Way," the authors write.

Based on comparisons to the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, Rubin-GC1 is most likely a cluster accreted to the Milky Way, associated with the Sagittarius leading arm. The Sagittarius leading arm is a massive tidal stream of stars from the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, torn away as that galaxy merges with the Milky Way.

The panel on the left shows the Sagittarius trailing and leading arms. (The DES images are not part of this work.) The image on the right shows roughly where Rubin-GC1 is located, shown with the gold star. The Milky Way's center is shown with the black cross, and the circle with the dot inside is the Sun. Image Credit: Left: By NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=139367207. Right: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âFinding new Milky Way satellites in Rubin Observatory data has been an exciting future prospect for most of my career,â said Marla Geha, a professor of astronomy and physics in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences, and co-author on both studies. âIt is remarkable this is now a reality.â

Rubin-GC1 was detected in the direction of the galactic bulge, where stellar density is very high and the dust is thick. Finding it in those conditions makes the detection even more impressive. "The discovery of Rubin-GC1 highlights the potential of Rubin to uncover faint, resolved satellites in dust-shrouded regions of the Milky Way, including remnants of the accretion events that have shaped the Galaxyâs hierarchical assembly," the authors write.

The panel on the left is what's called a 'smoothed isochrone filtered stellar density map.' It's a visualization tool in astronomy used to detect and map faint structures like ultra-faint dwarf galaxies by masking out field stars based on a color-magnitude curve. The panel on the right is a more familiar type of image used to show the region itself. Image Credit: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âThese discoveries are incredibly promising,â Geha said. âContinued discoveries will allow us to complete the census of satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, which is a key to understanding how the faintest galaxies form.â

The Vera Rubin Observatory is mostly known as a transient-detecting observatory, and as the maker of a ten-year long movie of the sky in its Legacy Survey of Space and Time. But it's more than that. As it images the sky repeatedly, dim objects will become clearer. "The sensitivity of Rubin LSST will steadily increase, and systems similar to Aquarius IV are ultimately expected to be detectable with >85% efficiency using the same search algorithm applied here," the authors of the first paper write.

Not only that, but its observations will work with observations from other observatories, like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, to detect even more objects. "The identification of Rubin-GC1 heralds an exciting era of discovery as Rubin, Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope pierce the shroud of Galactic dust to reveal faint satellites that were hitherto hidden by our Galaxy," the authors of the second paper write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and globular clusters are puzzle pieces in the history of the Milky Way's growth through mergers. The mergers are ongoing, as interactions between the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way show.

By finding more of the Milky Way satellites, a picture of all of these mergers, and the role dark matter plays, will become clearer. By mapping out these objects and the streams they're sometimes a part of, astronomers can detect where dark matter also concentrates in clumps. These dark matter sub-halos will show how our galaxy grew larger by consuming smaller galaxies with their own dark matter halos.
