How did the universe transition from an impenetrable fog of hydrogen into the bright and starlit cosmos we see today? Astronomers think they're onto the answer.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The mysterious force that cleared the cosmic fog at the dawn of the universe may not be what we thought, a new study suggests. The results hint that astronomers may need to rethink a major aspect of cosmological evolution, which led to the universe we clearly see today.

Around 400,000 years after the Big Bang, the fledgling universe finally cooled enough to form atoms — mostly hydrogen. But these neutral, non-electrically charged hydrogen atoms shrouded the cosmos in a fog that made it opaque to ultraviolet (UV) light.

Then, after the first stars flickered to life and gathered into galaxies, bursts of radiation ionized the neutral hydrogen. This turned the impenetrable fog of atoms into electrically charged protons and electrons, allowing light to pass through interstellar space unimpeded and, eventually, reach our observatories. This cosmic curtain parting is known as the Epoch of Reionization, or what a team of researchers studying it call the "last major phase transition in the universe."

A chart showing the evolution of the universe, from the Big Bang to today. The first stars started to appear from the hydrogen fog a few hundred million years after the Big Bang.

"We don't know exactly what objects caused reionization or how it evolved," Cody Carr, an astronomer who focuses on galaxy evolution at the University of Michigan and first author of a new study of the epoch, said in a statement. "We know that it took place, but we don't have complete answers to those questions."

Astrophysicists previously thought that this fog-clearing effect depended on supernovas, the violently explosive deaths of stars around eight to 50 times the mass of the sun.

But in the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Astronomy, Carr and colleagues presented evidence that supernovas exerted the opposite effect, trapping the so-called Lyman continuum (LyC) photons of ionizing UV radiation that dispelled the celestial fog instead of scattering them.

"The most interesting thing about our paper is the observation that the strongest LyC emitters do not have fast galactic winds," Carr told Live Science via email. "This challenges the notion that galaxies require fast supernova-driven winds to enable LyC escape."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers used the Hubble Space Telescope to observe an analogue of the ancient universe in the local cosmos: six star-forming, wind-launching galaxies around 3.5 billion light-years away.

These compact starburst galaxies are generally smaller than 6,500 light-years in diameter and form around 10 solar masses' worth of stars per year. That star-birthing rate is several times higher than that of the Milky Way, which is up to 20 times larger.

The galaxies' spectra, or light-based fingerprints, revealed the origin, chemical composition, speed and direction of their stellar winds, which were whipped up by the radiation from their newly formed stars.

The researchers also described how these processes changed as the massive young stars evolved and died in energetic supernovas several billion years later, with the resultant galactic winds overpowering the stellar winds.

These nearby galaxies highlighted a counterintuitive two-phase process.

In the initial phase, which occurred during the first 3 million years of star formation, the newly formed massive stars' stellar winds carved through their galaxies' neutral gas and dust at nearly 2,000 miles per second (3,000 kilometers per second). This allowed LyC light to escape the galaxy and ionize the neutral gas and dust in intergalactic space.

The second phase, which emerged around 3 million years after star formation, seemed to reverse this process. As O-type stars — the hottest, bluest and most massive stars in the cosmos — lived fast and died young, their expelled stellar guts added to the opaque galactic gas and dust, churning it and loading it with mass, which created a trap for LyC light.

The oldest galaxies in this study ‪—‬ and, therefore, the ones with the fastest supernova-generated galactic winds ‪—‬ allowed the least amount of ionizing radiation to escape their environs.

"In general, our results are in disagreement with most cosmological simulations, which typically show the LyC escape fraction peaking after the launch of supernova-driven winds," Carr explained via email. In other words, supernovas didn't drive the Epoch of Reionization, but they may have dampened it. The intense light of newborn stars now seems like the most viable source of reionization.

Future research could aim to obtain additional galactic samples and higher-resolution observations across other wavelengths.

O., Borthakur, S., Haye, M., Heckman, T., Ji, Z., Komarova, L., Reste, A. L., Leclercq, F., Marques-Chaves, R., . . . Xu, X. (2026). #6438. Why do flamingos dance while they eat? This scientist found out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Erin Garcia de Jesús, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

On a family trip to Atlanta, Víctor Ortega Jiménez spent time taking pictures and videos of flamingos as they fed in their pond. It wasn’t to admire their long legs or flamboyant pink color. Instead, he noticed the “beautiful” ripples spreading across the water as the birds ate under the surface. But he didn’t know why the waves were happening.

It took “more than four years to answer that question,” says Ortega Jiménez, of the University of California, Berkeley. “But I think the answer was fascinating.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Ortega Jiménez’s focus is biomechanics, or the study of how mechanics applies to animal movement and structure. His goal is to understand how animal behaviors might lead to human-made engineering feats.

He discovered that, by retracting their heads, flamingos produce vortexlike traps with water to scoop up algae. They stomp around — or dance, if you will — amplifying the vortex. The series of motions brings the food to their crooked beaks. The beaks then filter in food, releasing silt and mud.

The impressive process can weed out particles the size of a single cell. This kind of self-cleaning filter for extremely small particles can be applied to remove microplastics and so-called forever chemicals called PFAS from water, Ortega Jiménez says.

“Nature is always full of secrets,” he says. “And I think that’s the riddle that keeps me going, trying to understand nature. That’s my way to see science: by observation and trying to be inspired and trying to solve a problem.”

#6437. Deep ocean oxygen kept rising and falling long after animals appeared

Geologists found deep ocean oxygen built up and vanished again for over 100 million years after the Cambrian, complicating how animals evolved.

Researchers often explain the Cambrian Explosion, the burst of animal life half a billion years ago, with a lasting rise in ocean oxygen. In the deep ocean, though, the oxygen didn’t last..

Geologists studied mud that settled on the seafloor between about 485 million and 380 million years ago and later hardened into rock.

They found oxygen near the bottom building up for short stretches and then disappearing again. So animals may have evolved under less deep-sea oxygen than researchers once assumed.

Chadlin Ostrander, an assistant professor in the Geology & Geophysics department at the University of Utah, led the study. His team found no evidence of sustained oxygen in the deep ocean during that span.

The team concluded that oxygen didn’t settle into the deepest water for good until sometime after roughly 380 million years ago.

“Just a decade ago, it was thought that a deep ocean oxygenation switch was flipped around 540 million years ago. Our new dataset pushes that forward in time by at least ~160 million years,” he said.

The team didn’t measure oxygen directly. Instead, it read a chemical record in the rock that follows oxygen indirectly.

Researchers have invoked oxygen in the deep ocean to explain nearly every major step in early animal history. That includes the first animals and the Cambrian Explosion. It also includes a second burst of marine diversity from about 485 to 444 million years ago.

Other scientists have raised serious counterarguments to each. A common objection is that oxygen may have risen during these events, but not high enough, or for long enough, to fill the deep ocean.

Visitors to the Grand Canyon can see some of that early history. Its walls include about 1,600 feet (500 meters) of rock that settled in a Cambrian sea.

Ostrander’s samples start right after the Cambrian ended, about 485 million years ago, so the team didn’t sample that sea.

Geologists find tiny amounts of thallium, a heavy metal, in ordinary rock. It comes in two forms that differ by a hair in weight.

When a manganese mineral settles into seafloor mud, it pulls more of the heavier form out of seawater. That mineral survives in mud only where oxygen is steadily present in the water above it, and a few days without oxygen dissolve it again.

Mud formed in oxygen-poor places keeps a sample of the surrounding seawater, including its mix of the two forms. The team read a lower value, meaning more of the lighter form, as a sign that more seafloor lay under oxygen-rich water.

The team measured 82 shale samples from the Peel River in Canada’s Yukon. The river has cut into the rock, exposing fresh layers that stayed largely unweathered in the cold.

Erik Sperling of Stanford University and Justin Strauss of Dartmouth College led the expeditions that collected the Yukon mud.

Another 44 samples came from sites including Latvia, Libya, Wales and Montana.

For most of the record, the team found the same thallium mix as in ordinary continental rock. A seafloor with little oxygen above it should leave exactly that. In Yukon mud that formed between about 405 million and 386 million years ago, the readings dropped.

The lowest value came from a Marcellus Shale sample from the Appalachian Basin that formed about 388 million years ago. By the team’s calculations, that value means oxygen-rich water covered much more than 30% of the seafloor, well past the continental shelves and into the deep ocean.

Readings from the peak of the last ice age look similar, with surface oxygen reaching the deep ocean only slightly less effectively than it does now.

That high-oxygen stretch didn’t last. By about 378 million years ago, the readings returned to ordinary values and stayed there to the top of the rock. That could mean more of the deep ocean had lost its oxygen again.

Local conditions could have faked the dip, so the team checked. The 11 Yukon samples from the dip had the same chemistry as the other Yukon samples, and the Marcellus Shale, from a separate basin, dipped the same way.

By the time of those samples, Ostrander said, marine life was already large and doing energy-expensive work.

“You have some phenomenal changes in evolutionary biology happening during this time. And none of it seems to require substantial and sustained deep ocean oxygenation,” he said.

Animal life was changing fast before that window opened.

Paleontologists working at a fossil site in southwest China have found that many animal groups already existed before the Cambrian began. Researchers who analyzed fossil trails from about 545 million years ago reached a similar conclusion.

In rock about 520 million years old, researchers have found colonies of tiny filter-feeding animals and an early relative of octopuses and squid.

The deep ocean has had steady oxygen since then. The team can’t say when that began, only that it came after about 380 million years ago. Ostrander called that the study’s one disappointment.

Gaps remain. The team has only one rock sample for roughly every 450,000 years, so the real swings may have been even larger than the mud shows.

The team also couldn’t fully rule out that thallium cycled through seawater too fast for the mud to reflect the whole ocean. Its models and the match between basins make that unlikely.

The researchers wrote that long, closely spaced oxygen records from the late Paleozoic and the Mesozoic are still needed to learn when the deep ocean filled with oxygen for good.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6435. What an artist thought were ancient stone ovens in South Africa turned out to be termite nests at least 323,000 years old

Stone pipes near Calitzdorp, South Africa, once thought to be ovens, are fossil termite nests at least 323,000 years old and a new trace fossil.

In the early 2000s, a local artist named Tim Robson dug hard, pipe-like structures out of a river terrace. The spot was near Calitzdorp, a small town in South Africa’s Little Karoo.

He thought they were ovens built by early humans. They were fossil termite nests, and uranium dating now shows they are at least 323,000 years old.

A team led by Miengah Abrahams of the University of Cape Town’s Department of Geological Sciences has named them Columnanidus calitzdorpensis, a new trace fossil. No termite bodies were found with the nests, so the species that built them is still unknown.

The site is on a flat terrace of the Gamka River outside Calitzdorp, in the Western Cape. Nothing about Robson’s dig was recorded at the time.

Paleontology consultant John Almond heard about the oven theory from Tom Barry of CapeNature and from Bob Wood in 2003 and 2004. Several pieces were removed from the site. One went to the Calitzdorp Museum, and it is still there.

In 2005 Almond wrote a short entry on the pipes for a heritage study. It covered the Gamkaberg-Rooiberg conservation area, around CapeNature’s Gamkaberg Nature Reserve. He said they might be fossil termite nests, but no one was interested in returning to the site.

Emese Bordy, a University of Cape Town geologist, saw the entry and told Abrahams. Bordy had supervised her PhD. The work began in 2021, and Almond is one of the eight authors.

Barry guided the team in the field. Two pits had been dug into the terrace about 33 feet (10 meters) apart. Only the first one had nests in it.

Eight nests still stand there within 15 feet (4.5 meters) of each other. Some were built up against a neighbor, and a few share a wall.

The visible part of each nest is 14 to 41 inches (36 to 104 centimeters) tall. A nest is about 26 inches (65 centimeters) across, with a wall close to 5 inches (12 centimeters) thick.

River cobbles are stuck in the walls at all heights, and one wall holds a snail shell. So the nests were dug fully underground, the authors say, in an old soil lying on the gravel.

On the inside of the wall, the termites built rows of flat chambers stacked like shelves. Ramps link the levels. An average chamber is about 2.5 inches (6.4 centimeters) wide and less than a third of an inch (0.73 centimeters) high.

The inner chambers are lined with a dark organic layer. The paper notes that ants occasionally line their burrows too, but termites do so far more often.

Muofhe Tshibalangada CT-scanned pieces of the wall at Stellenbosch University. Megan Purchase-Wellman at the University of the Free State checked the minerals by X-ray diffraction.

“We determined that these were a unique ichnogenus and ichnospecies, because of their distinct cylindric nature,” Abrahams said in a university press release.

“The distinct zones in the shapes of the burrows and chambers within the nest wall have not been seen anywhere else before either.”

All eight nests have an empty center about 16 inches (40 centimeters) wide. The paper calls this feature curious and not understood. A soft hive may have rotted away, or the termites may have built around a tree trunk.

The team drilled 11 cream-colored carbonate layers out of the nest walls. Samples went through uranium-thorium dating, a method described by co-author John Hellstrom of the University of Melbourne, who works in the university’s School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences.

Two of the 11 carried too much detrital grit and were dropped. The other nine gave dates from about 422,000 to 206,000 years, which cluster at 401,000 (three dates), 323,000 (five dates) and 206,000 years (one date).

The single 206,000-year date came from a layer that did not follow the chamber shapes, so the authors did not take it as the minimum age.

The 323,000-year group was the largest and most precise, with an error of 12,000 years. The team took 323,000 years, give or take 12,000, as the minimum age, in the Middle Pleistocene.

Columna is Latin for column and nidus is Latin for nest. The second half, calitzdorpensis, is for the town.

Calcium carbonate built up in the sand the termites had worked and slowly set hard. Geologists call it calcretization.

Over the nests sits a honeycomb layer of carbonate lumps and an 11-inch (28-centimeter) cap of hardpan. In the second pit, 33 feet (10 meters) away, neither layer is there, a gap the authors tie to the termites.

Modern termites change the chemistry of the soil they live in and the way water moves through it, Abrahams said. “In ancient times such activity would have also provided good conditions for carbonate minerals to build up in the nests and be preserved.”

Living colonies build well-ventilated nests that move air and moisture through the ground. In dry country they dig deep for damp soil. The living species Hodotermes mossambicus nests as deep as about 11.5 feet (3.5 meters).

Other termite works have lasted a long time too. In Brazil, millions of mounds about 4,000 years old can be seen from space. In the Namib Desert, sand termites have been tied to bare rings known as fairy circles.

According to the paper, no single feature can fully discern a termite nest from an ant nest. The team calls the pipes “likely attributable to termites.”

The bottoms of the nests are not well exposed, and in the ones the team emptied out, the wall just stopped. The uranium dates show when carbonate grew in the walls, not when the termites dug, so the nests could be older. Few continuous climate records exist in the region to compare them with.

Next, the group will look at fossil termite and ant nests in the Northern Cape and near Ceres and Worcester. Abrahams will co-convene an ichnology symposium at the 7th International Palaeontological Congress in Cape Town, November 30 to December 3, 2026.

In October 2026 the researchers went back to Calitzdorp and gave the museum a poster about the find. “We hope visitors to the museum, especially children, will gain a deeper appreciation for the natural world around them,” Abrahams said.

The museum’s piece, once taken for an oven, is now the holotype. That is the reference specimen for the new name, accession number 93/01/01.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Quaternary Science.

#6434. A simple change could make lifesaving blood transfusions easier for dogs

A new study suggests refrigerated blood platelets could help control dangerous bleeding in dogs while making lifesaving transfusions more accessible.

Platelets, the tiny cell fragments that help stop bleeding, have long been stored at room temperature because veterinarians believed refrigeration made them less effective.

A new study of sick dogs suggests chilled platelets can still help control bleeding, and they can be kept for weeks instead of days.

Dogs given platelets stored for up to three weeks showed less bleeding within four hours, and no transfusion reactions were recorded.

A longer shelf life could make platelets easier for animal hospitals to keep on hand.

Jillian Haines, a veterinarian who directs the blood bank at Washington State University’s Veterinary Teaching Hospital, led the research.

Her team reviewed hospital records rather than running a trial, and no group of dogs was given standard room-temperature platelets for comparison.

“It is hard to overstate how important the ability to transfuse platelets is,” Haines said. “Many of us have seen patients die from bleeding complications because there was simply nothing we could offer them.”

“We went from having essentially nothing available to now having a really viable product that we can use.”

Bleeding on its own becomes a serious risk once a dog’s platelet count falls below about 30,000 to 50,000 per microliter, which is a millionth of a liter of blood.

At that point, a transfusion of platelets can be lifesaving for a dog with severe bleeding or one about to have surgery.

Getting those platelets is the hard part. Veterinary hospitals usually store them at 68 to 75°F (20 to 24°C) in constant motion, and a bag lasts about five days.

Warm storage also raises the risk of bacteria growing in the bag. Keeping platelets at 34 to 43°F (1 to 6°C) may slow that growth, stretch their storage time and make them easier to ship.

Human hospitals turned to cold-stored platelets during pandemic blood shortages, and reports found they controlled bleeding with no apparent rise in reactions or infections.

In dogs, Haines’s earlier lab work showed that refrigerated platelets could stay functional for up to three weeks, but no study had checked whether they help sick dogs stop bleeding.

Shannon Monaco, the study’s first author, worked with Haines and colleagues at the Washington State University College of Veterinary Medicine.

They found 24 dogs that had received 27 transfusions of chilled platelets between March 2022 and October 2024.

In nine of the dogs, the immune system was destroying their own platelets, a condition called immune-mediated thrombocytopenia.

Seven had cancer, and the rest had problems that included liver failure from a toxin, a twisted stomach and swallowed rodent poison.

Nine of the transfusions were given for bleeding that had started on its own. Six came before surgery, and 12 came before smaller procedures such as placing an IV line or taking a needle sample.

Each bag began as about 15 fluid ounces (450 mL) of donated dog blood, spun twice to pack the platelets into about 2 fluid ounces (60 mL).

The bags were stored at 39°F (4°C) without shaking, for an average of 12 days before use.

Clinicians judged bleeding with a bleeding score designed for dogs, which rates each site on the body from zero to two.

The team added bleeding inside the chest or belly, checked by ultrasound, for a top score of 20 points.

Six of the dogs showed no signs of bleeding before their transfusions.

Among the rest, the average bleeding score was 3.15 before the transfusion, 3.00 an hour later and 2.21 after four hours.

Only the improvement measured at four hours was statistically significant. In plain terms, bleeding had eased a little by the four-hour mark.

Clinicians recorded improvement within four hours after 19 of the 27 transfusions, or 70%. That meant bleeding slowed or stopped, or a procedure went ahead without bleeding.

Seven more transfusions were followed by partial improvement.

One case couldn’t be judged, because the dog’s heart stopped soon after the transfusion, which the team attributed to suspected cancer.

Nineteen of the 24 dogs, or 79%, survived to leave the hospital.

The dogs that died had higher bleeding scores before and after their transfusions, which fits earlier studies tying bleeding severity to survival in dogs with low platelet counts.

The platelet counts told a different story. Before transfusion, the dogs’ median count, the middle value in the group, was 17,000 per microliter.

An hour later it was 23,500, a change too small to rule out chance.

That wasn’t unexpected, the authors wrote. In people and dogs alike, a platelet count often fails to reflect how well a transfusion is working, especially in dogs whose bodies are destroying or using up platelets.

Chilled platelets also leave the bloodstream sooner than room-temperature ones.

Earlier lab studies found they clump together more readily and form clots faster, which may make up for their shorter stay.

The team didn’t test any of that in these dogs. They wrote that such properties may help explain the lower bleeding scores, although the cause can’t be determined.

None of the 27 transfusions was followed by a fever, an allergic reaction, an infection or any other reaction in the records.

The researchers noted that showing a lack of harm is an essential early step for any new way of storing platelets.

Records can miss mild reactions, though. Two of the dogs were also taking drugs that calm inflammation or suppress the immune system, which could have masked a reaction.

Three dogs did bleed later. Two with immune-mediated thrombocytopenia developed suspected bleeding into the belly 12 to 18 hours after a needle sample was taken from the spleen.

One of those two dogs stabilized after a second bag of chilled platelets, and the other stabilized without more treatment.

A third dog, a surgical patient, had mild bleeding from its incision a day after its operation that stopped on its own.

The authors suggested that these later bleeding episodes may be related to how quickly chilled platelets leave the bloodstream. Some dogs may need a repeat dose.

Nine dogs also received other blood products, such as red blood cells or plasma, on or near the day of their platelet transfusions.

Two received freeze-dried platelets during their stay, and those treatments could have helped steady some of the dogs too.

The bleeding score was modified for this study and hasn’t been formally tested, and some scores had to be rebuilt from clinicians’ notes.

The dose also varied from dog to dog, and the study didn’t determine the best one.

Even in people, the right dose is unsettled. A large human trial of preventive platelet transfusions found that low, medium, and high doses led to similar bleeding outcomes.

The university’s blood bank now keeps a routine supply of cold-stored platelets.

Haines said she has trained veterinarians and blood bank staff from other institutions in the method.

“It’s not needed often, but when it is needed, it is the only option,” Haines said. “These products can be lifesaving.”

Haines hopes to work out the best dose and find better ways to tell whether a transfusion helped an individual dog.

She also hopes to test whether the platelets still work after more than three weeks in the refrigerator.

The full study was published in the Journal of Veterinary Internal Medicine.

#6433. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

Each of Earth's hemispheres experiences summer, but how do they differ?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Each year, Earth's Northern and Southern hemispheres cycle through four seasons, including summer.

Given that the hemispheres are symmetric about the equator, you may think that, on both sides of the world, summers should be similar – both in terms of their climate and factors like their length. But are Northern and Southern hemisphere summers really the same?

Climate experts tell Live Science that they differ quite a bit — and that comes with a clear recommendation for sun enthusiasts.

The most obvious difference is that Northern and Southern summers happen at different times. According to NASA, this arises because Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees relative to the plane of our planet's orbit around the sun.

This tilt causes the Northern and Southern hemispheres to be oriented toward the sun at different times throughout the year. Between the Northern Hemisphere's summer solstice and autumnal equinox, the Northern Hemisphere is oriented toward the sun, resulting in summer, and vice versa in the Southern Hemisphere.

This means that summers between the Northern and Southern hemispheres sit six months out of sync with each other — with Northern summers spanning late June to late September and Southern ones going from late December to late March. (Summers are also defined meteorologically, or relative to changes in weather phenomena, as being the hottest months of the year. Under this definition, Northern summers run from June to August, and Southern ones go from December to February.)

Another difference between Northern and Southern summers is their duration. According to NASA, Northern Hemisphere summers are, on average, 4.5 days longer than Southern Hemisphere summers. (This is with respect to the astronomical definition; meteorologically, Northern summers are longer than Southern ones by two days in non-leap years, but this is due to February being the calendar's shortest month.)

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The 4.5-day difference occurs because Earth's orbit around the sun is slightly elliptical instead of perfectly circular, according to NASA. Consequently, Earth's orbital velocity (the speed at which our planet hurtles around the sun) isn't constant.

Earth isn't the only planet that experiences such a dichotomy in the duration of seasons. According to NASA, Mars does too: Northern summers on the Red Planet are 24 Martian days — 24.66 Earth days — longer than the planet's Southern Hemisphere's summers. This greater difference is because Mars's orbit is much more oval-shaped than Earth's.

During the Northern Hemisphere's summer, Earth is farther away from the sun and thus moving more slowly, said Georg Feulner, a senior researcher at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. This is due to Kepler's second law of planetary motion, he added.

This means that at aphelion ‪(the point at which our planet is farthest from the sun)‬ Earth is traveling at 18.2 miles per second (29.3 kilometers per second). This jumps to 18.82 miles per second (30.29 km/s) at perihelion ‪(the point when Earth is closest to the sun ) which occurs during Southern summers.

While this may seem like a tiny difference in speed, it causes our planet's path around the sun to be 53,686 miles (86,400 kilometers) shorter in a 24-hour-interval at aphelion compared with at perihelion. In other words, Earth covers more "ground" at aphelion than at perihelion over a 24-hour-interval. "Therefore, the time between the Northern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes is longer than the time between the Southern Hemisphere spring and autumn equinoxes, Feulner told Live Science in an email.

A third point of difference is that Northern summers are typically hotter than Southern ones. A 2015 study in the journal Climate Dynamics showed the precise value of this depends on whether temperatures are measured on the surface air, land or ocean, and the latitude at which they're taken. Nonetheless, when averaged over all domains and latitudes, Northern summers are 7.83 degrees Fahrenheit (4.35 degrees Celsius) hotter than Southern ones.

So what's behind this? Earth's changing distance from the sun isn't important. If it were, Earth's aphelion crossing during Northern summers should make them cooler than Southern summers during the perihelion crossing. Instead, several other factors are responsible.

One is the Northern Hemisphere's bigger fraction of land compared to its large water bodies like oceans. "Land has a lower heat capacity than water and so increases temperature more for a given heating than water does," Richard Seager, a professor at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, told Live Science in an email. As a result, the many inland sites in the Northern Hemisphere heat up rapidly and have higher summer temperatures, according to the UCAR Center for Science Education.

Additionally, Seager said, another difference lies in the way heat is distributed through air and water. The solar heat that land receives warms only the first few feet of the atmosphere, while the heat water absorbs gets mixed throughout its depths. This makes the Southern Hemisphere — with its larger fraction of water — cooler over summer.

The second factor for the North Hemisphere's higher summer temperatures are cross-equatorial ocean currents. Such currents cross the equator, transferring water and heat between the hemispheres. The primary current is the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC). "The AMOC transports heat from the SH [Southern Hemisphere] to the NH in the Atlantic," Feulner said. This warms Northern oceans and seas, which, in turn, heats up adjacent land-masses.

So, Northern Hemisphere summers are longer and hotter than Southern ones. If you want to stretch out your summer, you now know where to go.

#6430. Tiny Arctic bacterium has an unexpected strategy for capturing carbon dioxide

Scientists discover an Arctic bacterium with an unusual metabolism that combines acetone consumption, sunlight, and carbon dioxide fixation.

A tiny bacterium drifting through the surface waters of the Arctic Ocean has been hiding an unusual metabolic trick.

It can’t eat sugar and it carries one of the smallest genomes of any marine microbe. And yet it thrives by doing something no one had documented in the marine world before.

This unusual organism appears equipped to break down acetone while incorporating dissolved carbon dioxide into its metabolism.

Researchers at Concordia University in Montreal and Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh have described the organism, Porticoccus arcticus, in a recent study.

Acetone is one of the most common volatile organic compounds floating around in seawater. It’s produced by phytoplankton, broken down from organic matter, and deposited from the atmosphere.

Arctic surface waters contain concentrations above 40 nanomolar – enough, it turns out, to sustain microbes.

The researchers first confirmed the concept in a related species, Porticoccus hydrocarbonoclasticus, a bacterium previously isolated from a lab culture.

When they offered it acetone as its only food, it grew. Its cell density was directly tied to how much acetone was available.

Higher concentrations actually proved toxic, which makes a certain biological sense. This is an organism tuned for scarcity, not abundance.

P. arcticus caught the team’s attention through metagenome-assembled genomes pulled from Canada Basin water samples.

Its genome is strikingly compact – just 1.29 million base pairs with a GC content of 41.6%.

For context, its closest well-characterized relative, P. hydrocarbonoclasticus, carries a genome nearly twice that size at 2.47 million base pairs and 53.1% GC content.

Its streamlined genome suggests that evolution has favored a compact set of genes suited to life in nutrient-poor waters.

It has no sugar transporters. Its glycolytic pathway is incomplete. It can’t break down glucose the way most bacteria do.

What it has kept, though, is telling. A complete acetone carboxylation pathway sits right there in the genome.

The other surprise is the light-harvesting equipment. P. arcticus carries two proteorhodopsin genes – molecular light-driven proton pumps – and neither one appears to be ancestral.

Phylogenetic analysis shows they were picked up through lateral gene transfer from distantly related bacteria, one from a Gammaproteobacterium and the other from a Betaproteobacterium.

The blue-light-absorbing proteorhodopsin dominates expression by a factor of roughly 64 over the green-light version.

That’s a sensible adaptation for an organism living in Arctic surface waters, where blue light penetrates farthest.

A carotenoid biosynthesis pathway also appears nearby, suggesting that the bacterium has additional machinery involved in producing pigments and protecting its cells from light-related damage.

“This organism has evolved a fascinating metabolic strategy,” said corresponding author David Walsh, a professor of biology at Concordia University.

“It combines the use of acetone as a carbon source with light-driven energy production, allowing it to thrive in nutrient-poor Arctic waters where other bacteria struggle to survive.”

This isn’t some boutique organism lurking at the edges of Arctic microbial communities.

The team analyzed microbial samples collected between 2017 and 2023 across a broad stretch of the Arctic Ocean.

P. arcticus showed up consistently. At some surface sites in the Canada Basin, it represented up to 9% of all 16S rRNA gene sequences at 5 and 20 meters depth.

It had a clear habitat preference: oligotrophic surface waters with intermediate sea ice cover. It was abundant at open ocean sites experiencing dynamic, year-to-year changes in ice conditions.

At permanently ice-covered stations and in deeper water layers, its numbers dropped sharply.

The real biogeochemical kicker is the carbon dioxide angle. P. arcticus carries a cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase.

This is an enzyme that converts dissolved CO2 into bicarbonate, the form its acetone carboxylase needs as a substrate.

So the acetone carboxylation isn’t just about eating acetone.

The acetone carboxylation reaction incorporates one molecule of inorganic carbon for every acetone molecule processed, linking acetone metabolism directly to carbon fixation.

“It’s a form of photoheterotrophy we haven’t seen before in the ocean,” Walsh said.

“This bacterium uses sunlight for energy while consuming acetone and fixing CO2 – it’s operating at the intersection of several metabolic strategies that were previously thought to be separate.”

The Arctic Ocean is warming faster than any other ocean basin on Earth.

As Arctic sea ice retreats and ocean conditions change, the habitat available to P. arcticus could shift, potentially altering its role in regional carbon cycling.

An organism that simultaneously consumes a volatile organic compound and fixes CO2 while being powered by light could play a larger role in Arctic carbon cycling than previously assumed.

The team is careful to note that the acetone carboxylation pathway they’ve identified could exist in other marine photoheterotrophs as well.

Its abundance in Arctic surface waters suggests that this previously overlooked metabolic pathway could have broader ecological importance.

Acetone degradation via carboxylation had only been described in terrestrial bacteria before this work.

The discovery reveals an overlooked pathway in the Arctic carbon cycle, suggesting that even the smallest ocean microbes may influence how carbon moves through the environment.

The study is published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6428. Exercise may be one of the most overlooked treatments for depression

Psychiatrists say doctors should prescribe exercise more clearly because physical activity may improve depression, memory, and mental health.

A five-minute walk can sound easy until depression has taken away your energy. Then a doctor’s advice to get more exercise may leave you wondering where to begin.

Trials show that exercise can ease symptoms of depression.

Three Canadian psychiatrists argue that doctors should prescribe exercise with the same care and attention they give antidepressant medications.

Carl Zhou and Nicholas Fabiano work in the psychiatry department at the University of Ottawa, and Stanley Wong works in the psychiatry department at the University of Toronto.

Their opinion piece draws on earlier research, with no new experiment of their own.

“We still tend to treat exercise as general lifestyle advice,” Zhou said.

“The evidence we reviewed supports something more deliberate: a prescription that names the type of activity, the frequency, the intensity, the duration, the safety considerations, and a plan for follow-up, just as we would for a medication.”

A muscle doesn’t just move a limb when it contracts. It also releases molecules called myokines, which may interact with chemical pathways involved in mood and thinking.

Researchers call that proposed connection the muscle-brain axis. The authors discuss it as one explanation for what exercise does, while making room for several others.

The brain needs a healthy blood supply and metabolism, and it needs inflammation kept under control. Learning, meanwhile, means changing the connections between its cells.

Exercise influences the heart, blood vessels, immune system, and growth signals that help with learning.

Better sleep, more confidence and social contact, and lower risks of blood vessel and metabolic disease may help explain its effects as well.

Kirk Erickson’s team spent a year studying exercise and the brains of 120 older adults without dementia.

In that 2011 trial, half the volunteers did moderate aerobic exercise, while the rest did stretching.

The team was interested in the hippocampus, which helps us remember things.

This region grew by about two percent in the aerobic group, mainly at the front, but shrank in the stretching group.

The researchers described the increase as reversing one to two years of age-related shrinkage.

Among those who exercised, greater growth went along with greater improvement on a memory test.

Being active has also been linked to better thinking skills and lower risks of dementia and Alzheimer’s disease.

Those links come largely from watching people’s habits, so those studies alone can’t tell us that exercise made the difference.

Researchers have put exercise to the test for depression and anxiety in randomized trials, letting chance decide who goes into each group.

The results show that activity programs can ease symptoms.

Walking and jogging helped, as did yoga and strength training.

A 2024 review in The BMJ reached that finding after bringing together 218 trials with 14,170 people who had depression.

More intense exercise generally brought greater relief, but there were reasons to be cautious about the research.

Only one trial passed the reviewers’ strictest check for avoiding bias, and their confidence in the findings was low or very low.

Someone struggling to exercise may find the next finding more encouraging.

A 2022 analysis of 15 long-term studies, covering 191,130 adults, found a link with lower depression risk even below the recommended activity level.

People who did about half the recommended amount had an 18% lower risk than those who reported no activity. Those doing the full amount had a 25% lower risk.

These studies observed people’s habits, so the figures don’t prove cause and effect. The largest difference appeared between doing nothing and doing a little.

For patients who can’t reach the full target, the authors suggest about 75 minutes of moderate activity a week as a place to start.

That’s roughly half the usual recommended minimum.

Medicines for schizophrenia offer limited help with thinking difficulties, even though those difficulties affect how a person manages everyday life. Exercise may have something to offer there.

Ten trials involving 385 people with schizophrenia went into a 2017 analysis, which found better overall thinking with aerobic exercise.

Exercise also showed potential benefits for working memory, which helps people hold and use information, and social cognition, which helps them understand others.

People with schizophrenia and other severe mental illnesses tend to spend long hours sitting and have high rates of heart disease, metabolic disease, and early death.

The authors point partly to the illness, social disadvantage, and the metabolic side effects of some medicines.

“In schizophrenia, exercise can work on psychiatric symptoms, cognition, and physical health at the same time, in a population with substantial unmet needs in all three,” Wong said.

The thinking results came from only a few small trials, though.

The World Health Organization recommends 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week for adults, plus muscle-strengthening work on at least two days.

Brisk walking counts as moderate; for vigorous activity, such as running or fast cycling, the range is 75 to 150 minutes.

A patient doesn’t have to begin at that level.

If depression has drained their energy, motivation, and concentration, the first step might be a five-minute walk, a walk with the dog, or exercises in a chair.

“The starting point does not have to be impressive,” Fabiano said. “It has to be possible.”

For most patients, the authors suggest a low-risk activity that they can gradually do more of.

Pain or dizziness may signal a need to adjust the exercise plan, while chest pain or severe breathlessness calls for immediate medical attention.

Others may need a medical check, physiotherapy, supervision, or a brief pause before increasing their activity.

That includes people who are frail or have unstable heart or breathing symptoms, recent falls or fainting, an infection, or uncontrolled pain.

Wong wants larger trials to find out whether the thinking gains seen in schizophrenia hold up. The existing trials leave that question open.

Researchers are also exploring exercise mimetics, drugs or other agents that might copy some of the chemical changes exercise causes.

These could, in theory, help with depression in people whose symptoms, disability, or frailty prevent them from moving enough.

The authors see these as a possible addition to treatment, with safe activity continuing wherever it is possible.

They also point out that exercise prescriptions could widen health gaps if patients can’t get the help they need to follow them.

They want funded community exercise programs, help with transportation, and partnerships with recreation and community centers.

The goal is not to turn every patient into an athlete, but to make physical activity a realistic, supported part of mental health treatment.

The opinion piece is published in the journal Brain Health.

#6427. A striking Mars cloud may be born from surprising physics

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud might not need dust to kick-start its formation

The Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud emerges every day during spring and summer on Mars, a long wispy ribbon downwind of the Arsia Mons volcano. This image of the cloud was captured by a camera aboard the European Space Agency’s Mars Express mission.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

One of Mars’ strangest clouds may rely on unusual physics to emerge.

The Red Planet’s ribbonlike cloud — which stretches as long as four Grand Canyons laid end-to-end — may form without a speck of starting material to seed it, researchers report October 7 in Nature Geoscience. This manner of forming clouds, called homogenous nucleation, was thought to be possible on paper but not to occur naturally.

Tiny particles such as dust or salt floating in the air seed typical clouds on Earth. But that cloud physics doesn’t seem to apply to the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud. Beyond its impressive length, this wisp of water ice is remarkably consistent, forming daily in the same spot roughly 45 kilometers high on the slope of a Martian volcano for several months each year.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The team tried and tried but couldn’t reproduce the cloud’s formation, including its lengthy tail and consistent cycle, with computer models employing standard cloud physics, says François Forget, an astrophysicist at the Laboratoire de Météorologie Dynamique, or LMD, in Paris.

There’s no shortage of dust on Mars. The trouble is that high up in a thin Martian atmosphere, few cloud-forming dust particles stay suspended. Instead, they probably clump together and eventually fall, says planetary physicist Jorge Hernández-Bernal, who did the work at LMD. This left cloud formation without seeds as the most convincing explanation, he says.

Every day during some seasons on Mars, a long wispy cloud emerges along the flanks of the Arsia Mons volcano, as seen in the observations video spanning three Martian hours. How that cloud forms has been a mystery. A new simulation, bottom, included unusual physics, in which clouds form without starting material. That approach replicated the shape and timing of Mars’ Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud for the first time.

The team’s model suggests that the eye-catching plume originates when air flowing across the volcano triggers a rapid lifting of a moist parcel of air. The decrease in pressure at that altitude lets the air parcel expand, rapidly cooling it.

The newly cooled air now has 100,000 times more moisture than it can hold, the team’s model suggests. This excess moisture undergoes homogenous nucleation, rapidly forming more stable ice crystals. Winds sweep the forming cloud outward, creating the cloud’s distinctive long shape.

While the model doesn’t perfectly match satellite observations, it does capture how the phenomenon that leads to the cold air pocket reoccurs day after day, just like the real cloud does.

The study was surprising because “homogeneous nucleation is generally treated in our field as this theoretical concept,” says Samuel Atwood, an atmospheric and planetary scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., who was not associated with the study.

“It’s a pretty compelling story that they’re telling with the model, but it’s only one view or one perspective on it,” Atwood says, adding that future measurements supporting the team’s finding will provide more certainty. Hernández-Bernal says that he plans to validate the study by testing alternative explanations.

Even beyond Mars, the study provides food for thought. Previous studies have suggested that on Earth, meteor smoke provides particles for cloud formation in an upper layer of the atmosphere called the mesosphere, though a few studies have suggested homogenous nucleation could be responsible. Now that scientists are proposing homogenous nucleation on Mars, Hernández-Bernal says, “maybe there will be an increased interest in investigating this on Earth.”

The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.

The Hubble Space Telescope's optical light view of the Cat's Head Nebula.

Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in near-infrared light.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in mid-infrared light.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

#6424. Ancient viruses left behind genes that are still spreading millions of years later

Ancient virus genes moved between yeast species, possibly with help from insects, revealing a surprising way evolution works.

Genes usually move down a family tree, from parents to their offspring.

In a group of yeasts that live on rotting wood, a bundle of genes left behind by an ancient virus has also moved sideways, from one species into another.

A new genetic study found evidence of at least three of those crossings.

As far as the researchers know, it’s the first documented case of a whole cluster of genes from an ancient RNA virus moving between species.

Derek Taylor, a biologist at the University at Buffalo, did the work with master’s student Dominic Tringali.

They suspect that wood-eating insects, which carry these yeasts in their guts and leave them in their droppings, brought different species close enough to swap DNA.

“It’s an evolutionary whodunit, and wood-eating insects had the means and opportunity,” said Taylor, a professor in the university’s Department of Biological Sciences.

All of the evidence came from DNA. The team compared publicly available genomes from 18 yeast species and strains rather than watching a transfer happen in the lab.

The genes came from a totivirus, a kind of virus that infects fungi, including yeasts. It mostly passes from one generation of cells to the next when a cell divides.

Totiviruses carry their genes as RNA and have no built-in way to write themselves into a host’s DNA, the way HIV does.

Even so, a copy of one ended up in an ancestor of these yeasts, which belong to a group called Scheffersomyces.

Exactly how that happened isn’t known. The researchers propose that the yeast cell itself copied the viral RNA into DNA.

Taylor and a colleague first described the cluster in a 2009 paper, working with a yeast called Scheffersomyces stipitis. The cluster holds four genes in a row.

One of them carries both of the virus’s main parts, the instructions for its protein shell and for the enzyme that copies its RNA.

The other three are extra copies of the shell gene alone, made after the virus’s genes joined the yeast’s DNA.

The team named the cluster STORM. In the yeasts where it was first found, it has held the same spot in the genome for at least 15 million years. It may be much older.

If genes pass only from parent to offspring, their family tree should match the family tree of the species that carry them. STORM’s tree didn’t.

In two of the crossings, the cluster in one group of yeasts looked most like the cluster in a more distant group. Biologists call this kind of sideways move horizontal gene transfer.

It’s well known among microbes, and it has been documented in fungi and even plants.

To see how unusual STORM’s pattern was, the team built family trees for 3,527 other genes shared by all 18 yeasts. None of those trees reproduced any of the three STORM patterns in full.

“Now we have compelling evidence that an entire four-gene cluster has crossed species boundaries,” Taylor said.

Crossbreeding between species could in principle produce a similar pattern.

But it would have taken at least two separate episodes, and the team found no sign that the donor species’ DNA had spread widely through the rest of the genome.

The third crossing replaced only part of the cluster. In one strain of S. stipitis, the first three genes were swapped for versions that most resemble those of a related species, Scheffersomyces segobiensis.

The fourth gene and the DNA on either side kept their S. stipitis ancestry.

One crossing left more evidence behind than the others.

Beside STORM in a yeast called Scheffersomyces insectosa, the team found the broken remains of a jumping gene.

These stretches of DNA, known as transposons, can move from one place in a genome to another.

The researchers named this family of transposons YEET, short for Yeast Endogenous Element Transposon.

Its remains near STORM, and a broken yeast gene next to them, both looked like they came from the same donor group as STORM itself.

“Because STORM and a neighboring jumping gene show evidence of the same unusual evolutionary history, we suspect the transposon may have carried STORM between yeast species as extra cargo,” Tringali said.

YEET transposons appear to have crossed between these rotting-wood yeasts on their own, too, in at least five cases. How the other full-cluster crossing happened remains unclear.

Scheffersomyces yeasts share living space in rotting logs, in insect droppings, and inside the guts of wood-eating insects.

One species in the group, described as new in 2025, was isolated from the cocoon wall of a stag beetle.

“In order to exchange genomic material, you have to be in the same place at the same time,” Taylor said.

The authors wrote that these shared homes give different yeasts chances to swap DNA. Contact alone, though, doesn’t show how the DNA actually moved.

RNA viruses change quickly, and genes borrowed from them are generally expected to slow down once they become part of a host’s genome. STORM went the other way.

The team estimated that its proteins changed about seven times faster than those of related viruses that still infect cells.

Depending on how old the researchers assumed the cluster to be, the estimate ranged from just under six to nearly nine times faster.

“These genes have had an extraordinary evolutionary afterlife,” Tringali said. “Long after the original virus disappeared, its genes continued to evolve, multiply and spread between yeast species.”

The four genes didn’t all change in the same way. The fourth gene changed the most.

Tests suggested that natural selection weakened on that gene and let changes build up, rather than favoring new versions of it.

Yet that gene held on to a key part of one of the virus’s tricks. Related yeast viruses take the protective chemical cap off the front of the cell’s own RNA messages and use it on their own.

The fourth gene still carries the amino acids that form the virus’s cap-holding pocket.

Selection on the first gene grew stronger instead, compared with the second and third.

Computer predictions of protein shapes suggested that all four genes still carry instructions for proteins shaped like a virus shell.

The cluster isn’t silent. In genetic data from five yeast species and strains, cells were making RNA copies of all four genes, and the first gene was usually the most active.

In one species, the first and fourth genes were about three times as active in flasks built to mix in more oxygen.

Those growth tests weren’t designed to probe viral infection, so the genes’ activity could be tied to RNA handling, to the yeasts’ surroundings, or to defense against viruses.

There’s a hint for that last idea. In a 2018 experiment, a shell-like gene from another yeast, Debaryomyces hansenii, cleared a related virus out of baker’s yeast.

Of the two S. segobiensis strains, the one with an intact cluster carried no detectable totivirus. The one without an intact cluster was the only strain in the survey that did.

“Totiviruses are kind of like a frenemy for yeast. Under some conditions, they help the host deal with physiological stress,” Taylor said.

“So it might be useful for a yeast to keep a virus’ benefits around without having to worry about controlling the virus.”

What the four STORM proteins actually do inside a yeast cell is still untested.

The team hopes to grow the yeasts under different kinds of stress and see whether the genes respond.

The results could point to the job the genes now do for their hosts.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Biology and Evolution.

#6422. A generation feeling powerless: College students are overwhelmed by climate anxiety

New research reveals widespread climate anxiety among college students, with many feeling powerless and universities facing calls to provide more support.

Only four percent of college students in a recent survey reported feeling hopeful about the climate crisis frequently or “a lot.”

Many others reported a bleak mix of powerlessness, frustration, and anxiety.

Yet universities may not be doing enough to help students manage these difficult emotions.

That’s the uncomfortable takeaway from a pair of interdisciplinary studies out of the University of Utah.

Researchers surveyed hundreds of undergraduates about how climate change makes them feel and what, if anything, helps them cope.

The research team, led by environmental scientist Jennifer Follstad Shah and psychologist Monika Lohani, surveyed 547 students enrolled across three environmental studies courses and one communication course.

They asked a simple question: when you think about climate change, what do you feel?

Fifty-four percent of students reported feeling powerless frequently or “a lot.” Fifty-five percent said the same about frustration.

Anger, worry, fear, and anxiety clustered right behind, each hitting the “a lot” category for roughly one in five students. Meanwhile, 58 percent said they never felt happiness about the climate situation.

Only four percent reported feeling hopeful frequently or “a lot.” Even when students who experienced hope less often were included, the figure reached just 40 percent.

Here’s where the study gets interesting. Environmental studies majors did score higher on the researchers’ Climate Anxiety Index.

But once the statistical models accounted for other variables, a student’s major stopped being a significant predictor of climate anxiety altogether.

The final hierarchical regression model, which explained 52 percent of the variance in climate anxiety scores, pointed to different culprits.

These included political ideology, how often students encountered climate information, whether they ranked climate change as a top personal concern, and their levels of general anxiety.

“They’re not alone,” Shah said. “There’s a lot of students feeling that way, and likely a lot of adults feeling that way.”

The relationship between climate anxiety and generalized anxiety turned out to be striking.

Climate anxiety and general anxiety were closely related, although the researchers could not determine whether one contributed to the other.

Students with moderate-to-high climate anxiety tended to report low-to-moderate general anxiety.

These findings suggest that climate and general anxiety are closely related but remain distinct psychological experiences.

“It may be that climate anxiety is a contributor to general anxiety, as well as the converse,” Shah said.

Gender told a similar nuanced story. Women in the study reported significantly higher general anxiety than men, and initially appeared more climate-anxious too.

But once general anxiety was accounted for, gender dropped out as a predictor entirely.

The findings suggest that differences in general anxiety, rather than gender itself, may help explain the higher climate anxiety initially reported by women.

Not all information sources hit the same way. Classroom learning and online media – especially social media – were both significant predictors of higher climate anxiety.

However, information from friends, family, and co-workers barely registered.

Fewer than 30 percent of students reported getting climate information from family or colleagues with any regularity.

The findings suggest that climate change may come up less often in everyday conversations than in classrooms or online.

One interaction caught the researchers’ attention. For students outside environmental studies, more online climate exposure correlated significantly with higher anxiety.

For environmental studies majors, that link vanished.

Some of these students described engaging in “hopescrolling” – deliberately curating their feeds toward solutions-focused content rather than doom.

Lohani’s companion study dug into what students actually do with all this distress. Some found relief in nature, pets, self-care, or learning more about the science itself.

“The knowledge is empowering them to understand the intricacies. That makes them not feel hopeless,” Lohani said.

“All the progress in terms of technology that has come out to combat the carbon footprint actually made them feel more hopeful.”

But many students described shutting down entirely. One wrote: “Sometimes I just don’t feel like doing anything at all because it makes me so anxious.”

“Those who are overwhelmed, they might be catastrophizing or using avoidance or distraction, which ultimately is not good for their well-being, or efforts to address the climate change crisis,” Lohani noted.

“Those who are apathetic towards it, that is not bad for their well-being in the short run, but ultimately it is affecting them and their community.”

Both researchers argued that campuses need to stop treating climate anxiety as background noise.

Their recommendations are concrete: establish climate anxiety support groups within counseling centers, fund cross-departmental forums for open discussion, and train instructors to expect emotional responses to climate material.

The University of Utah’s own environmental studies program has already begun hosting Good Grief Circles, modeled on the Good Grief Network co-founded by Laura Schmidt, a 2014 Utah graduate.

These peer support sessions give students space to process ecological distress without judgment.

“Don’t be afraid to talk about it and let people know that you feel this way,” Shah said. “There’s power in those bonds.”

The study has its limits – the sample skewed female (66 percent), White (69 percent), and politically left-leaning (63 percent).

It was drawn from a single university in the arid Mountain West, where shrinking Great Salt Lake levels and megadrought make climate impacts impossible to ignore.

The researchers are calling for broader studies across more diverse campuses and majors.

Despite these limitations, the findings suggest that climate anxiety extends beyond students majoring in environmental subjects.

It is closely linked to general anxiety and affects students across academic disciplines, raising questions about whether universities provide enough emotional support.

The students surveyed said, overwhelmingly, that they want more opportunities to talk about it. The question is whether anyone’s listening.

The study is published in the journal Sustainability.

#6421. Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Madagascan flying foxes, easy targets for hunters, have shrunk since the 1980s

Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus) (shown) have skulls that are 6 percent smaller than they were prior to the 1980s. Large-scale hunting by humans may be the reason.

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.

With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).

“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.

To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.

Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.

“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.

As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.

It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.

The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.

“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”
