#6419. Restaurant cooking is becoming a surprisingly major source of air pollution

Restaurant cooking is emerging as a major source of urban air pollution, sometimes exceeding vehicle exhaust emissions during peak dining hours.

The smell of food drifting out of a restaurant rarely makes people think of air pollution.

Yet new research shows that in parts of central London and Beijing, cooking releases more fine particles than vehicle exhaust during lunch and dinner hours.

Cleaner vehicles and tighter exhaust rules appear to have helped change that balance. Kitchens have faced less attention: UK and European rules require them to extract fumes, but do not require filters.

Ben Langford, an atmospheric scientist at the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, led the research.

His team measured emissions from one central neighborhood each in London, Beijing and Delhi, three cities with more than 10 million people.

“Most people smell cooking but never consider it as a pollutant, yet cooking can release large amounts of fine particulate matter into the atmosphere,” Langford said.

The team placed instruments on London’s BT Tower, 623 feet (190 meters) above the street, and on a Beijing tower at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics, 335 feet (102 meters) up.

In Old Delhi, they worked 108 feet (33 meters) above ground at Indira Gandhi Delhi Technical University for Women.

Above the rooftops, a wind sensor and an instrument that identifies chemicals in particles took readings five times a second.

Matching the air’s upward and downward movements with what it carried showed how much pollution came from the surrounding neighborhood.

Frying oil, car exhaust and coal fires produce different chemical mixtures, which helped the team trace particles to their sources.

To measure pollution moving through the air, the researchers separated their readings into upward and downward air movements.

These tiny particles can travel deep into the lungs, and some may enter the bloodstream.

In London, cooking produced up to 83% of the measured particle emissions at midday and 87% in the early evening. In Beijing, those shares reached 61% and 76%.

Both towers overlooked areas with many restaurants, and the researchers think commercial frying produced most of the cooking smoke.

At some hours, traffic contributed less than 10% of local emissions in both cities.

Beijing’s cooking emissions were about 75% higher in winter than summer, partly perhaps because the wind changed direction.

Winter winds mostly brought air from restaurants and commercial buildings to the northwest, while summer winds brought more air from a highway to the east.

Europe has tightened exhaust standards in stages since 1992.

London also introduced a congestion charge and an ultra-low emission zone, and its restrictions on polluting solid fuels helped keep coal and wood smoke barely detectable.

Study co-author Eiko Nemitz, also at the UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, pointed to the success of traffic controls.

“Air quality policies targeting vehicle exhaust emissions have been highly effective,” Nemitz said. “As a result, cooking emissions are now a surprisingly important and poorly regulated part of the urban pollution mix.”

Earlier research in New York found a similar shift, with cooking, wildfire smoke and chemical products becoming increasingly important sources of summertime particle pollution.

Old Delhi told a different story: cooking accounted for 8% of direct particle emissions over an average day, while traffic contributed 56%.

Yet its cooking emissions per unit of area exceeded central London’s in winter and were only about 35% lower in summer.

Cooking’s small share reflects the much larger contribution from traffic and other burning.

The Delhi site stood near busy roads, a railway station and a large bus terminal, and the area released roughly two to four times as much soot as central London.

Both Beijing and Delhi restrict diesel vehicles to nighttime hours. The researchers suggested that looser emission controls and more older vehicles help explain Delhi’s higher soot levels.

Kitchen exhaust filters may have less impact in Delhi, where many homes have poor ventilation and more cooking happens outdoors.

The authors said traffic and other burning should remain the main targets there.

The sources releasing particles locally did not match the mix already in the air.

Cooking accounted for just 5% to 10% of airborne fine particles in London and Beijing, while traffic contributed 5% to 18%.

Much of the pollution formed in the air from gases, including ammonia, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide. Many of these particles formed across the wider region, beyond the city center.

Particles formed this way accounted for 59% to 63% of the total in London’s and Beijing’s air, compared with 30% in Delhi.

Most of Delhi’s particles were organic material, from both local traffic and burning and distant sources such as farm fires.

The towers measured neighborhood emissions, but the air above them also contained pollution formed or carried in from elsewhere.

Cutting local emissions alone may therefore leave London and Beijing above World Health Organization guidelines, the authors wrote.

Most official pollution inventories leave cooking out. The UK counts cooking fuel but not smoke from the food, while European and global inventories omit cooking altogether.

The London Atmospheric Emissions Inventory added cooking recently.

Most of the BT Tower’s measurement area lies in Westminster, where the inventory put cooking at 44% of annual emissions after excluding brake and tire wear, close to the tower’s 45%.

Still, the inventory estimated about 76% more cooking emissions than the tower measured.

The winter measurements took place during the UK’s Plan B rules for the Omicron variant of COVID-19, introduced on December 8, 2021, which may have reduced restaurant and pub visits.

Cooking smoke also raises health concerns, as chefs face a higher risk of respiratory illness than other people.

Earlier research suggests fatty acids in cooking particles may help them stay airborne for days instead of hours.

Langford said better kitchen filtration could offer a relatively quick way to improve air quality.

“Over recent decades we have dramatically reduced emissions from road transport, but we have paid far less attention to emissions from commercial kitchens and food preparation,” Langford said.

“Our results suggest this is an area where further improvements in air quality could be achieved relatively quickly through better filtration of kitchen fumes.”

The study is published in the journal npj Climate and Atmospheric Science.

Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale.

The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year.

This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing.

Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant.

"The hypothesis is that the whales are staying in areas with greater productivity [more food] farther south, in waters with slightly cooler temperatures," Daniela Alarcón, the expedition's leader and a researcher at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito's Galápagos campus and the Galápagos Science Center, told Live Science.

As to where the missing whales have gone, possibilities include the waters off Peru and offshore areas where the animals could go undetected. In this scenario, the unusually warm waters around the Galápagos Islands would act as a "temperature barrier," Alarcón said, preventing them from feeding in the archipelago's waters.

Blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can consume up to 12,100 pounds (5,500 kilograms) of krill — small crustaceans that make up the whales' primary food source — every day. That means they need to find areas with enough food to sustain them.

"These are very large animals that need to move to areas where they can keep feeding," Alarcón said.

It's not yet clear whether this year's El Niño caused a krill shortage in the waters off the Galápagos, but some indirect evidence points that way.

We thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing.

Past expeditions suggested that blue whales tend to feed in water layers around 71 F, which this season was identified around the Galápagos at a depth of about 197 feet (92 m). By contrast, peak chlorophyll concentrations, an indirect indicator of abundance of the krill's food source, phytoplankton ‪—‬ were recorded much higher in the water column, at between 39 and 121 feet (12 to 37 m) below the surface. Because krill abundance wasn't directly measured, that data suggests, but does not establish, that there was a mismatch between the whales' preferred feeding layer and the presence of their food.

"Honestly, we had never encountered such unusual conditions before," Juan Pablo Muñoz, a marine biologist at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito who was also on the expedition, told Live Science.

The whales' absence did not come as a complete surprise to the team. Sightings had already begun to decline before the most recent expedition. Reports submitted through Cetácea Galápagos, a citizen science network, began to dwindle between August and September 2025. There were two isolated reports of blue whales, in May and June 2026, but the team could not confirm either one, despite intensifying its search.

"We knew conditions wouldn't be the same, but we thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing," Alarcón recalled.

Despite nine months of looking, a recent expedition to search for blue whales around the Galápagos region did not spot a single one.

Part of that could be down to the elusive nature of the giant creatures. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae)are generally easier to spot, Muñoz noted. In some places, they can be seen from the shore or after a half-hour boat ride. Blue whales, by contrast, rarely approach mainland Ecuador's coast and tend to stay far from populated areas in the Galápagos.

Fernando Félix, a marine biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador who was not part of the expedition, was unsurprised by the result.

"We already knew there wouldn't be any blue whales in the Galápagos," said Félix, who is also a researcher at the Whale Museum (Museo de Ballenas).

Félix told Live Science that there are historical precedents for this behavior in the southeastern Pacific. During the 1982-1983 El Niño, which also brought substantial ocean warming, blue whales and other species, including fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and Bryde's whales (Balaenoptera brydei), were recorded shifting southward.

"We might think that because they are 'just animals,' they lack memory or don't understand these processes — but we would be wrong," Félix said. "They can clearly sense that when temperatures are unusually high as they travel north from the south, vertical mixing has been disrupted and there is no food in the Galápagos. They perceive environmental conditions and naturally direct their movements toward areas where they believe feeding conditions are better."

Sea surface and subsurface temperatures during the 2015 El Niño, showing a band of warmer water at depth. After that season, whale sightings bounced back, suggesting the missing blue whales will return once water conditions cool.

Rather than indicating a mass die-off, the whales' disappearance may reflect a shift in their movements in response to changing ocean conditions, Félix said.

"I don't think the whales have died," Felix said. "They simply didn't go to the Galápagos region. They went elsewhere, where conditions were better."

This response to environmental conditions may also have impacted dolphin movements. Pods may have moved toward colder waters, where food could be more abundant, or may have even dispersed, Félix suggested.

El Niño's effects will likely persist over the coming months. "Between January and May 2027, we'll have warm water coming from the north and warm water coming from the west," Félix warned. "This is going to hit us extremely hard."

Blue whales, humpback whales and dolphins would likely return to Galápagos waters once El Niño subsides and ocean conditions begin to normalize. He said pelagic fish (species that live in the water column rather than on or near the seafloor) ‪—‬ including tuna, swordfish, anchovies and sardines, which have also moved toward colder waters ‪—‬ would return as well.

Muñoz agreed. Krill populations can rebound just one to three months after cold, nutrient-rich waters begin to rise to the surface. More whale sightings were recorded in the years following the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events. Based on these precedents, he suggested that 2028 could be a promising year if cold water returns to the surface. "The system bounces back," he said.

Félix compared El Niño to a computer restart. "It resets the environment, allowing ecological processes to begin again," he said. He's confident that blue whales will return to the area. "I can guarantee that there will be large numbers of blue whales at this time in 2028," he told Live Science.

#6415. Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Fast east-west flights unlink birds’ internal clocks from the sun, scrambling navigation

A Manx shearwater soars in midflight. New research suggests that a phenomenon akin to jet lag can disrupt the seabirds’ ability to navigate using the sun.

Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.

Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.

For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.

Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.

Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.

“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.

The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.

This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.

“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

#6414. What Happens If Your Passport Expires While You're Abroad?

Most countries don't allow international travelers to enter their territory unless they have at least six months left before their passport expires. That might sound like an unnecessary ask for a week-long vacation, but the rule is in place for good reason.

That's because if you do find yourself in a scenario when your passport expires while you're abroad—say due to an unexpected medical issue or trip delay, for example—you could be facing a major bureaucratic headache.

However, although it might feel like a crisis, having your passport lapse while traveling is not the end of the world. There are procedures that travelers can follow to obtain a renewed document and get their trip back on track. Here’s a look at what happens if your passport expires while you’re abroad.

Many countries do not allow international tourists to visit unless they have a certain amount of validity left on their passport. A common rule of thumb that many nations observe is the six month rule: there must be at least six months before your passport expires in order to enter the country.

In some countries, including many popular destinations in the EU, your passport is required to be valid for an additional three months after your intended departure date. Before you board an international flight, airlines will verify your passport expiration and usually will not let you board the plane if your passport doesn’t meet the validity requirements. It's important to note that some airlines and cruise lines might have their own passport validity policies that differ from the country's official requirements, so be sure to check both.

Sometimes, it’s possible to enter a different country and stay past your passport’s expiration date. If that's the case, the protocol you’ll need to follow is similar to when a passport is lost or stolen abroad.

First, you’ll need to contact the nearest US embassy or consulate for assistance. If you’re not sure where the nearest embassy or consulate might be, you can use the search tool on the State Department’s website. You’ll need to then visit the embassy or consulate location in person in order to have them issue you a new passport. Keep in mind this could mean you need to travel to a different city within the country you’re visiting.

When you arrive, you’ll essentially need to apply for a new passport. That means you’ll need to bring:

“Even if you cannot present all these documents, consular staff will do their best to help you get a new passport quickly,” the State Department’s site says.

US citizens abroad who have urgent travel plans are usually issued an emergency passport, which is valid for up to one year. However, it’s also possible to get a full-validity passport that doesn’t expire for 10 years. It will depend on the specifics of your situation.

Replacement passports are usually issued by the next business day, according to the State Department.

If you’re a US citizen living overseas for an extended period of time, you might qualify for routine passport renewal by mail through the nearest US embassy or consulate. Processing times for renewal by mail are usually about four to six weeks, not including shipping time. Visit the website of the local embassy or consulate in your area and follow their instructions for passport renewal.

#6413. A Startup Wants to Put 50,000 Mirrors in Space. The Goal: Make Sunlight Available at Night.

For $5,000 an hour, Reflect Orbital will bring you the power of the sun no matter what time of night it is. Astronomers are sounding the alarm.

With the launch of Sputnik in October 1957, humanity officially entered the satellite era, and in the ensuing decades, the thousands of satellites sent into space have drastically changed life on the ground. These sprawling networks of orbital spacecraft provide us with constant GPS navigation, communication, weather forecasting, and an unprecedented level of scientific surveys. But for ground-based astronomers, satellites have been a steadily growing headache.

Problems really started back in 2019 when SpaceX launched the first cadre of Starlink satellites, and almost immediately their immense number and brightness disrupted ground-based observations of space. Today, there are more than 11,000 Starlink satellites, and scientists worry about their impact on next-generation telescopes, including the new Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile.

Now astronomers may have an even bigger problem on their hands: Reflect Orbital. If you haven’t heard of this company, that’s not surprising. Unlike SpaceX, they currently don’t have any satellites in orbit at all, but what they plan to do with those satellites once they’re nestled within Earth’s orbit has astrophysicists begging for the federal government to intervene.

“This is not a ‘concern’—this is like a bullet in your head,” Princeton University astrophysicist Gaspar Bakos told Sky & Telescope. “It’s the end of ground-based astronomy.”

So what exactly has astronomers like Bakos up in arms? Well, Reflect Orbital bills itself as a “sunlight-as-a-service” company whose constellation of 50,000 satellites, each armed with massive mirrors, directs sunlight toward dark areas of the planet. The company says users could conceivably call for sunlight on demand to power solar panels or aid in nighttime search-and-rescue operations. But this altruistic vision likely obscures more lucrative use-cases for the military. That seems especially likely given the going rate for sunlight: $5,000 an hour, according to Sky & Telescope. That price is well beyond the budget of most search-and-rescue groups.

Then there’s life on the ground. Plants and animals, humans included, depend on a day-night cycle that’s existed since Earth formed in the fiery cauldron of our star’s protoplanetary disk. Artificial sunlight could throw that rhythm off. Reflect Orbital CEO Ben Nowack dismissed these fears to the outlet Payload by saying that some people once feared light bulbs.

“I think a lot of people are scared of new things,” Nowack told Payload. “Similar concerns and fears were brought up when light bulbs were introduced to the world, and people were worried about circadian rhythm and like, is this godly?…I think it’s a sign that we’re doing something that’s really new and really important.”

On October 10, Reflect Orbital conducted a test of its technology near the town of Independence, California. As previously noted, the company doesn’t have any satellites in space yet, so instead they used giant, angled flood lights to mimic what the beam would look like from space and invited search-and-rescue groups to the demonstration. For astronomers, the blinding light confirmed their worst fears. Those fears have only grown since mid-July, when the Federal Communications Commission approved the company’s request to build a demonstration satellite called Earendil-1. The name continues the annoying trend of startups borrowing from The Lord of the Rings for their technologies.

“You might think a space mirror could illuminate a customer’s solar farm or a rescue site while leaving everything else untouched,” Macquarie University astrophysicist Richard de Grijs wrote for The Conversation. “That’s not quite how it works, because Earth’s atmosphere doesn’t respect sharp boundaries.”

A study in The Astrophysical Journal of Letters showed how molecules and aerosols would scatter this reflected sunlight, and another study detailed how a satellite with a 54-meter mirror (which is the operational goal) would still be brighter than our planet’s lone satellite if you were eight miles away from the beam. Within the beam, light would appear 40 times brighter than the moon, and the sky would be as luminous as after-sunset twilight. If Reflect Orbital reaches its planned 50,000-satellite constellation, the night sky would become three to four times brighter overall, according to the European Southern Observatory.

For now, the company is forging ahead with its plan to launch its first satellites with India’s Skyroot Aerospace, which will require authorization with the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre. This means the company could technically sidestep U.S. regulatory approval entirely.

“This whole question we have is: Who owns the night sky?” University of Alabama astronomer Michelle Wooten told Sky & Telescope. “I really feel that people should have a say on what their night sky looks like.”

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Roman-era Lycurgus Cup has a color-changing effect depending on the light source.

The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.

In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).

The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.

Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.

Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.

For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.

A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.

But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.

#6411. The Sky Today on Monday, November 2: The Moon passes Jupiter and Mars

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

The Moon slides 1.1° south of Mars at 9 A.M. EST, then passes 0.5° south of Jupiter at 6 P.M. EST. Some parts of the world will see these planets disappear behind the Moon, although this is not visible from North America. Instead, we’ll focus on the trio’s appearance before this in the early-morning sky, where they dominate in the hours before sunrise.

By 5 A.M. local time, western Leo is more than 50° high in the southeast. The Moon lies just to Mars’ upper right, roughly 1.5° southwest of the Red Planet’s position and 6.3° west-northwest of Jupiter. The gas giant is by far the brightest light here, shining at magnitude –2.0. This morning it lies halfway between the Moon and Regulus to its lower left (east), Leo’s alpha star and the base of the Sickle asterism.

This view offers a great opportunity to see just how far the Moon travels through our sky in a day. By tomorrow morning at the same time, Luna will have moved some 14° to the east, passing close to Regulus and standing southeast of the star in the early-morning sky at the same time. Make sure to check out the view tomorrow for comparison.

Sunrise: 6:30 A.M.Sunset: 4:56 P.M.Moonrise: —Moonset: 1:41 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (36%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

The Moon passes 0.8° south of the bright star Regulus in Leo at 4 A.M. EST on November 3. Some regions of the world will see our satellite pass in front of Regulus in an occultation, but again, the event is not visible from North America.

The pair rises together shortly after midnight on the 2nd, following Jupiter and Mars by roughly an hour. By 5 A.M. local time on the 3rd, the Moon-star pair is nearly 50° high in the southeast. Despite its brightness (it is ranked as the 21st brightest star in the sky), magnitude 1.4 Regulus will be the faintest object in this region, as magnitude 0.8 Mars and magnitude –2.0 Jupiter to its west (upper right) far outshine it.

The waning Moon has shrunk from roughly 43% lit yesterday morning to 33% lit today. It is just under a week from New phase, which occurs on the 9th. Between now and then, the phase will continue to diminish and the Moon will rise later in the morning each day, until it travels across the sky in tandem with the Sun when it is New.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6410. A proof-of-concept test can spot bladder cancer in urine

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Urine may also reveal the presence of kidney and prostrate cancers

A new proof-of-concept test surveys RNA in urine to spot bladder cancer. RNA carries information that can reveal what cancer is present and how it is behaving.

Andrew Brookes/Connect Images/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.

Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”

Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.

The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.

Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

#6409. Copenhagen is Opening a Stunning New Bathhouse Along Its Harbor This December—And It's Shockingly Affordable

Copenhagen is a swimmer’s city. "The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears, or the sea," Danish author Karen Blixen, who lived up the coast from Copenhagen, famously wrote in 1934. Locals and visitors alike have taken her words to heart ever since.

In the early 2000s, floating swimming pools were introduced to the Danish capital's harbor after the city's shipbuilding industry collapsed. These pools turned an unused space into a playground for swimmers, divers, water polo enthusiasts, and boaters, especially on hot summer days. In recent years, cold plunging has also risen in popularity as a way to help with mental and physical health—nowadays, you can expect winter swimming clubs with sauna access along the harbor to have lengthy waiting lists.

The new bathing house was designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates and has been 8 years in the making.

The next time you visit Copenhagen, there's even more reason to pack a swimsuit. The city’s historic waterfront welcomes a long-awaited new addition on Saturday, December 5: a public swimming pool set to become a new landmark along the city's harbor.

Designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates, Kai is the new 62,500 square-foot bathing house that has been eight years in the making. It promises ten pools in total, including an open-air rooftop pool and a heated onsen overlooking Copenhagen Harbor. Delayed due to the pandemic and its knock-on effects, the pool was originally slated to open in 2021 and now joins the list of architecturally distinct buildings lining Copenhagen Harbor, including the modern Opera House and the Royal Danish Playhouse.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag.

Pools will be spread across the several levels of the minimalist interior, with a 82-foot pool on the ground floor. The building also offers year-round access to the harbor with designated swimming and dipping zones in and around a timber boardwalk. While the harbor itself can get pretty chilly in winter, the outdoor first-floor pools benefit from a sustainable vertical ground-source heat pump system providing year-round heating.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag for visitors. Tickets are expected to be in line with other local city-run swimming pools—known as "water culture houses"—where entry is typically under 100kr (about $10). Capacity overall is capped at 380 swimmers. The 989 million DKK ($150 million) project was funded by the City of Copenhagen and Nordea Fonden.

Kai will open on Paper Island on December 5, 2026.

Swimmers all over the city are delighted with the news, including Copenhagen’s Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling. “I’m really excited about the opening of the Water Culture House,” she said. “Copenhagen needs more swimming facilities, so it’s incredibly important that we are now getting new pools for adults, as well as paddling pools for children. I hope it will become the city’s new gathering point for water-loving Copenhageners and visitors alike.”

The original idea for a new pool in the heart of the city came directly from Copenhageners. Surveys had pinpointed a desire for a new, central public swimming pool and the location on Paper Island could not be better. Once the site of a beloved food market, the area had stood empty for years, before being redeveloped to play home to restaurants, cafes and hospitality businesses. Directly across the harbor from the central tourist hub of Nyhavn and accessed by pedestrian and cycle bridge, the new pool brings renewed focus to the area, that links the old town with the rapidly gentrifying former military area of Holmen and the former shipbuilding area of Refshaleøen.

Copenhagen's harbor is the heart of the city's year-round swimming culture.

If you are keen to explore Copenhagen’s swimming cultures, the harbor is the place to start—but brace yourself for chilly waters. At Sandkaj in Nordhavn in the north of the city, a demarcated swim zone invites bathers directly into the deep harbor for lane swimming. It’s a great place for a chat with a fellow winter swimmer; changing room access is members-only, but there is space to change on the quay. Warm up with a sauna at Saunanor, where you can also try the distinctive Danish saunagus tradition.

Those seeking a more spa-like experience should head up the coast to Skodsborg Spa Hotel. The former sanatorium offers a superlative spa experience with 16 different bathing experiences, including saunas, steam rooms and access to a private swimming jetty on the beach. Alternative public swimming spots include Valby’s Water Culture House, a chic grey building a world away from typical leisure centre design with a slide, lane swimming and a hot pool area.

Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6404. What is the physical size of a 1-billion-solar-mass black hole compared to the Sun?

When a supermassive black hole is measured as 1 billion solar masses, what would be its actual physical size relative to the size of our Sun?

The size of a black hole is generally taken to be the size of its event horizon. The event horizon is a mathematical boundary around the black hole that marks the “point of no return” — anything that crosses this boundary is trapped inside and becomes part of the black hole forever.

The size of the event horizon can be calculated from Einstein’s field equations, and it depends on (1) the mass of the black hole, and (2) how fast the black hole is spinning. For a nonspinning black hole that has the same mass as our Sun, the radius of the event horizon (also called the Schwarzschild radius) would be about 1.8 miles (3 kilometers). A nonspinning supermassive black hole that is a billion times more massive than our Sun would have an event horizon radius that is a billion times larger, or 1.8 billion miles (3 billion km). This is 4,300 times larger than the radius of the Sun, or about the typical distance between the Sun and Uranus. However, if a billion-solar-mass black hole is spinning very rapidly, then the radius of the event horizon would shrink by about 30% (to around 1.3 billion miles or 2 billion km) because of the way the black hole distorts and drags space around it.

It is important to note, however, that while the event horizon is considered the outer boundary of the black hole, the mass inside the black hole has likely collapsed into a much smaller size under its own self-gravity, often referred to as a singularity. But we don’t actually know if the mass has collapsed into an infinitely small point in space, and, unfortunately, we can’t really say more than that because our understanding of physics breaks down under the extreme conditions that are present inside a black hole. So we use the event horizon as a convenient reference for the black hole’s size, because everything inside the event horizon is part of the black hole.

Misty BentzProfessor of Physics and Astronomy, Georgia State University, Atlanta

#6403. The Best Islands in the World: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best cities in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.

The six islands of the Bazaruto Archipelago—Bazaruto, Benguerra, Magaruque, Santa Carolina, Bangue, and Shell—are a protected conservation area and national park off the eastern coast of Africa. Nicknamed the Pearl of the Indian Ocean, the islands have only seen the arrival of big-name resorts within the past decade, like the impeccable andBeyond Benguerra Island in 2015.

Pro tip: This is one of the few habitats of the endangered manatee-like dugong, which sailors sometimes mistook for mermaids.

Getting there: Fly to Vilanculos on the coast of Mozambique; from there, take a seaplane to your final destination.

Instagram and Pinterest have created renewed interest in this island in the Indian Ocean, thanks to its so-called underwater waterfall—a visually stunning runoff of sand and silt best viewed from above. Roughly 550 miles east of Madagascar, Mauritius may also be home to a lost continent hiding beneath the waves.

Pro tip: Don’t trust the scales on Mauritius: The island has a stronger gravitational field, causing things (and people) to weigh more.

Getting there: The island’s Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam International Airport is your link for flights to other cities in Africa, as well as to major cities in Europe, Asia, and Australia.

With its white coral sand beaches, turquoise waters, and laid-back island vibe, few destinations offer a sense of escapism quite like Zanzibar. Add to that plenty of sunshine and consistently pleasant temperatures, and it’s easy to see its appeal. For the history buffs among us, don't skip historic trade center Stone Town, famous for its meandering lanes, minarets-crowned buildings, and the 19th-century House of Wonders where the Sultan used to live.

Pro tip: Visit the island during the dry season from June to October, when temperatures average out at 77 degrees. This time range also overlaps with the high season for safari, should a two-for-one trip be of interest.

Getting there: To get to Zanzibar, fly directly to Abeid Amani Karume International Airport (ZNZ), or arrive by ferry from Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

Our readers aren’t the only ones who consider this African nation one of the best islands in the world: Prince William and Kate Middleton and Victoria and David Beckham spent their honeymoons on the North Island of the Seychelles. Yet some stretches of sand are so deserted that parts of the movie Castaway were filmed here. The ultimate draw, however, is the nature—the white beaches here are so beautiful that visiting them borders on a religious experience.

Pro tip: Seychelles is one of the best spots in the Indian Ocean for snorkeling. Head to the islands of La Digue and Félicité for the best variety of sealife.

Getting there: Air France, Air Seychelles, and Turkish Airlines have regular flights that connect to Seychelles International Airport (SEZ), just south of the capital of Victoria.

A chain of 26 atolls and more than 1,000 islands in the Indian Ocean, the Republic of Maldives is one of the most sought-after tropical destinations in the world. It’s dense with villas and overwater bungalows, and the diving is unreal (though, sadly, some of the coral has been threatened by bleaching). Still, there’s a dive for all skill levels at Ari Atoll, where you can swim with rays and, deeper down, reef sharks.

Pro tip: Cheval Blanc Randheli, the number one resort in the Indian Ocean (per this year’s reader survey), has 45 luxe villas—some tucked among the coconut groves, some jutting out directly over the water.

Getting there: Fly into Malé’s international airport and transfer there to the appropriate resort or atoll.

If your idea of the perfect vacation involves three-day beach parties, Koh Pha Ngan is the Thai island for you. Famous for its full-moon parties at the Haad Rin peninsula's Sunrise Beach, this island is for hardcore partygoers and the anything-goes crowd. During peak season, the island can see upwards of 20,000 visitors dancing and cavorting on the white sands under a full moon. If you can't make it at the right time of month, don't worry—there are half-moon and black-moon parties in intervening weeks, too, and there's action every night of the week at the island's beach and cocktail bars.

Pro tip: There are secluded beaches far from the crowds (like local favorite Bottle Beach, arguably one of the best beaches in Thailand), and plenty of spas where you can check yourself in for an afternoon of recovery, from the basic to the deluxe (such as the Ayurvana Spa at Santhiya Resort on Thong Nai Pan Noi Beach in the north of the island).

Getting there: From Koh Samui, take the ferry or a high-speed boat from a nearby pier like Maenam or Bangrak to Thong Sala Pier or Haad Rin Pier.

India's Andaman Islands are chock-full of beaches for thrill seekers looking to snorkel among sea life and peer through shipwrecks, as well as relaxing sandy stretches for more meditative types who prefer their quiet strolls backgrounded by sherbet-hued sunsets alike. Whether you're enjoying Havelock Island's serene Radhanagar Beach or Elephant Beach, whose shores are a veritable water sports arena, these islands provide 365 days of sun, sand, and fun.

Pro tip: Beyond the beaches, hike through the Baratang Limestone Caves' striking natural corridors through one of the most renowned natural wonders of these islands.

Getting there: Direct flights to Port Blair's Veer Savarkar airport fly from Kolkata, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Delhi, and Vizag. Alternatively, travelers may also choose to arrive at Port Blair via ferry from Kolkata or Chennai.

The Phi Phi Islands lie in the cozy cradle between Phuket and the Straits of Malacca off Krabi Province. Each of the six islands—Ko Phi Phi Don, Ko Phi Phi Le, Bamboo Island, Mosquito Island, Bida Nai, and Bida Nok—have their own charms to offer. From silky soft white sand to dramatic limestone cliffs, the beaches found on these islands are among Southeast Asia's finest.

Pro tip: For a feel of local life, stop by Ko Phi Phi Don, the largest and most populated island of the group. If flopping in solace is more your speed, pop over to Ko Phi Phi Le, which lays claim to some of the island's most stunning vistas and coastal stretches.

Getting there: As there are no airports on any of the Phi Phi Islands, visitors will have to arrive via ferry from ports such as Phuket or Krabi.

Phuket is not exactly a hidden gem, but that's because it's such a magical place to vacation, whether you want a busy immersion in city life or a quieter experience. Since it’s the biggest island in Thailand, you’re sure to find something to fit your desired itinerary. In general, though, we recommend skipping the overcrowded west coast and heading to quiet corners like Cape Panwa, where you’ll find luxury accommodations and rum distilleries that feel a bit more removed from the oft-touristed track.

Pro tip: Phuket Town receives far fewer tourists than the western beach areas. Here you can sample colorful spices at markets, visit aging Taoist temples, and snap photos of the colorful street murals.

Getting there: There are more than a dozen daily flights from Bangkok to Phuket, with most trips clocking in at an hour and 20 minutes.

Nowhere on the planet offers the same combination of surfing, spirituality, and sun-kissed pleasure as Bali. The island has sadly become synonymous with the concept of overtourism, but there are still enclaves of hidden cultural treasures and undiscovered gems—if you know where to look. For a primer on everything Insta-famous and off-the-beaten-track, check out our list of the best things to do in Bali.

Pro tip: The shoulder months of April-May and September-October are the best times to visit Bali. Not only can you enjoy lower airfares and hotel rates during the low season, but you’ll also have the rare ability to see the island without its usual crowds.

Getting there: Many airlines fly directly from the United States to Bali, including Singapore Airlines, Delta, and American.

Thailand’s second-largest island is famous for its palm-lined beaches, buzzing nightlife scene, and luxurious hotels. AVANI+ Samui Resort was voted one of the best resorts in Thailand by our readers, though the hillside villas at Four Seasons Resort Koh Samui and floor-to-ceiling bookshelves at The Library are also worth checking out. In terms of beaches, be sure to visit the five-mile Chaweng Beach, lined with coconut trees and surrounded by a natural reef. Just note that the northern end of the beach is party central.

Pro tip: If you are looking for parties, check out Green Mango, one of Koh Samui’s oldest and most famous clubs.

Getting there: You can fly directly from Bangkok to Koh Samui. A more budget-friendly option may be to fly to Surat Thani and then catch a ferry to Koh Samui—it will add a couple of hours to your travel time, but the views are pretty spectacular.

Located off the northwestern coast of Malaysia, the Langkawi archipelago has pristine beaches, coral reefs, and lush mountains—plus that famous Sky Bridge you’ve definitely seen pictures of. This collection of 99 islands is also a foodie wonderland (eating is the unofficial national sport here), with spicy peanut satay skewers and macheted coconuts sold everywhere from high-end hotels to sidewalk stands.

Pro tip: The Ritz-Carlton, Langkawi was voted the best resort in Asia by our readers this year—chalk it up to a world-class spa, multiple beachfront restaurants, and a location in a 10 million-year-old rainforest.

Getting there: Take a one-hour flight from the Malay capital of Kuala Lumpur.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6402. NASA’s Swift telescope will face a fiery demise after a failed rescue

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable

This artist’s rendition shows NASA’s Swift Observatory in orbit around Earth.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s science tenure is ending, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. The Swift spacecraft is falling uncontrollably, destined to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in just a few days.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.

Swift is doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab/NASA

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.

And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.

“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”
